articles.text:
BY "SCOURGE."

No. lII.—THE LOAN OFFICE SYSTEM.
—ITS EVILS AND THE REMEDY.
SECOND ARTICLE.

IN large communities there will always be
< many persons,. such as the struggling trades-
-man with small capital, the professional man
just rising into practice and fame, but as yet
, destitute of rich patrons, and the clerk and me-
chanic, suffering under heavy domestic expenses
attendant upon long sickness, or from slack-
ness of employment, to whom temporary pecu-
.niary aid, obtainable at the right time, and re-
payable by easy instalments, is invaluable;
and any well-regulated system by which this
want could be supplied would be as great a
-public convenience as it is a commercial ne-
cessity. It is rather singular that in these
days of speculation and association some large
and powerful company, composed of commer-
cial men of weight and character, has not been
formed to meet this want—a company not
-formed on charitable 'or philanthrophic princi-
ples, but one purely and simply commercial in
its operation. - This has not, however, been
done;' and" as the demand existed, the supply
came from other sources. In the first instance
the demand was met by a number of tradesmen
in a neighbourhood clubbing their spare cash
together, taking an office, and advertising that
they had money-to lend on personal security;
in rwarly every instance confining the sphere
of their operations to the district or parish in
which they resided. The rules and charges of
these tradesmen's loan companies were gene-
rally fair and equitable.
.They were mostly
successful, and, being so, in process of time a
host of competitors came into the field, whose
only object was to make money,—" honestly if
they could," but to make it. Advances were
freely offered to parties "in all parts of town
and country," and borrowers, naturally prefer-
ring, for many reasons, to seek for accommo-
dation at places where their neighbours and
customers could not be aware of their need,
sought the aid of these general societies in
:preference to those previously existing in their
. own districts, the promoters 'of whom, being
men of character and prudence, and not pos-
sessed of sufficient capital, to take the risk of
lending to "strangers from a distance," retired
from the business, and the trading manage-
ment of loan societies, with some few excep-
tions, fell into the hands of extortionate money
lenders, Jew bill discounters, disreputable
attorneys, "accountants," that nondescript
and numerous class styling themselves "com-
mission agents," and adventurers of all de-
scriptions; converting what was a public con-
venience to poor, honest, and industrious men,
into a great moral pest and social evil, and in-
flicting more misery upon those classes of
society compellee to come within its influence
than any institution of modern times. Some
of the more prominent evils of this system were
brought before the notice Of the readers of the
BEE- HIVE in its columns last week.

The only effectual remedy that can be ap-
plied is that of legislative control and super-
'vision; the placing those persons Who embark
in the business of lending money on personal
security, in a position somewhat similar to
those tradesmen known as "pawnbrokers,"
who lend money on goods and chattels, and
personal property. There is not, on the whole,
a more respectable class of tradesmen than
those familiarly knowh as "our uncles ;" and
there is no reason why the tradesman who lends
his money on personal security should not be
equally as respectable and as conscientious as
the one who lends his money on chattel pro-
pert'. If he can be made so by legislative
enactment, by all means let it be done, and
done speedily. The tradesman who lends
money on chattel property conducts his busi-
ness under an act of Parliament of a very
stringent nature; not only is the charge which
he can make for the " duplicate," or receipt for
the goods deposited with him, and his rate of
interest, fix E d by •the act, but all the details
connected with the carrying on of his business
is regulated by it; and he is bound, moreover,
to exhibit publicly, in his shop, the table of
profits or interest allowed to be taken, and to
have his "Christian or surname painted or
written in large legible characters over the door
of such shop or place where he carries on his
business." Any default in these regulations
subjects him to heavy penalties. In short, the
Legislature has taken every possible means to
prevent fraud and extortion. Why, then,
should the tradesman who lends money on
personal security be exempt from some such
parliamentary control? Were loan societies
placed under an act of Parliament embracing
the following points, much, if not the.whole of
the present evil connected with them would be
eradicated. For instance ,

That all loan societies, whether composed of one or
snore persons, should be registered and licensed on
Payment of a small fee; that no person should receive
a license to open a loan office who has previously, or
within a certain number of years, been convicted of
felony or fraud; that the Christian and surname with
the previous occupation (Jr profession of all persons
-using such licenses should be registered; that the
names, addresses, and professions of all directors,
managers, or other officers as well as of all proprietors
or shareholders in a loan Office should be given in and
-deposited at the registration office, at the time of
opening the office, and renewed annually; and that the
same, so far as relates to the officers, should ho printed
on all prospectuses and forms of application papers
issued by the offiee ; that the name in full of the
manager should be painted legibly over the outer doOr
of the office; that the charge for application papers for
loans should be fixed; that the amount charged as
inquiry fees' should be also fixed and regulated by the
distance at which the parties live from the office; .ana the
amount of the advance required; that where 'inquiry
fees' have been paid, and the loan not granted, a cer-
tain proportion of the fee be returned; that where
inquiry fees' have been paid, and the loan not granted,
and it can be proved no inquiry has been made, the
party paying the fee to be entitled• to recover the
amount at law, and a penalty inflicted on the loan
office; that the managers be bound to state, when a
loan is refused,, the reasons why such • loan is not
granted; that the rate of interest, on all loans under
£5O, when paid by weekly, monthly, or quarterly in-
stalments, be at a fixed rate; that when a borrower is
in default with his instalment, the amount of such
instilment or instalments due only shall be sued for,
until the period for which the loan has been granted
and interest charged has elapsed, but that then pro-
ceedings for the whole amount due may be taken; that
the sureties for the loan shall not be proceeded against
-until after the borrower has been sued, and the Office
failed to recover their just demand from him; that a
return be made at the time of registration of the amount
of capital brought into the office to be used in lending
out, and that no office be licensed, or registered where
such amount of capital is less than £250; that' a
-quarterly return be made of all moneys received for
application forms, and of the number of such forms
deposited at the office with an inquiry fee, requiring
'an advance, specifying the amount of each inquiry fec;
that a similar return be made of the number ot *loans
granted-as the result of the inquiries, with the amount
of each loan; that no attorney having any money in-
terest, or being an officer or shareholder in the offiee,
shall be allowed to sue any of the Sureties or borrowers
.such office for any sums due to it; that where -it
can be proved by the borrower or surety sued be, the
office that the manager and the attorney acting for
hire, have agred, to divide the costs of such aetivn
between them, the manager shall be nonsuited ; th;tt
penny stamp be chard
a pen charged and affixed to all
forms of application when deposited for advances; that
all infractions upon, or neglect of these rules, be
visited either with fine or imprisonment.

articles.title: AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL
articles.text:
AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL

No. 5G .

An act of Parliament, embodying clauses of
the above description, would speedily, effect a
cure, and remove that commercial gangrene
now pervading d portion of the money-lending;
world. It would sweep away all those ficti-
tious loan companies now swarming over the
metropolis, existing on a system of fraud and
extortion, and just ketping within the bounds
of legality. It would cut the ground from
under the feet of a host of low attorneys and '
bill discounters, now fattening upon the misery
they create, and, vampire-like, sucking the
life-blood out-of their victims. It would intro-
duce a new and better element into the loan-
office system;' and, although they might be less
in numLer, they would be improved in quality,
becoming,, as they ought to be, amongst the
most useful institutions of the day, instead of,
as now, one of its greatest curses. The evil§
of
.the system are so many, and so wide spread,
that the Legislature will grossly neglect its
duty does it not apply a speedy and effectual
remedy.

A general meeting of this committee was held at the
BEEHEVE Office, on Tuesday evening last. The meet-
ing was attended by Messrs. R. W. Grey and Crabb,
delegates from the Paviour's Arms and North London
Lodges of the Masons' Society; Messrs. Burgess,
Hornsby, and Buckland, from the Ffiends of Freedom
Society of Carpenters; Mr. G. Pottei, from the Pro-
gressive Carpenters; also by Messrs. Hancock and
Walters, bricklayers; Messrs. Graham, Cromer, and
Tremlett, carpenters; Messrs. Medland, Wells, and
Glossop, painters; Messrs. 'Murray, Odgers, and
Castle, boot and shoemakers; Mr. Smith, ropemaker ;
Mr. Fast, zinc worker; Mr. Butler, tin-plate worker,
&c.; and a deputation from the London Trades'
Council.

Mr. Burgess having been called to the chair, and the
minutes of the previous meeting having been read and
confirmed,
Mr. Hartwell, the hon. sec., said he had, pursuant to
the instructions of the committee at their last meeting,
sent a letter to General Garibaldi, a copy of which
had been inserted in the BEEHIVE and other papers;
the reply, however, had not yet been received. He
i hen read the following letter from Mr. Richardson,
hon. sec. of the City Committee.
DEAR SlR,—Garibaldi will not he here in England
till about March. The committee, of which lam proud
to be promoter, will in two months' time be perfected,
and our arrangements also. I think it due to your
committee to state a few of our intentions, and I may
just add how delighted I am to know we shall be so
well supported by your energetic committee. As soon
as Garibaldi arrives in England we intend to organise
all the City authorities and others, who -will take
a part in the demonstration, in presenting to Garibaldi
a manifesto signed, we hope, by 20,000 to 30,000
people. We propose that this " welcome " shall be
presented at the Crystal Palace (as being the best
suited). I should propose to your committee, as the
time of his arrival draws nearer, th4tt we hold a joint
committee; for I feel so great a faith in the working
classes that I could not hope to succeed without their
aid. I hope to hear from Spezzia the supposed time
that great man Garibaldi will visit us.

_
Yours faithfully,
JNO. RICHARDSON.'
It was then moved by Mr. Tremlett, and seconded
by Mr. Glossop, That a copy of the address adopted
tiy the committee be sent otftcially to all Trade and
Friendly Societies.'—Agreed to.
It was moved by Mr. Cremer, and seconded by Mr.
Hornsby, That a deputation of five from this com-
mittee wait upon the Trade Delegate Meeting stout to
be convened by the London Trade Council on the
25th inst., to solicit their co-operation in the proposed
demonstration.'—Agreed to.
Messrs. Burgess, Cremer, Smith, Castle, and Crabb,
were appointed to form the deputation.
On the motion of Mr. Odgers, seconded by Mr.
Graham, the Secretary was instructed to communicate
with the Trade Councils and principal Trade Societies
in the provinces on the subject.
After the transaction of some important, though
routine business, the committee adjourned until Fri-
day evening, the 28th inst., by which time it was
expected the majority of the societies would have ap-
pointed their delegates.

REPLY OF GENERAL GARIBALDI
Since the above meeting, the following letter has
been received by the Secretary from Garibaldi, in reply
to the letter sent to him :

(Translation.)

Spezzia, Nov. 1, 1862.
Dear Sir,—You know how my heart feels. Pray
accept my heartfelt thanks, and communicate them to
the generous people of London, amongst whom dwell
the 100,000 working men who evince BO much affec-

tion for me. I, too, do belong to their class, and my
only pride is never to disassociate myself from them
Honour to the English people!
With every affection, yours, &c.,
Mr. R. Hartwell, London.

G. GARIBALDI.

GAI?IBALDI AND THE _LONDON CITY

3TEETING.

---
The following reply has been received from Gari-
baldi to . the letter enclosing the resolutions of the
London City meeting :

Spezzia, Nov. 1, 1862.
Honoured Sirs,—l owe you many heartfelt thanks
for the enthusiasm you have spread abroad in the
hearts of the English people in favour of the Italian
cause. Whir you in England public opiniOn is a
reality. This power-I can only compare to the Queen
of the Universe; but a power to which many, alas,
prove unmindful. If the good will and the influence
of your Government could weigh with the diplomatic
doings of the Pope's soldier, we would all of us thank
a kind Providence for the results which would flow
from it—namely, a flagrant immorality abolished, and
the peace of Italy, which is 'part and parcel' of the
peace of Europe, established. Once more let me tender
you my thanks, gentlemen, for what you have tried to
do on behalf of my country.—Ever yours,

- G. kirARIBALDI.
Western Wood, Esq., M.P. ; John Robert
Taylor; Esq., and John Richardson, Esq.,
Hon. Secretaries.

4
happened on 'the West London line of the London and

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1862.

THE CAB DRIVER'S DELEGATE

MEETING.

The meeting of the delegates of the metropolitan cab-
drivers, adjourned from the 7th ult., was held on
Wednesday evening at the BEEHIVE Office, 2, Bouyerie-
street, Fleet-street, to receive the reports from the
various districts, and on other business. Delegates
were present from the following districts :—West-
minster : Messrs. Wise, Walton, Turner, Barnes.
Highbury : Messrs. Lovell, Sibley, Eason, Earle.
Eastern Counties: Mr. T. Miles. South 'London:
Messrs. Cook, Towel!, Wellman. East London:
Messrs. Bates, Goodwin, Quin. Paddington: Messrs.
Good, Harris, Griffin.
Mr. Wise having taken the chair, called upon the
delegates to report the results of the district meetings
that had been held, to consider the minutes of revision
of the Hackney Carriage Act agreed to by the dele-
gates.

- The reports from the districts were generally in
favour of the minutes as passed' by the delegates, with
one or two exceptions. The clause relating to the pro-
prietors summoning the drivers for arrears to the
County Court, was altered to'Police Court, by a majority
of the meeting. The other alterations made were of a
verbal nature.

It was also reported that resolutions bad been
agreed to at all the district meetings to support the
delegates in all legal measures they may adopt to pro-
cure the revision of the present act. Many influential
proprietors had attended the district meetings, and had
expressed their cordial approval of the proceedings
taken by the men, proniising all the assistance they
could give.
The Chairman then declared the clauses of revision,
with the alterations made, finally adopted, and con-
gratulated the delegates on the attention they had
bestowed upon the subject they had undertaken.
Mr. Miles then drew the attention of the delezates
to the necessity of their appointing a corresponding
secretary and treasurer; their work was now about
to begin, and they must go to it in a business-like
manner.

Mr. Towell (South London), moved that
_Mr.
Bennett be appointed corresponding secretary.
Mr. Walton (Westminster,) seconded the proposi-
tion.

Mr. Cook, and other names, were proposed, but
eventually Mr. Bennett was eleetea by a large
majority.

Captain Fishbounm, R.N., a gentleman who had
ialcen the chair at the Paddington district meeting,
and had rendered great services to cab-drivers, was
then elected as treasurer.

Mr. Cook then proposed, and Mr. Bates seconded,
the following resolution That it is the opibion of
the delegates an aggregate meeting of the London drivers
be held on an early (ray, at one of the large central
halls.'

The resolution was unanimously agreed to.
Messrs. Towell (South London) Walton (West-
minster), Bates (East London), Miles (Eastern Coun-
ties), Earle (High bury), and Harris (Paddington), were
then appointed as a sub-committee to arrange the
details connected with the meeting, and prepare the
clauees for publication; and to report the same
to the general body of delegates to be called to-
gether for that purpose.
It was also arranged that the delegates for each
district should adopt such measuresas they might deem
most desirable to obtain subscriptions from their dis-
trict, to meet the general expenses connected with the
aggregate meeting, the sum to be paid to the treasurer
appointed by the delegates as above.
The meeting then adjourned.

EAST LONDON.—The adjourned district meeting was
held on Tuesday eveninglast, at the Horse and Leaping
Bar, High-street, Whitechapel, Mr. Bates in the chair.
The minutes were read and explained by the Chairman,
and after some remarks from Mr. Shrubsole, Mr. Brad-
ley, Mr. Cohen, Mr. Quin, Mr. Hayes, and Mr. Good-
win, were adopted, with some alterations suggested by
the latter. A resolution was.then adopted, condem
natory of the present Hackney Carriage Act, and
pledging the meeting to support the delegates in their
proceedings.

[NOTICE TO CAB PROPRIETORS AND DRIVERS.—It is
our intention, next week, to publish the revised minutes
of the delegates in full; and we trust that all proprie-
tors and drivers who may desire copies of the paper will
give their orders early, either to their news agents, or
direct to the office. We trust our friends the delegates
will take as many copies as possible for distribution
and sale, and by so doing benefit both the cause and
the paper.]

- EXPLOSION IN NEWGATE-STREET.—Considerable alarm
was created in Newgate-street on Wednesday night
by an exp!osion at No. 97, occupied by Mr. Lloyd, a
dealer in chemicals. The immediate cause of the
disaster wvs the bursting of a bottle of glevione, a new
spirit compound, which blew out the whole of the front
portion of the lower part of the building.

ALARMING EXPLOSION.—On Wednesday evening,
great confusion prevailed in the immediate neighbour-
hood of Tavistock-street, Covent-garden, owing to a
sudden explosion of gas at the Strand District Board of
Works, which demolished the glass windows on the
ground floor, and at the same time the front rooms and
passage on the same floor were, found to be on fire. A
man who was engaged upon the premises, and described
as the 'gas engineer,' was thrown down by the force
of the explosion, and so severely injund that he was
removed to the hospital.

THE FRENCH OCCUPATION OF ROME.—A. public
meeting of the inhabitants of Clapham, Stockwell,
Brixton, and the vicinity, was held on Wednesday
evening at the Educational Institute, Stockwell-green,
for the purpose of adopting a protest against the con-
tinued occupation of Rome by the French troops.
There was a large attendance. Mr. Thomas Webber,
a member of the City Common Council, occupied the
chair, supported by the Rev. Dr. Thomas, Dr. Smith,
Mr. Deputy Unwin, Mr. Richardson, and several
other influential gentlemen *belonging to the
locality. The chairman having opened the pro-
ceedings, Dr. Smith proposed the first resolution,
as follows :—' That this meeting is of opinion that
the occupation of Rome by French troops contrary
to the wishes of the Roman people, is a flagrant
violation of international rights, an encouragement to
anarchy, and injurious to the interests of civilised
Europe.' The speaker enforced the resolution in a
long and argumentative speech. Mr. Richardson
seconded the resolution. In doing so he entered into
a long and eloquent defence of Garibaldi, and stated
that the illustrious patriot might be in London in
March next, when it was intended both by the
citizens of London and the trade and friendly societies,
to give him a public reception. Dr. Thomas moved the
second resolution :—‘ That this meeting sympathises
with Garibaldi in ',that he has sufferee, 1 attempting to
vindicate the fight of Italy to Rome, and with the
Italians in being excluded from their capitol.' Mr.
Hart seconded the resolution, which was carried by
acclamation. It was then resolved that the foregoing
resolutions be transmitted to the borough mem-
bers, with a request that they support the opiniQns
therein. expressed in their places of parlioxamt.

articles.title: DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL OPERATIVES' RELTEP FUND.

The weekly executive meeting took place at the
Committee-rooms, Speak-buildings, Padiham, on Mon-
day last. Mr. James Heap (vice-president) took the
chair. Present—Messrs. C. Sutcliff, James Catlow,
and Wm. Hodgkinson (Burnley) H. Whitehead, G.
Hargreaves, and James Pollard (llalleyham), and
Messrs. James Morehouse, J. Howarth, Wm. Wilkin-
son, and Joseph Peacock (secretary). After the last
week's minutes were read and confirmed, the Secretary
read the report. A further remittance of £l3 had been
received from the Manager of the BEEMVE, Mr. G.
Potter, with a good hope of larger amounts shortly.
Mr. Lindsay, of. Aberdeen, was organising working
men's committees and concerts in that city, and early
promises of a goodly sum showed themselves. The
united trades of Liverpool were about to organise a
committee; also in London and Sheffield a movement
was going on. In various districts collections were
being made and committees of working men stirring.
Contributions were also expected from the Foresters,
Druids, and other benevolent societies. Altogether the
report was cheering, although the distress is already
over-matching all resources to cope with it.
'The Chairman thought the employers of Birming-
ham had been more than a match for the working men
in that town, for they had forced them into a kind of
union with them, and compelled them to send their
monies to the Manchester Central.

After the usual business was transacted and the
number of cases relieved and sums expended were re-
ported, resolutions were passed, and the usual grants
made to Burnley, Habergham, and Padiham, after
which the meeting broke up.

articles.title: TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
articles.text:
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sm.,—l beg to enclose you the accompanying letter,
received by us from what is called . the Birmingham
Working Men's Committee. At first I thought this
committee had been verily formed of bona fide workmen
and corresponded with as such, but upon inquiries
made it is discovered that the committee is merely a
sham, to decoy the working classes into subscribing
towards the Mayor's fund, which is sent to the Man-
chester Central. I hope the working men of Birming-
ham will not submit to such mode of treatment, but
resent it in a becoming spirit, and form a Relief Com-
mittee to correspond with us. We have no confidence
in the Manchester school, and never heard until now
of any working man or body of workmen that ever had.
I am sir, yours respectfully,
JOSEPH PEACOCK, lion. Secretary.
East Lancashire Central Flind,
Padiham, November 4th, 1862.

Cotton District Relief Fund,
Working Men's Committee, Town Hall,
Birmingham, October 31, 1862.
To Mr. Peacock,
East Lancashire Central Operative
Relief Committee, Padiham.
SIR,—In reply to your letters of October 10th and
18th, in which you make application to this committee
for funds, I beg to inform you that at our last meeting
on Wednesday, the 29th inst., a resolution was passed
to the efiect that this committee having perfect confi-
dence in the Manchester Central Committee they cannot
cntertain your application, and that all the funds raised
by this committee shall, as heretofore, be remitted to the
Manchester Committee. I may add, that we have under
consideration the amount at present being distributed
by the Central Committee, and that we feel that the
same is very far from sufficient, and that our views
upon this will be conveyed to the Central Committee,
and it is our earnest hope that they will be in a posi-
tion to largely increase their distributions throughout
the distressed districts.

I am sir, yours truly,
HENRY ARMS, Hon. Secretary.

LONDON.—A meeting of members of the London
Working Men's College was held at the College, 45,
Great Ormond-street, on Saturday evening, to con-
sider the propriety of establishing a fund for the
relief of the distress now prevailing in Lancashire.
The chair was taken by R. B. Litchfield, Esq., B. A.
(in the absence of F. D. Maurice, Principal of the
College), who, after expressing his concurrence in the
objects of the meeting, said he would content himself
with calling on Mr. Roebuck to read the first resolu-
tion. The resolution was as follows :--` This meeting
of members of the London Working Men's College
resolve to raise subscriptions amongst the members
and friends of the college in aid of the efforts now
being made for the relief of the distress in the cotton-
working districts, as a mark both of sympathy with
the operatives under their sufferings, and of admira-
tion of the •fortitude with which these sufferings had
been borne.' Mr. Roebuck supported the resolution
in an able speech. The proposition was then seconded
and carried unanimously. Other resolutions were
spoken to by Messrs. Shorter, Standring, and others,
and carried, by which it was arranged that a com-
mittee, to give effect to the first resolution, should
consist of Messrs. Litchfield and Roebuck, members of
the council of the college; Mr. Shorter, secretary of
college; and Messrs. Standring and Rawlins, student
members, together with a representative from each
class in the college, of which there are upwards of
t,hirty.

. -
WOOLWICH.— A numerously attended public meeting
of the inhabitants of Woolwich took place on Monday
night in the Town Hall, to adopt measures for:relieving
the existing distress in the cotton districts. Mr. John
Cowen occupied the chair. Amongst the speakers were.
Mr. Angerstein, M.P., the Rev. J. Rudduck, and the
Rev. W. Gill, all of whom strongly advocated the
claims on public sympathy of the suffering multitudes
in Lancashire. Resolutions in accordance with the
objects of the meeting were unanimously passed, and
an influential committee appointed to receive subscrip-
tions.

BRIGHTON.—A public meeting was held on Monday,
in the Town hail, Brighton. It was numerously
attended, and presided over by the Mayor. The object
of the meeting was to consider the best means of alle-
viating tho existing distress in the cotton districts. The
meeting was addressed by the Mayor, Mr. J. White,
M.P., Mr. Clarke, Mr. W. Coningham, M.P., and Mr.
P. D. Goldsmid. Resolutions expressive of sympathy
with the suffering operatives, and declaring the
necessity of entering into a subscription on their
behalf, were agreed to, and a considerable sum
was subscribed in the room at the close of the meet-

IEEDS.-A meeting, attended by many of the leading
inhabitants of Leeds, was held at the Town Hall on
Monday, to originate a subscription for the relief of the
distress in Lancashire. The Mayor (Mr. James
Kitson) presided, and the chief speakers were Mr. Wm.
Beckett, Mr. James Garth Marshall, Mr. E. Baines,
M.P., the Vicar, and Mr. John Hope Shaw. An in-
fluebtial committee was organised, and subscriptions
were promised, giving a total of upwards of £4,800. A
similar meeting was held On Monday, at Dewsbury,,
over which Dr. Fearnley, the Mayor of the borough,
presided.

MUNIFICENT SUBSCRIPTION TO THE WIGAN RELIEF
FUND.—At the last wkly meeting of the Wigan Relief
Committee, a letter was read from Lord Lindsay, ad-
dressed to the Mayor of Wigan, announcing his inten-
tion, jointly with his father, Lord Crawfordeto contri-
bute MOO a week to the relief fund in that town, during.
the next five menthe.

PRICE Two PENCE,

STATE OF AUSTRALIA.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEIIiVE.

have just received the following letter from
a personal friend, and, as it *ill be.read with pleasure
at this time when emigration seems taking another
start, I should be glad if you insert it. It must be.
highly pleasing to all who have friends in that distant
country, to find the colonists giving their attention to
the growing of cotton and the cultivation of the grape;
and, having been a resident in the Colony for 7 years,
I can have no doubt but that the climate is in every
way suited to the growth of cotton. Bat, Sir, I will
ever protest against the doctrine that the colony re-
quires more labotir at present; it is capital that is
wanted, and labour will soon follow. I can vouchior
the accuracy of the statements contained in the letter
from a highly esteemed and well-known colonist: I may
add that he promises me to become a monthly contri-
butor to our paper, giving next the price of wages and
provisions, and he hopes and wishes, as every true
friend of labour should, success to the BEEHIVE.
_ _

_
By inserting this, you will oblige yours, &c.,
Wm. PETHERBRIDGE.
Caledonian-road, Oct. 22nd, 1862.

The following is the letter alluded to by our corres
pondent :

SOUTH AUSTRALIA.

Adelaide, Aug. 23, 1862.
MY DEAR SlR,—The winter, now almost over, is one
of the wettest ever known in this colony. Our little
streams have been swollen into large rivers by the
torrents rushing into them from mountain and hill.
:ridges have been rushed down in many places, and
several persons drowned in trying to cross over what
used to be fords. The great amount of wet has rendered
out-door work impracticable, hence many are complain-
ing of want of !employment. Some of your old friends
are not thriving as fast as you could wish. Tradesmen's
wages have fallen considerably since you left; and
high prices for provisions, and low rates of wages, do
not constitute a prosperous state of things for the
working community. However, at this season, as you
are aware, things are always dull with us. In truth,
failures and bankruptcies, as you will see from the
papers I send you, are the only brisk business now
going on in this country of universal suffrage and ,
almost universal apathy to political privileges. Most
people come out here in the expectation of making
money in a little time, and when disappointed in attain-
ing that object, appear to sink into a state of political
torpor. The Political Association alone tries to rouse
them to a sense of their duties, and even that organ,
since you have left us, and Clark has vacated office, has
very much relaxed its exertions. In a few months our
M.P.'s will be going to the country again, when, I
hope, many of the constituencies will return more in-
telligent and more honest men, and that the Political
Association will display, at that important juncture,
some of its pristine vigour. I wish things would mend
here HO as to hold out some inducements to you to
come back to us, and stir up the working men, who
are allowing their crest to droop. Our present Ministry,
alias the legal one, so called from the number of
lawyers in it, on finding themselves in a minority on
the Australian Conference Bill, sent in their resigna-
tion, which the Governor accepted. However, though
the administration was one without a principle such
is the weakness of parties, that the house was Obliged
to allow the sa.mo Ministry, whose policy it had con-
demned, to return to office! The liberal party is, un-
fortunately, composed of elements •rendered incom-
patible by petty jelousies and mutual mistrust. The
House of Assembly has just voted the sum of £30,000 to
be applied to bringing out from home strong able-bodied
linen to compete with those here in supplying this
market with a cheap article, that can labour well for
ten hours laily under a broiling sun, and during the
prevalence of the exhaust* hot—aye, furnace-hot
—wind! Were it net for the lucky discovery of large
copper mines at Wallaroo, on the other side of the
Gulf, the condition of the labourer would be worse than
miserable, and yet the squatters and mining companies
cry out for renewed emigration. No fresh water has
yet been discovered near Wallaroo, so that the inhabi-
tants, who are chiefly men, will have to depend during
! the hot season, on the stills for a scanty supply of this
precious commodity. The future prosperity of this colony
depends a good deal on our being able to compete with
foreigners in your wheat and flour market. The Mel-
bourne market is now closed to us, the native supply
being nearly equal to the demand. The wheat and
flour sent to the Exhibition has been much praised.
We hope you will like our wines equally well, as with-
out your custom we shall not be able to get on. Atten-
tion at the present moment is turned to the cultivation
of the cotton plant, which is said to be easilycultivated
in a very hot and dry climate such as ours. Should
the experiments in the matter prove successful, there
will then be, in a few years hence, employment at fair
wages for more emigrants. Very many of the old
colonists have dropped off lately, as the Rev. Mr.
Stow and James, better known as Bully Chambers.
The cholera is raging in the Mauritius, which is not
far off, and in constant communication with this place.,
Its communication to this sultry country would be
attended with consequences too terrible to imagine.
Though rents and prices of provisions have fallen
in the last six months, I would not advise persons not
doing well at home to come out here now, as wages are
going down, and capital, not labour, is what we, for a
while at least, need. lam afraid our coming summer
will be a very hot one; winter is yet 'hardly over, and
the hot winds have already visited us. Hot wind!
What an incongruous expression to those who have
neVer experienced the ineffable sensation of a con.
tinuous furnace blast! Can we blame those who make
money for hurrying to English comforts and homes ?
G. N.

REPRESENTATION OF WESTMINSTER—It is currently
reported in Westminster that Sir De Lacy Evans will

articles.title: LITERATURE.
articles.text:
LITERATURE.

.Political Beonomy for the Million; or, a Handy-Book of
Social Intercourse. London: Longman, Green, and
Co. 1862. (Combinations.)
Handy-books are handy things; and 'Political
Economy for the Million' is a subject worthy of being
treated well in every way. We must do the author,
William B. Chorley, Esq., Barrister-at-Law, the
simple justice to say that, in mode and in matter
generally, he has far, very far exceeded the efforts of
writers upon this subject who are deemed authorities.
Indeed it would take a long essay to show how far,
often, and much we approve of and esteem his labour,
thought, talent, and good intention exhibited in this
handy-book; BUT,-but, we do not think him correct,
and therefore right on certain questions connected
with fact and conclusions vital to the interests of the
people. It is worth glancing at the fact, and
of asking ourselves if we can account, how a writer
so Able and evidently accustomed to think—and who
having a knowledge and research so extensive, with a
disinterested object to serve—how it is, that being so
true and correct on certain matters, he is so incorreat
and erroneous upon others.
In the, first place, we all know that a person
learned in law may not know anything of music, nor
do all naturalists become therefore historians. Men
may be well acquainted with some things, and be
really ignorant in others. So in the science of social
economy, a philosopher may be well grounded in cer-
tain facts, and be totally ignorant of others equally.
important. We hence see that inequality of experi-
ence will give rise to unequal estimates and repre-
sentation, and that .the same writer may teach truth
and fact; and falsehood and error, with equal
sincerity, and, so far as he is concerned, in
conscientious honesty and with equal merit. Now,
it often happens that 'philosophers, better accus-
tomed to their study, than to the practice of this world,
do not know the facts of practical lit.°' upon which .... s
they are wishful to systemise. But a knowhielge of
facts should precede a study. Of principles, as art does
science; and if knowledge and experience do not precede
theory, it is more than probable the theory will be
erroneofis, because the facts are either, faulty, or so
placed as to be irrelevant, and out of Place. .111. re-
lation to the book in question, upon the subject of
combinations of the men and masters,' the author, and
perhaps from no fault of his, is entirely in error on the
fact of the historical order and sequence of these com-
binations. Mr. Chorley, though a member of the
Barristers' Union, is not a member of a trades union,
and being neither employer nor artisan, he therefore
does know the facts of how their unions stand related.
But he still might have known, had it not been from
the operation of what would seem to be a law of
humanity,—viz., that we only see what we are looking
at, and many facts escape our vision, simply because
we are not looking at them. Mr. C. looks with the
eye of acapitalist, and hence he sees as a capitalist; and
thus he seems altogether ignorant of the simple fact
that combinations of capitalists always precede combi-
nations of the labourer. This common historic fact is
generally reversed. Adam StiaithVew, and stated the
truth in language unmistakably ext'ress ; b it those who
call themselves his followers only see. even in him,
what they have eyes to see. Thus herd Brougham, in
his address to the Social Science Co] gres at Bradford,
1859, says: The combination of miter is the inevit-
able consequence of the combination of men;' and
following him, Mr. Chorley says (p: 116) : We have
noticed that combinations among the men produce,
as is natural, combinations of the masters. * •*
* * But, generally, the masters have nothing
like the powerful unions of their workmen.
Indeed, they are mostly disinclined Ao this
agreement, except when forced by necessity, each
depending upon his own independent Course of action.'
But it is clear that his own independent course
of action' makes each employer a union in himself;
and that it requires the counter action of all ope-
ratives in unity, and by agreement, to equal the Voli-
tion of very few masters. But, that masters are not
inimical to united action; and that in the first instance
they do oppose all advance of the operatives for wages,
is a fact well worthy of placing the evidence of proof
before the world. In the first place, it shuttle]. be well
understood, that all large employers in trades, employ-
ing large capital, for any considerable length of time,
are, more or less, in one way or other, in union. The
evidence is clear; and taking the last cases first, we
instance, that the only strikes now before us, are those
of coal and iron miners in Lancashire, Yorkshire, and
Scotland.* And the coal and iron masters are all in
strict and well-defined union. See the Manchester
papers for September and October, 1862, for the facts,
Ist, that the coal masters met in Liverpool, and resolved
upon a second reduction of 10 per cent; 2nd, that the
men had no union in Wigan but on this notice, they
met, formed one, and resolved to resist or strike ; and
3rd, that on this resistance, the employers withdrew
their notice! In Yorkshire, and in Scotland, at this
very time, the same facts are progressing, in the same
way, in different stages. In 1858-9 there was a terrible
coal strike in West Yorkshire, and upon a history ()fits
origin and results being read at Bradford Social 'Science
Meeting, one of the employers admitted that the em-
ployers' association had, by their union and reduction,
caused the strike; and that their union had existed for 30
years before the men had attempted to unite, having.'
for its object the regulation of the trade as to weight and.
prices, &c. (see Social Science Transactions, vol. 3, p. 722).
The Anaster builders of London had an union well
defined in 1835; how long before is not known; and
it is well known that the engineers (we mean the em-
ployers) have all unions. The cotton spinners of Lan-
cashire down to the cotton brokers of Liverpool, have
all •associations ! The flax spinners of Yorkshire,
the stuff and woollen dyers, and dressers, have all price
union lists. Perhaps, however, the best illustration
of associations, or unions, and of their tendency in
action in modern times, may be gathered from the
history of the coal 'vend,' given in Porter's Progress
of the Nation,' and where we learn that a large volun-
tary association, in defiance of all principles of free or
fair trade, fixed prices and regulated supply of coal
to London, just at their pleasure, and invariably and
inevitably to- the loss of the public. And these were
capitalists!. Carrying our researches into the past, we
find that the first statute in our laws referring to the
labourers is in 1350, and was enacted, in the express
words of the legislature, with the direct object of com-
pelling the labourer to accept lower wages than he
would otherwise be able to obtain.'—(See Social Sci-
ence Report on Trades Societies, vol. 7, p. 339.) 4AII
other enactments of the law-makers, all capitalists
had the same object, and tended to their own advance-
ment, at the expense of the labourers, until 1824,
when Wade in the 'History ofi England% Greatness,'
and in his Chronological History of England,' statei
and admits, that thwepeel of all statutes against com-
binations of the labourers was on the ground that they
could be no longer maintained, because it was felt to be
unjust to prohibit union among operatives when
unions of their masters were fully permitted and com-
mon.' And Mr. Chorley states, p. 115—'The last trace
of legal interference with the free action of men, and
regulating the price of their labour has been very re-
cently abolished'— * * * 'as the rights of the
working classes have been better understood.' Who
it was that passed such laws, and what object they
had in view, will at once, if answered upon historic
facts, and on the very principles of human nature,
prove that capitalists, as such, and therefore, have
been always the first to combine,' and to violate,
as before said, the principles of both free and
fair trade. The result has been, first and
directly, evil to the labouring classes; and secondarily,
and indirectly (but inevitably) and in the end evil to
the capitalists themselves. When the 'million' are
not doing well, the few must in the end suffer. Trade
and demand can but prosper by numbers being a.ble to
pay for that which they require. A people thriving
must ensure a wealthy aristocracy of trade and com-
merce, and vice versa in general. Hitherto political
economists (?) have in action (and these are the
practical philosophers) always gone on the tack that •
the best way of obtaining capital, was to pinch it out
and from the labourer. Labour, they agreed, is a
commodity; and to buy in the cheapest, and to sell in
the dearest markets as true wisdom; and thus the
labourer has been kept down as near as possible at
starvation point. With what wisdom, may be judged
by applying the same action to farming. • Don't give
the earth manure or seed; don't cultivate it, and
grub up the weeds; save capital and labour, and so
riches will increase!' Glorious economy! from which,
we fear, neither theoretical nor practical plailosophers
are yet quite free. True, the results are daplored, and.
the (acts argued against by the author of the Handy-
Book; but -in the main he supports the views, and
enunciates those principles, which, if onliy strictly fol-
lowed out, necessitates all the evils of w'aich he and the
labouring classes complain. We have, at hand a flood
of evidence to prove this, but must 'ldes, on account
of space, recommending the book an .d. its truths to the
attention of our readers, in order Lb
.at they may profit
by its good and true, and reject • what is partial and
false, and therefore unjust and inj.asioas, J. H.

IRELAND.

prom the rift's correspondent) •
Dusnrig, Nov. one of my letters I reeently
. !lent you-a paragraph to the effect that some idea of the
state of the County of Tipperary may be formed -from
the fact that during the recent sittings of the Quarter
Sessions' Court a gentleman who was attending as a
witness was guarded during the day by two ,policemen,
who sat near him with their muskets loaded and capped.
This the Cork Examiner calls 'blackening Ireland,' arid
by way of white ashing Tipperary it gives a 'report of
, the case, which had been in the .editor's possession for a
few days' but which he had notdeeided upon publishing
until he found the circumstances connected with this
. gentleman were so 'improperly used.' He further adds,
for the information of these who take their opinions of
matters there from the Times, that Mr. Vincent Sculiy,
member for the county of Cork, has thought it necessary
to disclaim all re-ponsibility for the actions and conduct
which have of late acquired for his brother so 'much
curious and unenviable notoriety.' I am not aware that
any one was so fpolish as to consider the member for
Cork responsible for his brother's conduct, Mr. William
Scully being old enough to answer fur himself, and
being, besides' a man of property and independent
position. As, however, he is exceedingly unpopular, and
in the terrible Tipperary sense, 'a marked man,' it
was a prudent course on the part of the member, if he
hopes to be elected again, to express publicly his dis-
approbation of his brother's conduct. This was the more
necessary as Mr. William Scully has lately changed his
religion and become a member of the Established
Church, so that he is obnoxious to his brother's con
stituency not only as a landlord, but as a 'renegade.'
The report which the Examiner publishes in order to
contradict the statement which appeared in the Times
confirms it in every particular, and gives some additioial
facts which add .darker colours to the picture of
Tipperary. Mr. Scully appeared as a witness in an I
action of ejectment brought to recover £B7. The report
eta* that :

the ejectment was brought under a lea.e dated the
25th of March, 1839, made by Catherine Scully,
deceased, to William Dwyer, deceased, which was
granted for a•term of 31 years, and containdd several
clauses, among which was one th it if the tenant
meadowed more than a certain number of acres thp. rent
was to be increased from £43 10s. to £B7. Mr. William
Scully came forward from the side box, where he had
been standing, escorted by two armed policemen, who
usually accompany him, and mounted the table in a
slow manner, evincing a stiffness of gait which would
suggest the belief that he had on a coat of mail for the
protection of his person. He proved the handwriting.
of the witness to the lease—that of Mr. Francis Bcully,
his deceased brother, who had been shot some years ago.'
Mr. Scully was cross-examined by, the defendant's
Solicitor as follows:

Mr. O'Mara: Upon your oath, did not this man
always pay up the reserved rent?
' Witness : He did, but he allowed the lands to
be overgrown with weeds, and allowed the houses to
fall.

Mr. O'Mara: You are anxious to have the grapnel
irons on his.roof, and add to the desolation and number
of unroofed homesteads at Kilfeaele. I believe the
outhouse you, refer to was on a sandy foundation, an
we have a high authority for assuming that a house
built on sand_must fall?

Mr. Scully: No, the foundation was a good one.
'Mr. O'Mara: Is there a man in the United King-
dom save Mr. William Scully, of liilfeacle, would bring
this case into court?

'Mr. Scully: I consider it my duty as a landlord to
bring it. (Sensation in court.)
Mr,O'Mara : Did not this man's father expend £3OO
in iu_ipfovements on the farm?

Scully: He was bound to expend £lOO.
Mr. O'Mara: Did you serve him with a writ in
1859?

'Mr. Scully: What .do you mean by a writ?

Mr. O'Mara: As I mist be most technical with a
person so familiar with the law courts, which are ringing
with your persecutions and prosecutions, did you serve
him with a plaint?
Mr. Scully: I did.
The tenant was examined and proved an expenditure
of SlO6 on the farm by his father, and the erection of an
out-house by himself.
The learned Chairman retired from the bench and
called on plaintiff's solicitor to go into his chamber, and
on his return called for Mr. O'Mara, and intimated that
he was constrained in point of law to give a decree, but
would reserve his judgment with a view that some terms
might be agreed on, as from the terms of the lease
clogged with penalties no tenant could hold.'

ft-appears from another case in which Mr. Scully was
involved that the children are taught to stone him as he
passes along the road. He was prosecuted for striking
with his whip a child said to be only four years old, who
threw a stone at him. He was fined £5 for this, and he
appealed to the Quarter Sessions. Whether Mr. Scully
acted prudently or justly in enforcing one of the con-
Tenants of a lease and doing what he conceived to be his
duty as a landlord, it is a fact that the authorities consider
it necessary to have him constantlykuarded by policemen,
even in a court of justice, and it appears that he has
adopted the precaution of making himself shot proof by
wearing a coat of mail.' The style of denunciation
adopted towards him by the attorney is another fact
worth notice. This report, then, meant for a refutation,
fully bears out the statement in the paragraph complained
of, and warrants the assertion that the appearance of a
landlord thus armed and guarded in the most public
places, and in presence of the majesty of justice, enables
us to form some idea of the state of Tipperary.

THE NEW Posv-ovvica SOLICITOR. —The Post-
master-Gemeral has appointed Mr. W. H. Ashurst Soli-
citor to the Post-office. In accepting the vacant post,
Mr. Ashurst succeeds to his father, a man widely known
for his spotless integrity, his professional sagacity, and
his large practice; his high standing as a lawyer in no
degree cramping his activities as an outspoken and
equally practised Reformer. He combined in a remark-
able degree the qualities of courage and discretion;
while in private life he was beloved for his exhaustless
considerateness and kindness. When Rowland Hill's
plan of penny postage was still a project, it had the
valuable and effectual support of Mr. Ashurst; but
when it became a national institution he made no cldm
for his services. The choice of his successur, ho Never,
does not rest upon the father's claims • for Mr. W. H.
Ashurst has peculiar qualifications of his own, not merely
in his professional standing, but still more in the ex-
perience which he obtained under his father in the
particular department. That Lord Stanley's selection
will be appreciated by the le4al and mercantile com-
munity is evidenced in the remarkable testimonial by
which the candidate was supported. The list of the
• signatures includes, besides that of Mr. Joshua Bates,
the chairman of the Mercantile Committee on the
Reduction of Postage in 1838, those of Lord Overstene,
Sir Lionel de Rothschild, Morrison, Dillon and Co.,
Smith, Payne, and Smith, Sir Morton Pete, and, in
short, the very highest of the leading names in the City.
ELECTION OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.
The Dean and Chapter of Canterbury Cathedral have
elected the Most Rev. Charles Thomas Longley, D.D.,
of Christ Church, Oxford, Archbishop of York, to the
Archbishopric of Canterbury, in accordance with the
recommendation accompanying the Royal conge d' elire.
The election by the capitular body took place at Canter-
bury on Saturday, and it is almost unnecessary to add
that there was no opposition. The next step in the
elevationof the Archbishop-elect will be the confirmation
of the election, a ceremony which will take place in the
course of a few days in the parish church of St. Mary-
le-bow, Cheapside. That ceremony will ipso facto render
vacant the Archbishopric of York. Dr. Longley will
then do homage to Her Majesty, and towards the close
of the present month will be enthroned, with an elabo-
rate ceremonial, in the cathedral church of his diocese.
The diocess of Canterbury consists of 914,170 acres, and
has a population of 417,090, with 14 deaneries and 352
benefices. The ecclesiastical patronage in the hands of
the A tchbishop amounts in the aggregate to nearly
£BO,OOO .a year.
FALL OF A Housß AT EXETER. —SE VERAL CHIL-
DREN BURIED ALIVE.—On the 3rd the neighbourhood
of Colleton-buildings and Port Royal was thrown into
a state of great excitement through the falling in of an
old house, which buried several children. P. C. Cor-
nish, the constable of the district, was immediately on
the spot, and, with some assistance succeeded in
getting out five children from under the debris. Two
children were taken to the hospital, and three to their
respective homes, more or less injured. The house has
been in a dilapidated and dangerous state for some
time, but no owner could be found for it, the property
being in Chancery. The last person who was supposed
to claim it was the late Captain Perran, who died in
Plymouth some time since. After his leaving the
house it was let to-a woman, who was obliged to leave
it from its dangerous .condition, and a week after she
left a portion af the roof fell in, and it has since been
resorted to by children for play. The windows and
everything that wa3 removeable had been taken away.
On Monday, about the middle of the day, several chil-
dren were upstairs at play, pulling out laths and other
pieces of wood, and one young urchin pulled a plug
which supported a lot of briers. On the removal of
this support the bricks fell and a portion of the front.
This was followed by th e roof, and, indeed the entire
house. After the removt ii of the five children it was
reported that other ehiidreo were under the ruins, and a
body of police, under the dil-ection of Sergeant Mitchell,
were quickly on the spot, and they amtinued their
search throughout the day. Vip to five o'clock no more
bodies had been found, but Bev -era children's caps were
dug out. About eight years ago a portion of a row of
houses, not 160 yards from this spot, fell in the middle
of the night, and buried several pers 0118.— Western Morn-
News.

ITHE D YAi 'll4' AXITIBITION.

On.Sattirdw the public were admitted for the last
time to the International Exhibition of-180. Already,
as an exhibition, it is a thing of the past. Those who
visited it on Monday, in the character of buyers, found
the Picture Galleries and Machinery Annexe closed,
cranes electing at the British and foreign entrances,
and busy hands removing the articles that have b,en
sold, or arranging for the disposal of the small amount
that still remains without purchasers. To prolong the
time. of closing further would have been to court a
f.ilure and dim the eclat of a great success by a most
lama and impotent conclusion. It has already exceeded
the span allotted to our former Exhibition by 17 Jays.
Later than this month it could not have been, delayed
with safety to its popularity at home or satisfaction,to
those whom we have invited from all•parts of the world,
and'whoin courtesy compelled to stay until we, as hosts,
had given the signal of departure. This farewell
signal was given on Saturday, and before Monday
closed hundreds of exhibitors took advantage of it, and
bid adieu to what has been a scene of triumph and a
source of honourable profit to so many. The few days
that have yet to run are emphatically days of sale only,
for the Exhibition clos,d on Saturday last.
Beyond the simple ceremonial of singing our national
hymn nolormalit y of any kind marked the occa.ssion.
There were crowds of visitors, though neither more 'nor
less than might have been expected on such a miserable
day.
At 3 o'clock,the building seemed more full than it has
ever been, save on the memorable State days, and when
so much .was expected and so very little seen. Some
little excitement was caused at this time by the prema-
ture and exit rely unexpected strains of the organ at the
east end, commencing with the National Anthem,
*lila led the visitors pell-mell back to that part of the
building. The false note of termination, however, was
soon checked, and popular confidence so far restored in
the integrity of. the simple progiamme that, every one
contentedly stood ~or sat round ,the west dome, till
galleries, side courts,,and every place from which every-
thing could be seen or heard, and very many from which
little could be heard, and nothing seen at all, was
thronged with thousands of visitors.
The members of the Sacred Harmonic Society were
partly in the west gallery, by the side of Messrs. Walker
and Mr. Hedgeland's organ among the finest and richest
toned in all the building, and partly also round the dais,
under the west dome, used at the opening on the Ist
of May.

As le clock struck 4 the well-known words of our
National Anthem were begun, at first with diffidence,
but gradually swelling out into a sound which, if it
did not fill the building, at least sent its clear, solemn
tones up the nave, bringing together the scattered
groups from all parts' hurrying down on tiptoe and
bareheaded, to assist by their presence at what to all
Englishmen is almost a religious ceremony. For a few
moments after its close there was a pause, and then, as
at a signal's loud cheer broke forth, with clapping of
hands and waving of handkerchiefs, which was renewed
again and again, and one cheer more' led to another
and a louder, till there was no method of restoring silence
but by singing natant pour la Syrie.' To this com-
pliment to eur foreign visitors the same respectful atten-
tion was paid and the same cheering greeted its termina-
tion, when again and again came the heavy rolling cheer
and calls for an encore which made the building, large
as it is, echo again. To this fresh demand the
members of the Society kindly lent an indulgent ear,
and sang Rule Britannia,' and, to do them justice,
the audience spared no efforts to make them sing it half
a dozen times more, so loud and long-ststained was their
applause. But there was no response to this emphatic
and vigorous encore. Some concession was however,
made to popular opinion by playing Auld Lang Syne,'
but even the plaintive strains of this fine old melody
were soon overwhelmed and buried under the tremen-
dous clamour with which every bell in the building
commenced ringing out.' They seemed at once to
open at full cry from every nook and gallery,—high
overhead, in side courts and main avenues, and down in
secluded bays where no one dreamt that bells lay lurk-
ing,—all gave tongue at once, filling the air with such
a hideous jangle of various sounds as ought at once to
have emptied the building, though it did not.
The practical question which will occur to every
Englishman's mind, now that the excitement and the
triumph, too, is done, is, Has it paid its way ? ' or,
rather, will there be any such deficit as the guarantors
may fairly be called upon to make up? Witholit pro-
fessing to have any official information on this important
subject, we may safely venture to announce that, as far
as the guarantors are concerned, the Exhibition has
paid,' and they will not be called upon for a single
fauthing. There will be a deficit on receipts as com-
pared with expenditure, as all in any way interested in
this question have known there would be for months
past. The daily returns of money taken at the doors
show a total received of nearly £315,000, excluding, of
course, the admission by shilling day tickets. The
season tickets have, it is said, realised nearly £BO,OOO,
and the shilling tickets also a considerable sum. Alto-
gether, the receipts from every source, including
refreshment and photographic contracts, waiting-rooms,
umbrella stands, sales of catalogues, &c., have been,
we believe, up to the present day within a very
small amount of £500,000 sterling, and are not unlikely
to be £510,000, or even £520,000 before the final clos-
ing of accounts after the distribution of prizes by the
Prince of Wales. The expenses of constructing the
building according to the original plan have, it is stated,
been within the £200,000 originally advanced by the
Bank of England, though, of course, the Commissioners
have incurred the usual supplementary estimate in the
way of extras, such as the annexes, gilding, foundations
for machinery, &c., -which bring the total cost up to
nearly £70,000 more. The office and staff expenses
have been unusually, indeed almost parsimoniously low;
but road-making and hire of police account for large
sums as do also the charges for receiving goods, &c. in
the blinding, the redelivery of which outside the E;hi-
bition will be almost as much more. In shert, there-
fore if every claimant were paid in full, the guarantors
would be liable for some 9 or 10 per cent. upon the
amount they individually underwrote.
The Paris Exhibition of 1855 was attended in six
months by 3,626,934 visitors to the industrial depart-
ment, and by 906,530 visitors to the fine arts depart-
ment—in all 4,633,464, who paid for admission to each
department the sum of £117,666. This display left a
deficit larger than our surplus, and which had to be
made good by a grant from the Imperial Government.
The present Exhibition has also been open six months,
or 17 days longer than of '5l. The total number of
visitors, excluding the staff and exhibitors' attendants,
has been 6,117,450, or 87,000 over the gross numbers on
the first occasion. This would give the Exhibition that
has just closed a majority of quite a million over its
predecessors, while its gross receipts will, we believe, be
between £BO,OOO and £90,000 greater than on the first
occasion, if we• exclude from the total of 1841 the
£67,400 subscribed throughout the country at the first
conception of the scheme, and which it is quite needless
to say was never returned to the subscribers.

Notwithstanding the famine in our manufacturing
districts—a famine of the worst kind, as arising from the
enforced idleness of the people; notwithstanding the
death of the great originator of the plan, with a Court
absent and in mourning, a wet summer' a bad harvest,
and trade generally in such a state of depression as it
has seldom been in before in this country, the Exhibition
has in all popular and practical results surpassed the
hitherto unapproachable standard by which all similar
efforts have been judged, the Exhibition of 1851. That
this result will be a bitter grievance to the prophets of
evil is likely enough, but the day when these could
injure it is now long past, and the Exhibition of 1862
will find in its results an ample answer to all detraction
(tad ill-will.

THE MANSION HOUSE RELIEF FUND.—The aggregate
donations to wards this fund have reached the amount
of £lOO,OOO. This speaks strongly for the noble private
benevolence of Englishmen; but large as the sum is, it
is quite inadequate to meet the necessities of the great
emergency. . It seems now pretty certain that if the
Government does not render the movement in favour of
the sufferers a purely national one, making it the con-
cern of the whole country, the gigantic evil will never
be completely mastered. A shilling or even a sixpenny
poll tax on persons whose means exceed a hundred a-year
would be far more than enough to make the Lancashire
operatives comfortable, until the cotton trade should
recover its old activity.
INDIAN Corrox.—lt is pleasant to find by the last
mail from India that we are really now likely to be
made independent of America for a cheap supply of good
cotton. Up to this time we have had such Indian
cotton as we could get from Bombay or Surat. But
now the people of Bahar and the Gangetic valley are in-
dustriously sowing cotton for the English market, to be
shipped at Calcutta, and we are informed that we may
expect four times the ordinary supply from India in the
course of next year. The native princes and capitalists
are taking up the matter in earnest, and under the
strongest local encouragement large tracts of land are
now sown with cotton. If the cultivators could only get
a few intelligent, active, and energetic Europeans to
superintend their operations, India might soon supply
good cotton not to England only, but to the whole
world.

TM: INCOME OP THE LATE CITY SOLICITOR.—The
City Press writes The-net annual receipts of the late
CI, y solicitor from 1848 to 1862 averaged very nearly
£2,100. It the year 1860-61 the net receipts were
upwards of £2,200; in 1861-2 more than £3,000. The
income WIS blerived from several sources. Prom the
city cash there as paid to the late solicitor an average
yearly sum of about £1,400, for Parliamentary work
nearly £3OO, from the Commissioners of Sewers some
£7OO, from the Iri-h society about £150,, and from

articles.title: P.RESENTATION OF THE LORD
articles.text:
P.RESENTATION OF THE LORD

MAYOR-ELECT.

On the 3rd inst., in accordance with an ancient cus-
tom, Alderman Rose (the Lord Mayor-Deet) was pre-
sented to the Lord High Chancellor to receive the
sanction of the Crown to his election to the office of
Lord Mayer of London. The ceremony took place in
the fine hall of the Society of the Middle Temple, in
the presence of the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex,
with the Under-Sheriffs, some o: the Aldermen, and all
the principal officers of the Corporation. The civic
dignitaries had previously assembled at Guildhall, and
thence in carriages escorted the Lord Mayor Elect in
procession to the Temple.
Mr. Russell Gurney (the Recorder) approaching- the
Lord Chancellor, said :—lt was wholly unnecessary
that he should say a single word to his Lordship as to
the natuns of the duties which devolved on the Lord
Mayor of London, or on the qualities which wet e
neccessary to insure a right discharge of them.. That
those qualities were possessed by Alderman Rose in a.
remarkable degree was the firm conviction of those who
had had the best opportunities of forming a correct
opinion upon the subject. He had,already filled various
municipal offices with credit to himself and advantage
to the public; arid his, fellow-citizens, having seen that
he was active • and intelligent in business, amiable in
private, and independent in public life; had now raised
him to the highest office which it was in their power to
confer, and they had instructed him. (the Recorder) to
express to his Lordship their hurable but confident hope
that they would learn from his Lordship that the
choice they had made had met with the sanction of the
Crown.

The Lord Chancellor, addressing the Lord Mayor-
Elect, said :—I have her Majesty's commands to signify
to your Lords-hp her Royal approbation of the choice
whiell the Livery of Londonland your fellew-citizens
have made in electing you to fill the office of chief
.magistrate. I congratulate you very -ranch upon. the
occasion. I have had the good.,fortune to receive your
predecessor in office on an occasion similar to this, and
it was a great satisfaction to me to felicitate him, as I
have now to felicitate you in like manner, on being
elected the chief magistrate of London. He has left
you one duty to perform of a somewhat melancholy
character, it is true, but not new in connection with the
corporation of the city of London, which, first in
hospitality, has been also generally foremost in works
of charity; and in the committee formed by the Lord
Mayor for relieving the prevailing distress in the cotton
manufacturing districts you will be occupied in a work
of humanity and benevolence. Upon whomsoever the
duty may devolve of receiving your successor, I hope he
may have to congratulate you, as I have now the grati-
fication to congratulate your predecessor, in his absence,
on the mild dignity, the gentle wisdom, and the
invariable kindness and courtesy which have cha-
racterised him—qualities which, while they have gained.
him many friends during life, have left him, I may say,
without a single enemy; and that is a very honourable
termination of a public career. •
In the evening the Lord Mayor-Elect entertained
about 60 gentlemen at dinner at the Albion.

SUDDEN DEATH OF COLONEL LLOYD, C.B.—Whilst
Colonel Lloyd, C. 8., was speaking at the Music- hall,.
Chester, on Monday night, on the occasion of the pre-
sentation of the prizes to the Chester Volunteers, he
suddenly dropped senseless from an attack of disease of
the heart. Drs. Powell, Waters, and Brittain endea-
voured to promote artificial respiration, but in ten
minutes the gallant colonel expired.
THE HARVEST IN THE NORTIL—rn the hilly districts
of Yorkshire the frosts and winds of the past week have
enabled the farmers to secure a good portion of their
crops, but the harvest is yet far from complete in some of
the most exposed positions, and in places crops are even
yet uncut. As may be expected, the grain is much de-
teriorated in quality, but, owing to the low temperature,
not so greatly sprouced ' as might have been supposed.
The moorland farmers must, of course, be sufferers to
some extent.

A remarkable instance of the influence of town drain-
age en the public health is shown in a report which has
just been issued by the sanitary committee of the Hali-
fax corporation. Great sewarage works have been con-
structed since 1851, and between that period and the
present the death rate has decreased from 25.39 per
1,000 to 21.48 per 1,000. This is in the town of Hali-
fax itself; in the union the mortality has only decreased
1.1 per cent.—a Lid which shows more clearly the bene-
fisial operation of the sanitary improvements in Halifax.
A NEW THEOEX.—Professor Bache, connected with
the United States Coast Survey, in a recent article :on
the physiology of sea-sickness, advances the idea that
this torment of ocean travellers is a disease of the brain,
and not of the stomach. His view is, that it is owing to
the fact that the mind is not able to understand the vary-
ing motions of the vessel as rapidly as the senses feel
them, thus causing a conflict if impressions, and a con-
sequent affection of the brain, which in turn deranges
the nervous system, and produces nausea. As soon as
the mind can conceive the ides of each motion as soon
as it is felt, sea-sickness ceases. The deck is conse-
quently the best place for one suffering, as there the
sight can be best educated to the movements of the
vessel.

LORD WESTBURY'S CARRIAGE STOPS THE WAY.—
During several hours on the 3rd, in consequence of the
course adopted by the Lord Chancellor, of holding his
levees to initiate the business of the term in the new hall
of the Middle Temple, instead of at his private residence,
as has been usual, there was a continuous flow of
carriages freighted with gentlemen of the long robe
through Temple bar, and this so interfered with the
usual street traffic as to entirely impede it. The City
police undertook the duty of making the necessary
arrangements to facilitate the passage of so great an in-
flux of vehicles within the City boundaries, but the
effort so overtaxed their ingenuity, that they had to give
it up in despair, and the only solution they could find
of the difficulty in which they were placed was, to pre-
vent all the omnibuses, cabs, and waggons going east-
ward from proceeding beyond the limits of the Strand
until such time as the barristers had paid their respects
to the official head of their profession. This caused a
regular block all down Pickett-place so far as Somerset-
house, as the vehicles referred to cqu'id neither move
forward or return to seek some bye way into the City,
to the great annoyance of t.4e passengers who were in a
hurry to attend to their business there.

CANADA.-4 For, gentlemen, depend upon it, we can-
not in the North America of our day—in this new.
American age which announces its advent like the first
boom of a conqueror's salvos of artillery—we cannot go
on as we have gone on in the piping times of peace.
We have three choices be ore us—either to continue the
connection, or to, set up for ourselves, or to drift into
annexation with the Northern Democracy. Not one per
cent. of the people of Canada desire annexation; not one
per cent. of the people feel that the hour has come for
our entering on an independent political existence; and,
therefore, practically the only choice left us is to pro-
vide for the proper maintenance, on our side, of the
imperial connexion. I say frankly, I place this alter-
native on no impalpable ground; but I do place it on
the clear ground of common sense, of self-interest, of
self-preservation, as well as on the sense of duty and
conscientious obligation. I put it to you on Canadian
rather than on imperial ground. I say the connection
is worth paying for, and the only que,tion is
whether as to a militia or a military road, what can you\
pay, and when and how will you pay it F—Extract from
a recent speech of the Hon. Mr. 314 Gee, at Ottawa.
THE SOLDIER'S GREATEST PERIL.—The experience
of this war confirms that of nearly all campaigns, that
soldiers are in far greater danger from the diseases inci-
dent to camp-life, than from the weapOns of the enemy.
There are many surpris ng facts illustrating this in the
history of the English and French armies. The 92ri
English Regiment lost more officers and men in fort.:
months from the climate of Jamaica, than by the enemy
in an active war of twenty-two years, in which it was
twenty-six times in battle. The French sent 309,268
officers and men to the Crimea war, of whom 200,000
were under medical treatment, 50,000 being for wounds
and 150,000 for diseases. Among the soldiers there
were 69,229 deaths, of whom only 7,500 were killed on
the battle-field or nor afterwards heard of, being eight
deaths from other causes to one in battle. It is the
deliberate opinion of Scrive, an intelligent investigator,
that the losses occasioned by the most murderous batles
do not equal one-fourth of the total losses to which an
army is ordinarily subjected.--Boston (U.S.) Paper.
THE STEAMER ALABAMA.—This vessel appears still to
keep about the banks of Newfoundlind, and conse-
quently out of reach of the Federal men-of-war who
recently came to European waters in search of the Con-
federate privateer. The ship Travancore, which arrived
at Liverpool on Monday from St. John's, New Brunswick,
reports that when off the banks of Newfoundland, about
300 miles S.E., she saw the Confederate steamer Alabama.
The steamer made for the Travancore, and fired a gun
across the ship's bows. ' The Travancore immediately
hoisted the English ensign, and the steamer seeing her
mistake at once hoisted the Confederate colours, dipped
them three times, and then steered away. There was a
rumour in Liverpool on Monday to the effect that in order
to stop the career of the Alabama the swift Federal
steamer Vanderbilt had privately left New York for the
cruising ground of the lemons Confederate.
