articles.title: TINDERG.ROUND RAILWAY AND
articles.text:
THE TINDERG.ROUND RAILWAY AND

IT STATIOA S.

Prom a close inspection on Saturday of the whole
length of the Metropolitan Railway there appears but
very little doubt of early opening of this great under-
taking, which, in its various stages of construction, has
engrossed the attention of the public so long. Few rail-
way works of such short length have ever presented the
difficulties encountered in the formation of this line, and
the popular expectation, which had assigned its opening-
to an earlier period of this season, has been disappointed,
partly through the bursting of the Fleet Ditch at
Clerkenv4 ell, and partly from the desire of the authorities
to have the works completed throughout before the train
, commenced running. At the Farnngdon-street station,
(the city terminus), the works are• in a. very forward
state. Erected. principally of wood, covered with slat-
ing, and provided with the necessr booiiing-offices and
three commodious platforms, it is as well lighted by day
as any of the other London termini, while the globular
lanterns which hang from its roof will be more than suffi-
cient for this purpose at nighttime. There is also a capa-
cious gasholder erected here for the supply of gas to the
trains., The signals are being, fast completed, and the
:workmen are busily engaged on the switches and an
immense turntable. In the Clerkenwell cutting there
is still a little work to be done, but the permanent way
is. complete, with its double lines of broad and narrow
gauge. Leaving the cutting, which has been well
ballasted with dry gravel, and entering the tunnel (near
the workhouse), at the mouth of v,ldch is a switchman's
box, nnthing, of interest occurs ti. 1 the line reaches
another -open cutting just bef,re entering the fine station
at King's-cross. Here are the junctions with the Great
Northern and Midland' Railways, and the station itself
is_considered to-bathe finest on_the line. The -booking-
offices, supported on light bronzed latticed giriers and
ornamental pillars,bridge the-railway, beneath the lofty
curve& of the magnificent iron and- glass roof: Stair-
cases, with handsome bronzed balustrades, descend to
'the platforms lighted, as at arringdon-street station,
with the glob ;F
ular lamps, which are being supplied to
all the stations. Little beyond a few decorative
works and the signals remains to be done at the station
itself. Passing through toe tunnel beneath the New-
road (now the Euston-road), we come to the Gower-
street station, which only wants a few finishing strokes
to complete it, besides painting and placing of the
signals. This station, which is simply a portion of the
tunnel, reached by staircases from the offices on each
side of the Eustom- road, derives sufficient daylight from
the ingeniously contrived loopholes in the sides of the ,
tunnel; it will be lighted at night-time in a similar
manner to King' s- cross station. Continuing the journey
through the tunnel, the next station reached is the Port-
land-road and Regent's Park. The interior architecture
of this is very fanciful, the principal features consisting
of two small towers with cupola roofs, the latter
supplying a portion of daylight to the station
beneath, which is a part of the tunnel. This
station is also nearly finished, and from here to the
Baker-street station, which is almost a repetition of that
at Gower-street, the lime still runs through a tunnel.
The works at Baker-street., are likewise in a very
forward state. Another piece of tunnellinc, intervenes
between this latter and the next station at Edgware-road,
which has an iron and glass roof like that at King's-cross.
A little work has yet to be done here on the permanent
way, but the station itself is nearly finished. Leaving
Edgware-road station, the line again passes through
a tunnel, at the other extremity of which is the-
Paddington station, the most unfinished portion of the,
line. A great deal of work. yet remains to be done
here, as the station is incomplete and the roof un-
finished. At this spot the workmen are still engaged
upon the permanent way at the junction with the
Great Western., R4ilway. The Paddington station
abuts upon the bridge over which the Bishop's-road
is carried. It will be entered from the latter place
and also from the Great Western terminus. Here
are several of the new carriages, both first and second
class, each compartment being furnished with two lights
supplied from the reservoirs on their roofs. They are
broadgauge carriages, with the initials G. W. H.;' the
first-class carriages are luxuriously furnished, and the
second-class are neatly and comfortably cushioned. The
telegraphic communication will soon be perfected, the
wires, contained in grooved planks fastened to the sides
of the tunnels, being nearly continuous from one end of
the line to the other. The whole of the tunnelling and
the permanent way are in first-ratecondition, the former
being extremely dry, with an exception or two (Clerken-
well, forinstance), and thelatter well laid and ballasted
throughout. Probably, therefore, by Christmas the
public will be in possession of a short and expeditious
route from the city to Paddington, the distance (about
four miles) being accomplished by express trains in ten
nainates and by the ordinary trains in 15 minutes; at
extremely reasonable fares.

articles.title: CUSTOMS REVEIVUE..
articles.text:
CUSTOMS REVEIVUE..

Despite the distress prevailing in the cotton-manufac-
turing districts, and which week by week for months
past has become more and more intense, the revenue
derived from customs duties is not only sustained, but
considerably increased.
On an analysis and comparison of the official accounts
for the first nine months of the years 1861 and 1862, it
appears that cocoa, currants, pepper, brandy, sugar„
molasses, tea, tobacco and the chief cereals, have to-
gether brought into the Exchequer upwards of £400,000
more this year than were collected from those commodi-
ties in the same period of 1861. Of wheat, £1,375,917
quarters were entered for home consumption in excess
of 1861, a year in which the importations and deliveries
were more extensive than any on record.
Of wheaten flour, likewise the increment is more
than half a million of hundredweight over the nine
months of the last year. Oats, peas, beans, and Indian
corn, however, appear on the. adverse side for nearly a
million of *hers.
Brandy has increased 60,267 gallons, sugar and mo-
lasses upwards of 372,000 cwt. tea 339,702 lbs., tobacco
471,382 lbs. Rum and wine have decreased, the former
121,423 gallons, the latter 1,059,676 gallons: but, as
respects wine it should be borne in mind that a large
quantity on which duty was paid in the first months of
1861 had been held over from 1860 to render it admis-
sible at the reduced rates of duty. Opposing these
decreases against the increases, the preponderance is
greatly in favour of 1862.

Importing Tea without colour on the leaf prevents
the Chinese passing off inferior leaves as in the usual
kinds. Horniman's Tea is uncoloured, therefore, always
good alike.
A CARLYLIAN CERTIFICATE.—Mr. John Macrae Moir
has been elected, out of one. hundred and thirty candi-
dates, Secretary to the Scottish Hospital and Kinloch
Trust, Crane-court, Fleet-street. His selection, by a
very large majority-183 votes to 114—is chiefly to be
ascribed to the unusually powerful recommendations
which had been given to him by his old college and
other literary friends. Amongst the other well-known
names on the list of testimonials were those of Professor
Blackie, Professor M‘Gillvray,
•Stansfeld, Colonel
Sykes, Mr. Grant Duff, Sir Wm. Dunbar, Mr. Craufurd,
and, greatest of all, Mr. Thomas Carlyle. The last has
been printed and circulated pretty largely. It is very
characteristic :---‘ I have had the pleasure of meeting
Mr. J. M. Moir different times in late years and am
willing to testify that I consider him a man years,
and
vigorous intellect, of honest solid notions, ideas, and
aspirations; generally of a robust, substantial, and
manful turn of mind. A man, I should guess, capable
of much labour, and of doing it in a faithful, energetic,
and efficient manner. Of his private habits and modes
of working and living, I have heard nothing that was
not favourable.—(Signed) T. CARLYLE.-5, Cheyne-row,
Chelsea, May 6, 1861.' Among those who voted for
Mr. Macrae Moir were Lord Clyde, Rev. Drs. Cumming,
Hamilton, Young, Mlames, Grant, &e,
A PICTURE OF ANCONA.—Ancona it a nasty place to
live in. Walk down to the port to see the 'handsomest
triumphal arch the Romans ever erected,' and your path
is crossed by a gang of desperate-looking galley-slaves.
Go past a cafe, stand before the door of a church, or go
up to its altar, you are beset by loathsome beggars. Out
of the most squalid mud-holes, unmatched for dirt and
poverty, even in Ireland, without windows, without
chimneys, and doing duty for houses, stables, high lofts,
and pigstys altogether, whining brats swarm, whining
audibly, and chuckling inwardly, making fun of the
verymisery which affects to appeal to your benevolence.
The whole army of beggars garrisons the sanctuary and
its approaches. Its stronghold is the church, the door
of the shrine, the steps a the altar. Before that black
doll, all swathed in glittering jewellery, on the threshold
of that treasury to which the vanity even more than the
munificence or piety of monarchs so lavishly contributed,
you see sturdy idleness and vice counterfeiting want and
starvation. Through that hideous throng of abandoned
ruffians, of cripples, of lepers, of plague-strickim
wretches, whom a well-constituted society hides float
sight, and which is here displayed, you have to fight
your way, heart-wrung, sickened, your blood boiling
with rage at a system which has tainted the race to the
very core and which you feel will long baffle the well-
meant efforts of the humane rulers who are now bent On
grappling with it.
Inlsu CoNvlar SEnvicE.—ln consequence of the
increased number of prisoners at present in .Mountjoy
Male Prison' owing, in a great degree, to the closing of
Philipstowa Prison) the Lords of the Treasury, on the
recommendation of the Director of Convict Prisons,
have sanctioned the appointment of six additional
warders to the staff of that prison, and directed that the
warders should be selected from those placed on the
redundant list on the abolition of their office as wardens
on Philipstown Convict Prison staff.—Civil Service
Gazette.

articles.title: LATE STORM.
articles.text:
THE LATE STORM.

On..Frilay. the screw-steamer Panther,- Captain
Rutter, belonging to Messrs. Brownlow and.Co:, arrived
at Hull, from Cronstadt, after• a very heavy, passage of
twenty-two days, the Panther having sailed from Cron-
stadt on the 11th of October. The wind at the time was
blowing a gale from the E.S.E., and the sea rolling
mountains high. The vessel, however, proceeded on
her course, and arrived at Copenhagen on the 15th,
where she took in coals and left the 5a.:143 evening. She
proceeded down the Cattegat, and passed the Skagen
lighthouse at six o'clock next morning. At seven
o'clock on the evening of the 16th Holmen lighthouse
was passed. The Panther continued to beat about in
the North Sea from this date until the 23rd, when the
captain determined to run for the Elbe. Owing to the
strong wind, the heavy sea, and Click -weather, they
were unable to get into the river, and brought up out-
side the Elbe lightship. The vessel rode very heavily;
with 100 fathoms of chain out. The engines were also
going ahead at full. speed.. The sea was rolling com-
pletely over the ship, and but few on board expected to
see the light of another day. About midnight every
preparation was made to cut away the masts. Fortu-
nately, however, it was not found necessary to resort
to this extremity, and on the following morning the
weather had somewhat moderated. The anchor was
therefore weighed, and the ship ran into Cuxhaven.
Having taken in a stock of coals and provisions, they
left on the 29th ult. Captain Rutter said that it was
heartrending to see the number of vessels either already
on or driving towards the coast of Jutland, as; owing to
the nature of the coast, most of the hands must have
been lost. A large bark let go two anchors when near
the Panther with 100 fathoms to each. She rode
gallantly for some ,time,, but the force of the hurricane
was such that, before long, she dragged. both anchors,
drifted on to the shore, anctevery soul on board perished.
A report spread on shore next morning that some of the
hands were to be seen in the rigeing, and a Cuxhaven
steamer went out, notwithstandieg -the heavy sea, but
no trace of a living being Could- be found. Captain
Rutter reports that when he left Cronstadt-the freights
were much better than for some time past. The Panther
brought five men belonging to the Lord. Gambier, whi,h
was lost in Davis' Strait, and who were taken by a
Danish vessel to Copenhagen.

articles.title: TWO PRISONERS UNDER SENTENCE
articles.text:
TWO PRISONERS UNDER SENTENCE

OF DEATH.

On Friday afternoon the Sheriffs, Mr. Alderman J
C. Lawrence and Mr. Hugh Jones, accompanied by
Messrs. Farrar and Mackrell, the Under-Sheriffs, and
the Rev. Mr. Davis and Mr. Jonas the Governor of
Newgate, proceeded to the cell in Which the prisoner
Robert Cooper was confined, and the Chaplain an-
nounced. to him that the Sheriffs had fixed Monday, the
17th inst., as the day for carrying out the sentence of
the law; he alsotxhorted him to make the best use of
the short time that remained to him in this world, and
by a sincere repentence to endeavour to obtain pardon
for the great sin he had conmitted. The wretched man
appears to be quite prostrated by his position, and to
feel an excessive terror at the thought of losing his life
upon the scaffold. He has never, it appears, attempted
to cast any doubt upon the propriety of the verdict of
the jury, but still he seems to think that there was a sort
of justification for the act he committed in the conduct
of the deceased. He has repeatedly stated that no one
could tell what his feelinc,s were at discovering that his
wife,' as he always called the deceased, was unfaithful
to him. On his being reminded that she was not his
wife, and that he had a wife living, he stated that, on
account of his being in the army, he could not live with
the woman whom he formerly married, and that they
mutually agreed to separate; he had not seen' her for
many years, and thought she was dead at the time he
contracted the second marriage with the deceased girl.
This prisoner evidently entertains an idea that mercy
will be extended to him, and he has ,-xpressed an inten-
tion of sending his own statement of his cam to the
Home Secretary, and making an appeal to the Crown
for mercy; but it is not probable, from the character of
the crime, that this will be likely to havo any effect.
The prisoner has repeatedly stated since his conviction
that on the day the fatal affair happened he went to
Isleworth quite by chance, and he declares that he en-
tertained no intention to do mischief to the deceased,
but alleges that the object for which he carried the pistol
about him was to destroy his own life. The other con-
demned culprit, Samuel Gardner, the sweep, who.was
convicted on Friday of the murder of his wife, appears
to exhibit much more fortitude than his wretched com-
panion, and it seems that he has all along persisted in
declaring his innocence of the crime of which he was
accused.. It will be remembered that the circumstances
of the case were very peculiar; but, although the jury
were in deliberation more than an hour and a half before
they returned their verdict, it appears that eleven of
them had made up their minds in a very short time that
the evidence had established the guilt of the prisoner,
and only one of them entertained any doubt upon
the point. The Lord Chief Baron, who tried the pri-
soner, is understood to have expressed himself perfectly
satisfied with the verdict, and the prisoner's attempt, if
he be really guilty, to fix the crime upon an innocent
person—a similar proceeding to which, it will be remem-
bered, was adopted by the man Mullens, who was con-
victed of the. murder of Mrs. Emslie—is evidently a
great aggravation of his offence. A similar announce-
ment to that had been made on the previous day to
Cooper was made to the prisoner by the officials on
Saturday afternoon. He heard it with perfect calmness,
and merely observed that he was prepared to die, and
did not utter any of those protestations of innocence
that were made by him after his trial. On Friday even-
ing, after the jury had delivered their verdict, the girl
Elizabeth Humbler was liberated from custody, and
taken away from Newgate in the charge of her mother.

Gatignani says :--‘ Considerable agitation has been
caused at Heidelberg (Palatinate of the Rhine) in con-
sequence of the effects which have been caused to the
castle by the construction of the tunnel out under it for
the new railway of the Neckar. In consequence of the
continual shaking of the foundations of the building
from the passing of the trains, the castle is threatened
with destruction. The front, facing the town, has
already cracked in several places, and it has been found
necessary to use strong iron cramps to prevent the en-
largement of the fissures. Should the castle, or even a
part of it, be thrown down from this cause the loss
would be irreparable, as it is one of the most curious
monuments of the Renaissance.'

THE EXODUS mom LivEnPooL.--=According to the
official returns from the Government Emigration Office
at Liverpool, it appears that during the month of October
there sailed for the United States 13 ships under the
act,' having on board 358 cabin and 2,012 steerage pas-
sengers; and to Victoria, 3 ships, with 24 cabin and 605
steerage passengers—making a total of 16 ships and
2,999 passengers; 1,204 of whom were Irish, 1,167
English, 64 Scotch, and 183 other countries, showing
an increase over the same month of 1861 of 471 pas-
sengers. Of vessels sailing not under the act, there left
for the United States 14 ships, with 457 passengers; to
Canada, 5 ships, 650 passengers to Victoria, I ship, 29
passengers; to South America, 4 ships, 19 passengers;
to West Indies, 2 ships, 10 passengers; to Africa, 1
ship, 27 passengers; to East India, 2 ships, 6 passengers;
to China, 1 ship, 4 passengers—making a total of 30
ships and 1,202 passengers—showing a decrease, as
compared with October, 1861, of 306 passengers. Total
emigration for the past month, 4,202; total same month
last year, 4,036; increase in favour of 1862 of 166
passengers.

THZ HARVEST ON THE CONTINENT. A Belgian
journal gives the following general retrospect of the
last harvest All accounts agree in stating that the
harvest in Brabant and the neighbouring districts has
been very satisfactory; for if the yield of rye is small
it is amply compensated by the abundance and good
quality of the wheat crop. As to other products—
barley, buckwheat, bay, potatoes, flax, colza, &c.,—
they leave nothing to be desired. If we take a wider
view ,a e shall have equal reason to be thatLkful for the
harvest of 1862. In the country north of the Danube
the wheat crops are very good; in Hungary, and the
region watered by the Theiss and the Danube, the
yield is an average one; while the dryer.districts show
a general deficit of one-tenth, and in some places as
much as one-third. In the whole of North Germany,
Posen, Eastern and Western Prussia, the yield is good;
in Silesia, very good; in Wurtemburg, Baden, and the
Palatinate, a good average; in Franconia, better than
in 1861; Moselle, Holland, France Belgium, Luxem-
burg, a good yield. As fur rye, the yield is about the
average; in Bessarabia, the Ukraine, and Poland,
above the average; still better in Silesia and Saxony;
not so good on the lower Elba and the Weser. In
South Germany, Wurteraburg, Baden, the Palatinate,
Franconia, Luxemburg, nearly an average one. A
good yield itt the valley of the Maine, Wetteravia, on
the Rhine, the Moselle, and in Holland. Of barley
and oats ,the crops are universally good, except in
Hungary, where they suffered from drought. As for
potatoes, though slightly affected with the disease in
some .places, they are generally abundant, and will
amply supply the deficiPncy of rye.'
Amongst the visitors at the International Exhibition
on Monday lea was W. W----, a native of a village
near Wirksworti?.. Although totally blind he could not
be prevailed upoti to forego a visit to the world's great
fair, and might have been seen threading the courts and
avenues of the vetst building with all the rapidity and
eagerness of those who wish to see a great deal in a short
time. Whatever, his motive was we know not, unless it
be that he might be enabled to tell his friends that he
had been in the 'Exhibition—certainly not that he had
leen it.

Stenography is now universally taught in the Bava-
, rian rammar schools.
, It is now stated'that, in the• event of an early
tion of the House of Commons, Mr. S. Laing will solicit
the suffrages of the electors of Sligo.
The statue of George 1. has disappeared from the
centre of the Great Globe, where it was supposed to
reside during the time that locality was an exhibition.
It is to be hoped it will come to light in due season.
A lady fell down the other day whilst walking on the
King's-road, Brighton, when a man very civilly picked
her up, and said gently, I hope, ma'm you are none the
worse.' 'Well, then, indeed I am just as little the
better,' she replied, quite savagely.
The Emperor of Russia has just given an Order in
diamonds, which was certainly well merited. It was the
ingenious amongst the engineers, M. Jules Alquine, who
had the 'construction of the railway between Warsaw and
St. Pete-sburg.
It is teought that the first public act of her Majesty,
after the year's mournimr, will be the opening of Parlia-
ment in person. This rumour tends to the belief that
the Houses will meet at an early date next year.
The Charivari amuses its readers with a travestie of
the sympathy expressed by Punch for the Southern
Slave-owners. Punch is made to say, by his Paris
brother, that we English have a monopoly of the right
to create freemen, and a commercial interest in the
maintenance of Southern slavery.
Dr. W—, on one occasion, received no fee for
marrying a parsimonious couple, and meeting them
several months after at a social gathering, took up
their baby, and exclaimed, 4 I believe I have a mort-
gage on this child.' Baby's papa, rather than have an
explanation before the conapany, quietly handed over
a sovereign.
How far inwards towards the Strand did the Thames
extend previous to the erection of the Adelphi Terrace
by Adams? The Strand has, it is well known, be the
highway between the City and Westminster for centuries,
following prob ibly near the same course as it does at
the present day; but the river, it would seem, must•for--
merly have approached it much more nearly.—Notes
and Queries.

A private letter from one in close attendance ea the
Emperor Napoleon contains the following paragraph:
—4 The Emperor has not changed in favour of the Pope,.
however much laiy politicians • have tried to influence
him ; depend upon it, before many months have passed,
his troops will be withdrawn from Rome. I know
exactly the Emperor's vi,ws, and M. Drouyn de Lhuys
is just the man to carry them out—patience therefore.
Mr. Kinglake's History of the Crimean War' has
changed publishers before it has reached the public.
After being advertised for several years by Murray, it is
now undertaken by 'Blackwood. • It is. understOod that
some difference of opinion between the author and, Mr.
Murray, as to the .extent of the disclosures with regard
to the secret history of the war, has been the reason of
this step.
While working near the Graving Bank, Watfrford,
on Wednesday last, the dredge Yes el brought up a bone
with about sixteen ounces of lead run into the socket
at one end, and apparently so prepared as a weapon.
There was little doubt that it was a human shinbone!'
It was imbedded seven feet, at least, below the surface'
of the mud.

The Bishop of Liege had a narrow escape two evenings,
since. When passing along the Rue LouVrex, in that
town, one of the wheels of his carriage ran against the
ropes of a pair of sheers with which some workmen were
raising a large stone to the top of a new house. The-
shock threw down the sheers which fell on the carriage
and smashed part of it, but fortunately without injuring
the prelate, who was speedily extricated from the wreck
by persons who .happened to be near.
Walking, the other day, on the beach at Biarritz, the.
Emperor Napoleon, it is said, happened to meet an in—
telligent-looking boy about eight or nine years old, who.
took off his hat as he p tssed. The Emperor courteously
returned the salute, awl said, 'Are you English?' 'No,'
answered the boy very quickly, and drawing himself
up, I'm American.' 'Oh! American, are you? Well,
tell me which you are for, North or South?' 'Well,.
father's for the North, I believe, but I am certainly for
the South. For which of them are you, Sir?- The.
Emperor stroked his moustache, smiled, hesitated , a
little, and then said, lam for both.' 'For both, are
you ? Well, that's not so easy, and it will please.
nobody.' His Majesty let the conversation drop, and,
walked on.

It is said, and on good authority, that the Southern.
leaders, pressed by want of men, are turning their
thoughts to plans of partial emancipation. Their idea is.
to 'abolish the law under which a man with any negro
blood is held to be a negro, and substitute as a principle
that any,white blood makes a man civilly white, pro-
vided he is in the army. They calculate that this Will
give them a vast body of recruits, and create inextin-
guishable jealousy between the two coloured races, the
mulattoes thus acting as buffers between the purely
black and white races. That plan might succeed if all.
whites were statesmen, but they are not; and the mu-
lattoes, incessantly insulted by low whites, are sure, as
in Hayti, to ally themselves with the blacks, and act as
guides and officers.
Earl Russell is of opinion that British vessels making
for any point of the Circassian coast between the ports
which have been opened by Russia to foreign commerce
would not be secure from interference on the•rart of the
Czar's cruisers, and that, consequently, any such attempt
, to open a communication with the people of Circassia
'would only bring about complications with the Russian
Government, and result in losses to the persons engaged
in such an enterprise.'
In anticipation of the speedy inclosing of the famous
training-ground, Langton Wold, near Melton, a move-
ment has been set on foot to secure the northern training
establishments at or near Scarborough. There is a wide
waste of moorland, known as Seamer Moor, the property
of Lord Londesborough, who is a supporter of the turf;
and. it is on this moor the proposed training ground and
race-course are to be. A gentleman has returned to
Melton, after having made an official inspection of the
place, and reports favourably. It is thought the Malton
Race Meeting will scarcely survive the inclosure of the
Wold, and it is proposed to inaugurate a spring and an
autumn meeting at Scarborough, where at present there
are no races at all. - - _

A Paris paper seems rather hard-pushed to make some
excuse for duelling , if we may judge from the follow-
• ing :—` A duel is the last resource of civilisation. It
offers to the offended a noble revenge, for, instead of
quietly assassinating one's antagonist, we struggle with
him hand to hand beford. witnesses.' It is, indeed, a
noble revenge for one who would quietly assassinate,
but the nobility does not go much farther. The sen-
tence we have quoted occurs in one of the most respect-
able Parisian papers!
The scheme for the union of the City churches was
completed on Saturday. It was originally proposed
that there should be 17 amalgamations, with the sup-
pression of as many churches; but from the circum-
stances that emerged in the course of the examination
three of these amalgamations were given up, and only
14 churches are to be suppressed. The patrons have
yet to give their sanction, but this, though it may
delay, is not expected to prevent, the nnion. A corre-
sponding number of churches to those suppressed are to,
be built in the centres of poor and dense localities out-
side the City walls.
At the battle of Inka the desperation of the 'enemy
was astonishing. Several of them endeavoured to tear
our colours from the hands of the men by main strength,.
and either perished in the attempt or were taken priso-
ners. In one spot next morning I counted seventeen
rebels lying dead around one of their colonels. Sixteen
feet square would cover the whole space where they
died with their commander. Between two caissons of
the 11th Ohio battery lay sixteen dead horses, and the
battery lost ninety-three in the fight. In one place- a
rebel and a Union soldier, the Unionist shot through
the breast, and in falling fie had plunged his bayonet
into the breast of the man who had shot him, and they
fell together, the rebel clutching our boy by the throat.
They lay in this position on the field next morning, and
it was with difficulty they were separated.—New York
Herald.
Mr. Lancaster has at present a gun undergoing at
Woolwich an endurance' trial. It has already stood
more than 2,000 charges of powder, each of 61b., and,
from all we can hear, is as far off from being burst as it
was on the first day. Cui bono, may we ask, to pursue
the experiments to,a further extent? The gun is now
admitted to be a good and strong piece of artillery; and,
as the cost of testing it up to its present condition has
already stood the country in about £l,OOO, it appears to
us that any more expenditure of cash upon it would be
useless, and therefore scarcely justifiable. If it be posi-
tively determined to destroy the gun) we would suggest
that it should be removed from the slings which it now
occupies, and where the effects of recoil cannot be ascer-
tained, to a carriage of the precise character on which
it would be mounted supposing that it were required for
service, and where it would receive all the jarring inci-
dental to a working piece, and that it should be loaded
e
with gradually increasing charges until all connected
with the trials declared themselves satisfied, or the gun
itself put hors de combat. This plan would soon settl
the matter, and would have the great merit of being
.
practice.—Army
more economical than the one now in
un
and ravy Gazette.

_REVOLUTION LV GREECE.

The following diary of recent events at Athens is the
most detailed account of the revolution that has yet been
received :

_ .
Athens, Oct. 23rd, 8 a.m.
The morning before last
.we received the exciting
news that the -whole of Acarnani, with the countries
adjoining the Gulf of Corinth--,in a word, almost the
whale el the country—had raised the standard of
insurrection. The shops were at once closed, and every
ame collect d in the streets to watch the progress of
events. The Government, the legations, in short,
every one, heard
,on the following day that the insur-
rection would commence at Athens in the evening at
8 &dock, and at the -hour fixed reports of muskets were
heal d in every part of the , city, until about 10, not,
however, for the purpose of attack, but of rejoicing.
There was then. a moment of calm, and some persons
might have imagined that the movement was
.not
'serious. Such, however, Was the case, for preparations
were then being made for going •further. The place of
rendezvous was the open space called Liberty-square.
The battalion of military firemen were the first to
arrive, and afterwards came the cavalry, the artillery,
•and the line, the whole' amounting, with the peoPle who
had collected, to about 4,000 -men. At daybreak this
body of insurgents, headed by Commandant Papadiaman-
dopoulos, marched into the University-square, close to
the Chainber'of Deputies. It afterwards went to the
square near the Palace, and then returned to University-
square; and there the following decree was read
ATHENS, Oet.. 22.—The misfortunes .of the. country
have ceased. The provinces and the capital, having
.come to an understanding, have put an end to our state
.of misrale. By tilt, common decision of the Greek
people . there have been decided and decreed :—The
deposition of. Bing Otho ; the fall. of
.the Regency of
Queen Amelia; a Provisional Government is, composed
in the following manner, in order to direct the affairs of
the country. until the meeting of a National A.ssembly :
—Demetri Bulgaria, Presiet_nt ; Constantin Canaris, and
Benizelo ROufos. A National Assembly will be imme-
,ditely convoked. to draw up a Constitution and elect a
big. Long live the nation! Long live the country!'
A few persons were accidentally wounded, and one
gendarme _killed. Those are the only casualties attend-
ant on the revolution, which it will be seen has not
been a very terrible one. It could:not have been otherwise,
for all.were of the same mind. The gendarmery did not.
join the people until the revolution had been accom-
plished ; but they refrained from resistance, and those
who were on duty at the palace only fired a few shots in
the air for form sake.

•. 23rd, 10 o'clock, p.m.
Admiral Canaris has given in his resignation as mem-
ber of the Provisional Government. M. Roufos, who
is at the head of the movement at Patras, has
not yet arrived et Athens, 'so 'that M: Bulgaris
governs alone. He has. formed a Ministry. The
people are waiting for a proclamation from the Go-
vernment, and the city is illuminated. Daring the
whole day bands of armed men have patrolled the
'streets, rand are still doing so. Muskets are still fired
from time to time by way of rejoicing. Some few lamps
have been broken; the royal garden has been laid waste,
.and some of the, Palace windows smashed. All, or almost
9411, the persons attached to the personal service of the
.ex-king have fled. No one was either molested or even
insulted, except the Grand Mistress, the Baroness de
Pluscow. She was well known to have exercised great
influence over the Queen, which reacted on the King,
-and also to be devoted to Austrian policy. She could
not escape the sarcasms of the -people who met her in
laer flight, but that was all she met with.
24th (Noon).
The departure of the King has just been announced.
31. Kalifrounas, Minister of Marine, went to signify to
his Majesty the fall of his dynasty from the throne of
'Greece. The King is said to have assured the Minister
that he was ready to accord to the people all they asked
for, when the latter replied in the well-kno phrase—
'lt is too late.' •.The, King tprotested, but tte Foreign
Ministers are said to have advised him to leave. All the
Government officials are at their posts.
24th (Midnight).
The houses ha've been again illuminated to-night, and
processions of the people have taken place. • ,
The following proclamation has been issued by the
Provisional Government : •

a Fellow Citizens !—A system of policy which debased
thefnational dignity and a system of governmext which
trampled under foot #9 respect due to the. laws of the
Sfate and the consciences of citizens must naturally
'excite against it_the convictions ofthe Greek 'nation, and
impel it to revolt. It is in consequence of such a state
of things that at first afew and afterwards all the other
provinces rose, put doWn_ the existing Power,-ana;sup-
ported 17 the noble and generou.s army, established new
authorities. The same wants and the same wishes, have
now raised thepopulatiOn of the capital, who, equalling
the patriotism of the provinces, have called for, the
'overthrow of the previously established state of things.
The troops, who , have remained the inflexible and
faithful guardians of 'the duty confided to then: by
the nation, and to their path to Support the, laws,
and worthy of the name of a Greek army, have sup-
ported the undertaking of the people,, and .by common
accord the established state
,of things has been over-
thrown, and the people have proclaimed the downfall of
him whO sat on the throne of Greece. They have also
'declared the downfall of the rights of his wife to the
regency. A Provisional Government has been estab-
lished, composed of Demetri Bulgari (President), Con-
stantin Canal-is, and Benizelo Roufos. The President
of the Provisional Government has formed the following
Ministry :—(Here come the names already announced.)
The mission which the new Government has received
from the people and from the army consists in preserving
the Constitutional MOnarchiCal Government, and to
always profess in an-unchangeable manner the grati-
tude of Greece towards the, three protecting Bowers;
to -always keep up- friendly -relations 'with- the other
States, and to convoke :without delay the National
Assembly, observing' during the interval order and tran-
quility, and maintaining the laws of the country. We
will, fellow-citizens, fulfil that duty with exactitude and
fidelity. We are ready to deposit the power into the
hands of the National Assembly which will be convoked.
Bat, in order that the great sacred work may be realised,
it isinecessary that the patriotism of all be maintained in
its full force. It is to your patriotism, therefore, that
we address ourselves for that work, and we hope from
you, not only order and tranquility, but also that abne-
gation which always characterised the Greek nation in
the critical moments of the past. It is thus that we hope
thatthe powerful hand of tha Almighty, who has never
abandoned the country, will protect our feeble, but
sincere efforts, and that He will bless this work by
strengthening the new order of things for the glory of
name.'—(Signed by the President and the
Ministers)

GARIBALDI AIVD AZERICA.

In a letter addressed on behalf of General Garibaldi
by Colonel Vecchy to a friend in London' the General's
views on the American question are set forth as fol-
lows:

Garibaldi being a humane man, and who never denied
his noble and generous soul, could not have answered
otherwise to one who had asked him to offer the power
of his mind and arm, in order that he might solve
the Gordian knot which unfortunately involves and
ravages America. In explanation of this letter,
what your great English people have wished and
carried out—the redemption (manumission) of slavery
in the islands and dependencies of you, Crown—
Garibaldi wishes .and wills the same, because the
clanking of the slave's chains is an abomination in his
high and true -hearted soul, and wherever there are tears
to be dried' he is always eager and ready to help the
oppressed. Not caring to be called filibuster or rebel,
he .was going to Rome to cause to -vanish from that
place of human grandeur and scatter to the. winds that
fcetid imposture which keeps enthralled so numerous a
portion of Mankind. In America he does not see a
question of commerce, but a human problem to be
solved. He cannot, think without great emotion that
in a land where, as an exile, he was honoured ;with the
citizenship, there are human beings sold by. auction like
sheep or horses. He thinks and trusts that the Federal
Government will abolish slavery. This, he says, is
their duty, and it will and must be their decision. Such
then is the explanation of the note 'that Garibaldi has
written to the American Ambassador.

. The Levant Herald bf the 22nd says that M. Lafette,
who went to Turkey on a mission connected with the
Bank of Turkey project, had failed in his efforts to
obtain a concession.

A great fire occurred in Constantinople on the 20th.
The _Herald says :
On Monday night, one of the most calamitous fires
which has devastated the northern side of the Golden
Horn for several years, broke out in the quarter of
Tarla-bashi, Pera, and was only subdued, or rather
exhausted itself, after eight hours' desolating play over
the quarter. It is believed to have originated in the
shop of a greengrocer, about ten o'clock, and though
the night was calm, in less than half an hour had
risen and closed over that and more than a dozen of the
adjoining houses in a rolling irresistible tide of flame,
which gradually lighted up the whole face of the sky
from Hakkeui away over to Scutari. The municipal and
other squirts—miscalled fire-engines—speedily gathered
from all parts of the capital, but their, feeble jets of
water seemed rather to feed than to check the blazing
torrent, as it rolled on with multiplying strength from
house to house and street to street, till the whole
quarter seemed engulphed in its waving billows of fire.
Their Highnesses the Grand Vizier, Capitan Pasha, and
Seraskier were on the spot soon after the conflagration
had assumed unusual proportions; but in spite of all the
energy their voice and example could impart to the
efforts of the firemen and soldier st the devouring storm
swept en, till the usual remedy of pulling down houses
in the line of its progress at length checked its further
course. This, however, was not achieved till 573 houses
and 80 shops had been consumed. We regret to say that
five fatal casualties also occurred, four men and, a boy
having fallen victims to the flames. The calamity, how-
ever, will have at least done one great public good—in
having cleared a densely-populated neighbourhood, and
given the authorities an opportunity of compelling the
erection of houses less grossly outraging every known
law of sanitary economy.
In the suminasy of miscellaneous news are the follow-
ing items :
His Majesty has restored the 23,000 p. recently reduced
from the salaries of the late Sultan's daughters--an act
of generosity which will meet with proper local appre-
ciation.

The newly launched frigate Rdhber-Nusret, arrived
in the port ,froni Ismidt yesterday, in tow of one of. the
Government tugs. Her armament will be put on board
in the Arsenal.

A disastrous acadent occurred at Yenikeui on
Wednesday last, resulting in the death of four men, and
the injury, more or less serious, of several others. The
scene of the catastrophe was the house formerly owned
by Djezaorlioglu, but recently presented to Nevres
Pasha, for whom it was undergoing Lextensive repairs
and alterations. One of the main walls, on or about
which some twenty workmen were employed, fell in
bodily, burying the whole amid its debris.
The Water Corordission reports that there is only
water enough in the Belgrade bends for an eleven days'
supply of Pera and Galata. The third of the reservoirs
. has only three feet of water left.

BUSINESS IN THE COURT OF CHANCERY. - The
:learned judges of the law and equity courts break-
fasted with the Lord Chancellor on Monday the 3rd, at
Middle Temple Hall, and then proceeded to their're-
spective courts. About 300 causes are set down for hear-
ing in Chancery, and the largest number to Vice-
Chancellor Wood.

HYDE PARK. There was again a very large
assemblage of people in Hyde Park on Sunday, fully
equalling in number that of the previous Sunday, and a.
strong body of police were again on duty. The au-
thorities considered that all fear of future disturbances
has now passed away; and it is understood that on Sun-
day next there will be only alew additional constables
placed in the park beyond the number ordinarily on duty
in that locality on the. Sabbath day.
ALARMING ACCIDENT ON THE SOUTH YORKSHIRE
~RAILWAY.—Onthe Ist inst. an accident occurred within
about four miles of Doncaster, on the above line, which
might have been attended with very serious conse-
quences to both life and property., ,Fortunately,. how-
ever, the only human injury sustained did not go beyond
a few cuts and bruises, although the'first tidings of the
accident created great excitement in Doncaster, for the
rumour went to the effect that the whole of the passen-
gers, with one exception, had been drowned, and the
engine-driver and stoker killed on the spot. The simple
facts Of the case, however, appear to be these. The
market train left Keadly at 8.25, and -proceeded all
right until it arrived near Barnby Dun, when a very
,rough and uneasy motion was perceived by the passen-
gers, who became very much alarmed. The fears of the
travellers were soon brought to a climax by the engine
jumping off the line at a most dangerous curve on the
banks of the canal and plunging into the water, dragging
with it the tender and a first-class carriage. , Most pro-
videntially the , passenger carriage happened to be
uppermost, and the inmates were quickly rescued from
their unpleasant position, with nothing beyond a severe'
fright and much shaking. The next carriage, a second
class, did not fully enter the water, one end only being
immersed and the other resting on the bank. The
engine was completely submerged, the only portion
above the surface being the funnel. The driver was
severely cut about the head and face, and the stoker
saved himself by swimming.
~Ma. COBDEN AND THE LEEDS WORKING MEN'S
REFORM A.ssoCIATIoN.—The following correspondence
has been published Diekinson's.yard, Leeds;

Reform Association to forward to you a copy of the
following resolution, passed at the annual meeting of
the association, held on the 13th ult. That this
meeting desires to express its sense of obligation to
those liberal representatives who have to the utmost
resisted the extravag,ince of Parliament during the late
session, and especialy tenders to Richard Cobden, Esq.,
M.P., its sincere thanks for the masterly exposure, at
the close Of the session of the inconsistency of a liberal
• government—having unscrupulously: discarded promises
and questions it was distinctly pledged to maintain_
turning to and relying upon the forbearance of a conser-
vative opposition in order to retain its posse, sion of
plaee;and power."--I have the Nikitur to be, Sce., w.

1.862.—5ir,—1 heg to acknowledge the teceipt of your
letter inclosing a copy of a. resolution, passed by the
Leed's Working" Men's Parliamentary Reform Associa-
tion, thanking me for the course 'Which I thought it my
duty to take a the close of the last session of Parlia-
ment respeiting the reactionary conduct ef the Govern-
ment. In thanking your body for this kind expression
of their approval, I beg to refer'you to the proceedings
at the meeting of my

to the first re
so e. ion calling on the Goveriment to
pledges
.or to retire from office. If other

A SINGULAR OCCURRENcE. —A few days ago two
Ladies, coming in the direction of Sunderlwad, dis-
covered that they were minus four Bank of 'England
five-pound notes, which they had carefully wrapped in
a pocket handkerchief, and for safety had carried in the
hand of one of them. In haste they returned in search
of their treasure, and agreeably surprised to find
the whole of the notes flying before a gentle breeze in
the centre of the turnpike-road. The handkerchief was
nowhere to be seen, and it is believed that some person
had found it, and supposing its contents to be only pieces
of valueless paper, had contented himself with what he
considered the only thing worth having.
ALLEGED DISCoVERY LN ELEOTRICITY.—The Man-
cluster Guardian states, on what it considers to be most
respectable authority, that a wonderful discovery has
recently been made in electricity as applicable to pur-
poses of the electric telegraph Incredible as it may
seem, it is said that experiments have established the.
fact that intelligible signals can be exchanged between
distant stations without the intervention of any artificial
conductor whatsoever, and with equal success whether
the intervening space be wholly or partially land or
water.'

articles.title: LATE GALES.
articles.text:
THE LATE GALES.

SHIELDX.

Several vessels that have been missing since thesale
have cast up within the past two or three days, among
which may be mentioned the Rosa, the Ann and
Elizabeth, the Clarendon, the Elizabeth, the Lord
Seaton, and the Agility; The Catherine Hannah, and
the George Clark and Nlary Clark have got into ports in
Norway. To the surprise of every one the Austrian
barque the Franciska Maria, which was towing up from
Scotland light at the time the gale came ()n, and which
was abandoned by the steamboat off the Fern Islands,
and for the safety of which every one had given up
hoping, has been towed into the harbour, having been
picked up by a Tyne steamer knocking about at sea.
he Italian brig Nueva 'Elisa has also arrived in the
Tyne, having on board the crew of the Fergus, of New-
burgh. The Fergus, which was bound from Hamburgh
for Shields in ballast, was during the late gale struek in
raidships by a heavy sea, thrown on her beam-ends, and
completely disabled. The crew, after clinging to the
wreck for three days, were rescued from their perilous
position by the captain and crew of the brig at great
risk to themselves. The Margaret Knight, belonging to
Blyth, is lost, and has drowned all her crew but two.
There is every reason to fear that a new iron steam
screw collier, of 800 tons burden, the Addison Potter,
which sailed from the Tyne the morning before the gale,
somewhat deeply laden with coals for Hamburg, has
foundered and drowned all hands. She. had a crew of
seventeen hands, and she has never been heard of since
she left the Tyne. There is every reason to fear that
she went down in the terrible night of the 20th of
October. There are three or four laden collier brigs
missing, and of their safety also there is but little hope.
Tht Port Mulgrave, iron screw • steamer, belonging to
Messrs. Palmer, of Jarrow, which was stranded upon
Souter Point in a fog this week, while on her passage
from Rosedale, in Cleveland, with a cargo of iron ore for
the Tyne, is likely to become a total wreck. She ap-
pears to be breaking up.
It will be about a week yet before a complete list of
wrecks of vessels belonging to this port can be made up.

articles.title: THE- NORTH SE.A.
articles.text:
THE- NORTH SE.A.

On Friday the screw steamer Panther, Captain Rutter,
belonging to Messrs. Brownlow and Co., arrived at Hull,
from Cronstadt, after a very, heavy passage of twenty-
two days, the Panther having sailed from Cronstadt on
the 11th of October. During the course of the voyage
she was obliged to run into Cuxhaven for provisions
and coals, and left that port on the 29th ult. Captain
Rutter reports that it was heartrending to see the num-
ber of vessels either already on or driving towards the
coast of Jutland, as, owing to the nature of the coast,
most of the hands must have been lost. A large barque
let go two anchors when near the Panther with 100
fathoms to each. She rode gallantly for some time, but
the force of the hurricane was such that, before long,
she dragged both anchors, drifted on to the shore, and
every soul on board perished. A report spread on shore
next morning that some of the hands were to be seen in
the rigging, and a Cuxhaven steamer went out, notwith-
standing the heavy sea, but no trace of a living being
could be found.

AN INCIDENT AT NIAGARA.—Luna Island is, as I
have said, on the very verge of the Falls, and was the
scene of a fearful accident in 1849. A family from
Buffalo were at the Falls in June of that year; they had
been enjoying an evening's ramble upon Luna Island,
and were about leaving it when a young man of the party
playfully seized one of the children, the little daughter
A Mr. D., and held her over the edge of the river as it
raced by, exclaiming, lam going to throw you in.'
The child, hfrigtened at the sight of the rushing water,
sprang from his hold and fell into the stream. With a
cry of horror the young man threw himself after her to
save her, and in another moment they were both carried
over the Falls before the very eyes of the wretched
parents of the little girl. Their bodies were discovered
some days after the accident, which is not always the
case with those who have met with the same awful
death. The celebrated American jumper, Sam Patch,
jumped into Niagara River once too often. In 1829 he
leaped it from a height of 125 feet; he never rose, and
his body was never. found.—Bentley's Miscellany.
A deep gloom at present hangs over the town of Win-
canton (says the Salisbury Journal), two of the leading
medical men of the place having, by an extraordinary
coincidence' been summoned from their sphere of use-
fulness by death, Within twelve hours
.of each other.
Mr. Bruorton, who for upwards of thirty years practised
here, died on Thursday morning, after a painful illness
of between two and three years' duration, borne with
truly Christian fortitude and resignation to the Divine
will. And at mid-day, Mr. Eastmenth, his senior in
practice (who but a few hours before was at the bedside
of his dying friend), was seized with a fatal illness,
which terminated his life in less than two hours. By
these sad events not only have their families been
plunged into the deepest afiliction, but their friends and
neighbours have been deprived of two of the best men
and most skilful practitieners, while the poor have 'lost
friends to whom they never applied in vain, whether for
medical advice or pecuniary help.
LORD BROUGHAM ON THE GLASGOW MURDER CASE.
—The quarterly epistle of. Lord. Brougham to the Earl
of Radnor, published in the Law _Magazine, refers to
various subjects of interest relatieg to the administra-
tion'of the law; and in advocating the principle that
accused persons should be allowed to offer -theiaselves
for examination, he alludes to the Sandyford murder
case, which has recently excited so much general
intereet. He characterises the agitation upon the sub-
ject as a scandal, and remarks that Jessie M‘Lachla.n
would have desired to be examined, and that her sifted
testimony would either have led-to an acquittal or con-
•firmed the verdict: in 'either case the public mind
would have been satisfied. As it is the woman has been
convicted of murder, and, though sentence of death is
not to be carried into execution, she has not received a
pardon, though the respite was granted on the ground
of the doubt which exists as to her guilt. Lord
Brougham considers that the only objection urged
against the proposed extension of the Evidence Act—
that any party declining to be examined would be sup-
posed to be guilty for that reason—would be entirely
removed by the judge's explanation.to the jury.
CHILD STEALING AND .CHILD SELLING.—PymouTH,
Monday.—Messrs. Green's ship Vernon arrived in
Plymouth Sound on Sunday afternoon, en route foe
Sydney. On her arrival she was 'boarded by George,
Peake' a cattle-drover, of 38, Clayton-street, Caledonian_
road, London who Charged . two Scotch ladies, Mrs.
Maria Sutherland and Mrs. Sarah Stewart, with hlvine
stolen his child, a fine little boy twenty months old'.
The child and the ladies came on shore, and to day
(Monday.) the case came before the sitting magistrates
at the Plymouth Guildhall, when the ladies proved that
they advertised for a child to adopt in the Clerkenwell
News, had forty-two answers, and selected the com-
plainant's child, 'for which they paid £3 to his wife, with
nis knowledge, and that he had since, on his arrival on
board the Vernon at . Plymouth, attempted to induce
them to give him £3O more, for which he was willing to
resign all claims to the.child. This they refused to give
on account of his having made the matter public on
board the ship. The child was given up to the man, and
the ladies dismissed.

• RIGHTS OF BELLIGERENTS AT SEA. —At a Special
meeting of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, held
on the 3rd, some discussion took place upon the above
subject, in connection with the presentation of a report
upon the recent visit of a deputation to Manchester to
bear Mr. Cobden's address. The system of seizing
neutral property when on board belligerent ships was
yery severely condemned, and the seizure of the property
on beard the Emily Farnham and the Tonawanda pro-
minently pointed, out as being acts of , great injustice,
particularly the demand made for. a bond upon the cargo
of the latter vessel, which was almost exclusively
British, and the permission given to the ship to proceed
on a cartel, to carry the prisoners of one of the bellige-
rents. The following resolutions, after considerable
discussion were agreed to .—Moved by Mr. Campbell
That the Secretary convey the thanks of the council to
the MancheAer Chamber of Commerce for the Opportu-
nity given to its members to be present on the -oee..sion
of Mt'. Cobden's address to that, chamber on belligerent
rights at sea, and to assure the Manchester Chamber oi
the readiness of the council to co-operate with them in
urging this subject upon the attention of the chambers
of commerce throughout the kingdom,
_and also upon
the attention of the Legislature.' Moved by Mr..
Patterson That.a special committee he appointed 'to
meet on Wednesday next to consider the questions that
have arisen and may arise with regard to the seizure and
destruction or seizure mid release and ransom of British
property by a belligerent cruiser, and especially to report
upon the propriety of communicating with her Majesty's
Government with reference bitereto.'

DURHAIL—The Right Rev. Dr. Baring, Bishop of
following circular to the
Durham, has addressed the
clergy of his diocess :—Auckland Castle, Oct. 27. 'Rev.
..-
and dear Sir,—The increasing distress in the cotton
manufacturing districts, and the 01emplary patience
with which the operatives have hitherto borne their
sufferings, demand the hearty sympathy and liberal aid
of all classes throughout our country. lam aware that
in many parishes in my diocess collections have already
been made for die relief of the distressed artisans; but
as in others the clergy may be waiting for a request
from their Bishop before they invite the assistance of
their flocks, I do not any longer delay to ask that, if
you have not hitherto done so, you will have a collection
for this charitable object upon some Sunday before
Christmas. The amount of the collection can be paid
by check or through any local bank, either'to Mr. J. W.
Machin, Hon. Secretary of the Central Executive
' Committee, Town-hall, Manchester; or to the Right
lion. the. Lipid Mayor, Mansion-house, London, E.Q.

articles.text:
THE REGISTRAR - G ANER 'r 8 1?E-
T URN AND THE DISTRASS IN
LAN CA SHIRE.

The Registrar-General's return of marriages, Births,.
and deaths for -the quarter has just been issued. It
comprises the births and deaths registered by 24199
registrars in all the districts of England during the
summer quarter that ended on September 30, 1862.;
and the marriages in 12,665 churches or chapels,
about 4,672 registered places of worship unconnected
with the Established Church, and 6.37 superintendent-
registrar's offices, in the quarter that ended on lone
30, 1862. Marriages were not numerous in the spring
quarter of this year, During a period of eighteen
months, embracing the whole of 186-1 and the earlier
half of the current year, the marriage rate was low,
and the concluding three months exhibited a remark-
able inactivity of .the rate at which new families are
formed. But the birth-rate was well maintained in
the last summer quarter, and in each quarterly period
during the last eighteen months children were born in
a number exceeding the average. It is still more
satisfactory to add that the health of last summer was
unusually good. The death-rate has not risen above
its average 'in any quarter of the year since June, in
1860.

•
MARRIAGES.—The total number of marriages in the
spring quarter of 1860 was nearly 44,000; in that of
1861 it was about 42,000; and in the same quarter of
the present year it fell to 40,771. The annual marriage-
rate in the spring quarter of this year—viz., persons
married to a hundred in the population—was 1-610.
This proportion is lower than any result obtained in
the same season during an extended series of years, for
in the ten years 1852.61 it fell to its lowest point,
which was 1-638, in 1856; and the average of the
whole series is 1.709. It maybe remembered that a
decree- e of marriages in the cotton manufacturing cliff-
tricts in the first quarter of the year was mentioned in
the last quarterly report. In the three spring quarters,
of 1860-2 (ending 30th June) the marriages in Cheshire
numbered respectively 993, 941, 017; those in Lanca-
shire in the same times were 6,331, 6,126, and 5,484.
By comparing the marriages in both counties, the
number in last spring with the mean of the number in
two preceding springs it is found that the decrease is
equal to 12.4 per cent. By a similar mode of arm-

prison the next greatest- decrease occurred in the
Eastern Counties, Essex, Suffolk, and Norfolk, where
it was 9 9 per cent. Sussex may be mentioned as an
example of a single county in which there was a de-
crease of equal amount. The decrease in Monmouth-
shire and Wales was 6.4 per cent.; in Yorkshire it
was 4.1. The Northern Counties also show a decrease,
but it was less.than 1 per. cent. London stands alone
in the eleven divisions as presenting an example of
increase, but as this was only 1 per cent. in an ever
growing population the marriage-rate even in the
metropolis was not unusually brisk. The decrease in
the marriages of all England was 5 2 per cent.; and it
may be inferred from the above facts that a large por-
tion of that class of the population by which families
are established did not consider that their circumstances
justified the foiltnation of fresh alliances. Lancashire
in its season of calamity has borne,witness 'to the
operation of a law of prudence which has not been
without its effect in most of the other parts of the
kingdom.
BIRTHS.—The total number of births in the quarter
that ended 30th September was 172,237. It showed
an increase of 4,427 above the mean of two previous
summer quarters (1860-1). The birth-rate was 3.356
per cent, of the population, against an average of
3.285 in ten corresponding quarters in (1852-61). In
Cheshire and Lancashire the numbersof 'children born
in three summer quarters were 25,691 in 1860; 27,184
in 1861; and 27,984 in 1862. The last number, as
compared with the mean of the' two previous numbers,
represents an excess of 5.9 per cent. This increase is
higher than that shown by any other of the groups of
counties distinguished as the Eleven Divisions.'
INCREASE OF POPTILATION.—The excess of births
over deaths •in the last quarter was 80,012. The
natural increase of the population was therefore at the
rate of 870 daily. As the stream rises, part of it over-
flows into other regions of the globe. The number of
emigrants to all parts who left ports in the United
Kingdom where there are emigration officers, in the
three months that ended 30th September, was 33,240 ; •
and in this -number the 'English emigrants may be
stated approximately as 12,866. The emigration to the
Australian colonies has much increased; the English,
Irish, Scotch, and others who went thither last quarter
was 12,071; in either of the two previous summers
they were little more then 7,000. British North
America alsodrew a larger company. The number who
sought the United States was 14,170, the number in the
same quarter of 1860 having been 21,104, and in that
of the following year 6,348. Of the 22,866 English
who emigrated about 5,255 went to the United States,
and 6,536 to the Australian colonies.
PRICES AND PAUPERISM. The average price of
Consols was 93k; it has been above 93 in 'the four
quarters that have elapsed since September of last
year. Wheat (the average price 565. 10d. per quarter)
was dearer than in the same period, of last year, when
the price was 525. Id. The average of the highest and
lowest prices of beef at Leadenhall and Newgate was
bid: per 111,And of mutton 50. Best potatoes were
115 s. per Lou; they were dearer than they had been at
the same time, last year. The return of the Poor Law
Commissioners are heavy for the summer quarter. The
increase of pauperism' is seen in the following state-
ment, which shows the quarterly average of poor persons
relieved on the first day of each week: Quartcr
ending. 30th September, 1860---in-door 101,680, out-
door 667,680; ditto, 1861 in-door 112,932, out-
door 693,649; ditto, 1862 —in-door, 119,592, out-door,
789,914.

articles.title: WiLLS AN_D BEQUESTS.
articles.text:
WiLLS AN_D BEQUESTS.

The will of Owen Wethered, Esq., of Remnantz, Great
Marlow, Bucks, who died in May last in. Cumberland-
street, llEyde Park, was proved in London under £60,000
personalty, the executors nominated being the testator's
brothers, the Rev. F. J. Wethered, M.A., vicar of Hurley,
Berks, and Lawrence W. Wethered,.Esq., and his (the
testator's) sons, Thos. Owen Wethered und Owen Peel
Wethered, Esqrs. The will is of considerable length,
and was executed, with a codicil, in June, 1861, and a
second codicil in February, 1862. The dispositions are
confined to the members of his family. To his wife he
has secured an annuity of £1,500, and has left her an im-
mediate legacy of £l,OOO, and has also bequeathed to her
a life interest in certain estates, which latter property,
upon her decease, is to pass to their eldest son. The
rest of of his estate, real and personal, is to be divided
amongst his children. To each of his younger sons a
legacy of .£lO,OOO is bequeathed, and to each daughter
£7,000. The ultimate residue he laves to his three sons,
amongst whom he has distributed his stock of wine. The
testator expresses a wish that his business of a brewer
should be continued by his son, iiv partnership with his
(the testator's) brother Lawrence.

A 'SHARK FOUND IN THE ,KENT.—On Friday after-
noon last a young.man of the name of Dover dragged
from the river Kent, near Nether -Bridge, at the
southern extremity of the town, a young shark. It was
found at the bottom of the river, and he drew it out of
the wfor by means of click-hooks. It measured five
feet in length, from snout to tail, and was dead when
taken out of the river. During Saturday it was exhi-
bited in the Mechanics' Hall, and afterwards sold to Dr.
Gough, for the Kendal Museum. The shark had, three
rows of teeth, and had, several bruises on its body.
There are various conjectures as to low it got into the
Kent; some think that it had been blown and frightened
out d its latitude, by the late storms, into Morecombe
Bay, from whence it had entered the mouth of the Kent
at the head of the bay, and ascended the river, where it
perished.
THE FENS.—In connection with the recent disaster
at the Marshland Smeeth -and Fen drain, it may be
stated that the Commissioners have agreed to have adam
made across the breach, and a 'new sluice built. Mr.
Page, civil engineer, who .has been consulted by the
Commissioners, promises that the darn shall be com-
pleted in a fortnight, and that the new sluice shall also
be finished in ten weeks' from this time, and if these pre-
dictions are realised the Smeeth and Fen will,be restored
to its former position. As regards the 'Middle Level
drainage, it may be added that the nine siphons erected
have worked satisfactorily. When they were put in
operation last week for two days the water was reduced
at March-bridge, a distance of 16 .miles from the
laboriously-constructed dam, from 7ft. 91n. to 4ft. 7in.
When the other seven siphons proposed to be erected are
completed, of course the discharging power organized
will be proportionatelyincreased, and all doubt as to the
efficiency of the arrangements which Mr. Ilawkshaw
and his assistants haveably devised and carried out may
now be considered at an end. Under the powers of an
important Act of Parliamentpassed last Session, a new
Board of Commissioners is to be formed this week for
the purpose of securing the drainage of the Middle
level ; and one of the first acts of the new Board will
to borrow on mortgage the sum of £52,000. This
amount represents the injury thus far 'sustained' by the
Commission from the disasters against -which it has had
to struggle.
THE INDISIVITION OF THE DUKE OP NEWCASTLE.
—The Duke of Newcastle has quite recovered from his
recent indisposition.
THE NEW PUBLIC COMPANIES ACT.—On the.3rcl the
Public Companies Act will take effect to incorporate,
regulate, and wind up trading companies and other asso-
ciations. In 212 sections the law has been amended and
consolidated, and the rights of shareholders defined and
the liabilities of 'contributories' set forth. The

SIR ISAAC NEWTON'S HOUSE AT KENSFSGVON.—
Having identified, Sir Isaac Newton's house in 1727,
the next point to, consider -was how to prevent the
house from again being lost sight of. This may very
soon take place, without some permanent record. The
writer applied to the vestry for permission for a
memorial to Sir Isaac Newton to be placed against the
garden wall of Bullingham House. This having been
granted, it has been suggested that a chamber for
deposits should be formed underground, and to be opened.
every half century for examination, and to report or
make- additions as may then be- thought desirable, to
perpetuate Newton and his-discoveries. Photographs of
the front and other parts,. on glass, burnt in and en—
amelled, have been suggested. Sir Isaac's town house.
may then also be thus recorded,.not forgetting a piece of
the old glass, if even a square has, to be taken out for
that purpose. A slate slab has been temporarily fixed
against the-garden wall, on which a sketch for part of a
design for a memorial has been made. That has already
attracted the notice of thousands who, pass that way to
and from Kensington Gardens, through, the new passage
by the barracks.—Leisure Hour.
A ROYAL OPINION ON 'run' INCOMES OF THE
CLERGY.—' The Duke of Cumberland, heard a Mr.
Mudge, one of our angelic order (a clergym-in), who had
a most seraphic finger for the harpsichord, play him a
tune at some friendly knight or squire's house, where he
was ambushed for him on his way to-or from Scotland,
and very honestly expressed great satisfaction at the
performance. "And would your highness think," says
his friend, "that with such a wonderful talent, this
worthy clergyman has not above a hundred a year ?"
"And do you not think, Sir," replied his. highness,
"that when a priest has more it generally spoils him ?" '
—George Selwyn and his Contemporaries.
LOOTING IN DELHI.—I stuck. into a circuitous lane
near the canal, leading from the Loll Surrak 'or red
street, to the Begum Sumroo's garden (Dyce Sombre's
Begum), and selected, for my-first trial, a ruinous buffalo
dairyman,'s shed, which stood (or tottered) close by a
dirty little hut, then deserted, where one of the chief
gold-workers of the place had formerly flourished. I had
excavated for a little time without success, and with
much offence to, the narine nerve!ets—for a Delhi dairy
is not at all like a Dundreary dairy, and the flooring was,
geologically speaking, of disintegrat ed coprolite—when
an acute coolie,. whose intelligence I afterwards rewarded
with four arinas, 6,-Id over and above his lawful wages,
suggested a mine under the party-wall. It was easily
made, for the wall had no foundation, and was built of
kuccha,' or sun-dried bricks of clay, quite friable from
age. I read the English news with as much interest as
I could while my men were rooting; but I was soon
interrupted, by a heavy fall of rotten bricks, a shout
from my coolies and the apparition on the other side of
the tumbled wall of my jolly friend Pintle, of the Royal
Bengal fire. workers, mattock in hand, with his great
red cheeks, covered with dust and sudor, his khalee '
tunic dirt-coloured indeed, and wet through with per-
spiration, his whole appearance like &navvy's in a solah
topee. The rascal was a licensed digger like myself, but
he worked alone, on principle; and there were, in conse-
quence, even uglier stories about him- than about myself,
and that's saying a good deal. We cried simultaneously,
Halves with you!' and struck a partnership on the
spot. He knew Delhi better than I did, and worked, as
I afterwards found, on more scientific data; but my
sources of information were- better than his, and he
acknowledged that solitary digging was an error. The
natives began to clear away the rubbish, and while I
watched them, Pintle, pulling a small chisel out of his
pocket, tested knowingly every likely-looking brick in
the jeweller's-wall. I shouldn't' wonder at all,' he said,
as he went round tapping, if the swag were here.' Ile
had scarcely spokcn, when, by a neat wrist-turn, he
extracted a brick which was a trifle more firmly set than
its neighbours, and thrust his chisel into the cavity.
Something soft, at all events,' he whispered, peering
in eagerly.- A little scooping produced a small dirty rag
tied m& knot. I lent him a knife ;'the- rag contained
about a dozen uncut sapphires and diamonds of unques-
tionable value, and a splendid cat's eye'—one of those
gorgeous dusky orange opals with as many-changes of
coloar in different lights as a cameleon, a real talisman
stone.' We looked at each other and sighed;' there was
at least two hundred pounds' worth of gems in that rag,
and there were two of us.—Cornhill Magazine.

`Tax•Rien HOLLANDER.—No one can visit one of the
old aristocratic merchant families in Amsterdam without
perceiving theo immence advance made by the Dutch.
two centuries ago beyond any other mercantile cora-
mtmity in the world, except the Italians. Take as a
specimen the mansion of the V.— L—s, in the
Heeren Geracht. Notice the large marble flags that pave
its handsome lobbies and line their walls—the stately
rooms—the large mirrors—the soft thick carpets—the
tasteful grouping of old handsome furniture, and beauti-
ful side-tables with rare and costly china, and exquisite
filagree work in silver from Japan;. and the perfume of
choice flowers which- makes every apartment odorous.
But, above all, gaze upon those pictures that cover the
walls of the drawing-room and library. How fresh!
They seem as if they had just come from the .hands of
the painter. Exquisite flowers, with ,pearly drops of
water, by Van Huysen ; Roman scenes, by Ulft ; land-
scapes, by Both and RuiSdael ; sea pieces, by Black-
huysen ; old women, by, Gerard Dow; village scenes and
huge noses, by .osta.de ; with other masterpieces,. by Van
de Velde; Weenix,` ' Berghem and especially a magnificent
Wouvermans and Metzu. These have not been picked
up suddenly at some sale, nor are they of doubtful author-
ship; but the best of 'them, upwards of twenty, were
painted for the family, and have never been out of the
house since framed in those plain black frames, and hung-
up on their walls by the hands of the famous artists
themselves. Here, too, are two grand full-length
portraits of their ancestors, Burgomaster 5---- and his
wife, painted by Rembrandt. —Good Words.
SANGUINE MEN THE LEAST SUCCESSFUL.—III my
recollections of school and. college I remember that as
between two yauths of equal ability and ambition the
odds of success in rivalry were always in favour of the
one least sanguinely confident of succeeding. And
obviously for this reason :—He who distrusts the security
of. chance takes more pains to effect the safety which re-
sults from labour. To find what you seek in the road of
life, the best proverb of all is that which says, 'leave no
stone unturned.' As all men, however, have in their
natures a certain degree:of hope, so he is the -wisest who
husbands it with the most care. When you are engaged
in.any undertaking in which success depends partly on
I skill, partly on luck, always presuppose that the luck
may go against you for that presupposition redoubles
all•your efforts to Obtain the advantages that belong to
Hope nothing from luck, and the probability is
that you will be so prepared, forewarned and forearmed,
that all shale.* observers will call you lucky.—Sir B.
B. Lyttonin Blackwood.
THE Gun FROM THE WORKROUSE.—What have we
to shOw for the thirty thousand a year spent on the
teaching of the young in workhouses ? Instruction with-
out education. Next to nothing in the ewe of boys.
Worse than nothing in the case of girls. There the girls
are—not young criminals as in a reformatory, but simply
destitute .of means, and dependent upon those who under-
take to teach them how in after years they may earn
bread for themselves and be of some use in the world.
These children are poor without blame: they cannot
help having been born dependent upon parents unable,
whether, through misfortune or misconduct, to give them
requisite support. They cannot help their orphanhood.
Still Of the age when nature makes them dependent upon
adult help for maintenance and education into ,the futute
duties of their lives' the 'charge of them, ,dropped from
private. lands, falls into those of the guardians of the
poor. No young girl can be rightly trained into a
woman's sense of work and duty, under conditions that
exclude all part in home affections, alllperception of the
varied duties of farailylife. Where nothing is done -to
cultivate into strength wholesome affections, where wash-
ing.is done by 'machinery, where cooking is done upon a
great system having nothing in common with the pot on
the cottage fire, and.where the thriftless vicious talklof the
elder ne'er-do-wells of their sex.is common in their ears,
girls are ill bred into.th.e power of self-help. They, leave
such a place with little sober thought of becoming useful,
earnest, happy wives. they must come back as their
lives draw to a close, to live again upon the rates. The
number of girls who do"eo return is twice that of the boys
—Dickens' s the Year Round.'

RURAL WALKS IN ENGLAND.—The chief enjoyment
of my several visits to Leamington lay in rural walks
about the neighbourhood, and in jaunts to places of note
and interest, which are :particularly abundant in that
region. The high roads are made pleasant to the.tra-
yeller by a border of trees, and often afford him the hos-
pitality of a wayside bench beneath a comfortable shade.
But a fresher delight is to be found in .the footpaths,
whichgo wandering away from stile to stile, along hedges,
a
and across broad fields, and through wooded.parks, lead-
ing you to little hamlets of thatched cottages, ancient,
solitary farm-houses, picturesque old mills, streamlets,
pools, and all those quiet, secret, unexpected, -yet
strangely &milkr features of English scenery that
Tennyaon shows us in his idyls and eclogues. These
various by-paths admit the wayfarer-into the very heart
of rural life, and yet do not burden him with a sense of
intrusiveness. He has a ri:4-ht-to go whithersoever they
lead ; for, with all theirshaded privacy, theyare
.as much the .property of the public ,as the dusty high-
road itself, and even by an older tenure. Their antiquity
probably exceeds that of the Roman ways; the footsteps
of the aboriginal Britons first wore away the grass, and
.the natural flow of intercourse between village and
.village has kept the track bare ever since. An American
farmer would plough across any such path, and oblite-
rate it with his hills of potatoes and Indian corn; but
here it is protected by law, and still more by the sacred-
ness that inevitably springs up, in this soil, along the
well defined footprints of centuries.-14. W. Emerson,
in the Atlantic Monthly.

foreign grain this week have been good, of English wheat
small, and no oats. The attendance at to-day's market,
although small, included a few country buyers from a
distance; busitess was much interfered with by a dense
