SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1862.

SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

GREECE goes on without a monarch, and to
the present week has not done anything else
very remarkable. Bavaria protests that a king
should be found in its dynasty for the Greeks;
but the three principal powers, Britain, France,
and Russia decline to interfere.

These three powers will, it is said, immedi-
ately offer terms of mediation for the Northern
and Southern States, beginning with an armis-
tice, proceeding with re-opened cotton ports,
terminating with peace. Probabilities of dis-
disturbance exist in carrying out this pro-
gramme.

A British merchant ship, the Blanche, with
cotton from Mexico to Havannah, drawn pri-
marily, no doubt, from the Southern States,
intended ultimately, we have as little doubt,
for Lancashire, was chased in Spanish waters
by the Montgomery, an armed Federal ship,
and took the ground six miles from liavannah,
A Spanish Alcade boarded the ship and
hoisted the Spanish flag as the signal of pro-
tection, but the captain of the Montgomery-
went on board also, slapped the Spanish ma-
gistrate on the face, turned him on shore, and
burned the ship. A Spanish frigate went in
search of the Montgomery, but the Federal
was too quick for the Spaniard, and escaped
the latter's vengeance.

The Federal ambassador has apologised at
Madrid, and on the part of his government
disavowed the doings of the captain of the
Montgomery; but the Spanish government
require the punishment of that officer and his
men. They are more exacting than our go-
vernment, and their demand will be complied
with, for France would probably in this busi-
ness back up Spain. We have not heard that
our government have demanded the price of
the cotton and the ship, with compensation to
the owners and seamen.

From Nev Granada come gratifying reports
of the success of the Liberal party in a great
battle which we hope may terminate the con-
test for religious freedom in that republic, so
long a field of strife.

The Perm, ians have not only doubts re-
garding the acceptance of a loan made for them
here during the summer, but have badly en.:

treatei and imprisoned some English subjects,
Tor which they are likely to experience a close
Teckoning. They may deserve it, but other
people deserve it also, on whom the Civis
Romanus principle has not fallen heavily.
The Mexicans continue to organise means of
resistance to the French, who also receive
reinforcements, and have now reached the
season of campaigning in these regions.
The Federals are deep in the election move-
ments, and the Democrats beat the Republi-
cans, that is to say, the present Governmental
party, in nearly all the Northern States yet
tried, excepting New England, which many of
them propose to cut off and leave to solitude,
or perhaps a junction with British North
America.

in the cotton districts is not in any degree
improved. Other trades are in a condition of
average acEvity.

A Trades' Committee is proposed in London
to collect subscriptions for Lancashire. We
trust that it may be efficiently and soon
organised. One of our correspondents suggests
that a great part of the night and day clothing
now deficient has been pledged and might be
redeemed. A gentleman in Manchester offers
£lOO to be expended in that manner. Perhaps
a trades' committee in London might adopt the
suggestion, and provide for its accomplishment
by their correspondents in the district.
A meeting has been held in Manchester,
with the hope of reviving the movement for
complete reform. The measure is required
by the suffering of the time. Famine is
present, fever is threatened, because the Go-
vernment and the Legislature long neglected a '
clear duty. The productive classes need an in-
dustrial policy and means of enforcing it. The
nation has lived under a mercantile middle-
class policy for years, and the end in a county
with two millions of population is riches to
speculators famine to operatives.
The examination of Mr. Stiffe, before the
Bankruptcy Court on Tuesday, brought out
the facts that on the Morning Chronicle in three
years OEII,OOO were lost; and that the Weekly
Ttines from its reduction to one penny had
been "a disastrous loss."

Mr. John Van Buren, a son of the former
President, Van Buren, said, at New York,
that the application of President Lincoln's
proclamation on slavery would justify the in-
tervention of foreign nations.
The meeting cheered this opinion. So there
is one purpose for which the Democrats would
tolerate foreign intervention.
Bragg, the Confederate General, has eva-
cuated Kentucky through Cumberland Gap,
carrying off immense trains of provisions,
captured or purchased in that State. Buell,
the Federal General, who should have inter-
cepted him ,has been superseded, and Rosen-
crauz, who successfully defended Corinth, has
his place. Buell appears to have been defeated
at Perrysville, and Bragg retained 1,200 pri-
soners on the first, and 7,200 prisoners on the
second days' fighting._ _

The precise sum is not given, but is only
described as "disastrous," although inciden-
tally the fact crops out that £l,BOO were lost
on forty publications of the paper, or £45 on
each No., yet at twopence the profits were £4O
per week.

Corinth, from Nvhich after two days' of hard
strife, the Confederates, under Van Dorn, were
repulsed by the Federals, has been abandoned
by the latter. The Confederates have also
changed the leader under whom they were re-
pulsed from Corinth, for some other person
deemed more skilful.

- On this " established " journal, therefore,
£B5 per week were sacrificed, from a selfish
desire to suppress all other weekly papers.

DISTRESS.

the absorption of all other committees, in making
a national effort to relieve the famine, and all
its results, in our manufacturing districts; want-

necessarily contemplates Manchester as the

scheme. Manchester has not a good title to
the position in this national effort, claimed for

The European Continent furnishes few re-
markable occurrences for the week. The medical
consultation on Garibaldi's case has given a
favourable report, and he expects to be here in
March next.

The Chinese intelligence is gloomy-. A Ma-
hommedan insurrection has been successful
in one region, and the leaders hold twenty-five
towns. The Taeping-wangites have disap-
peared from the neighbourhood of Shanghae,
but they had formed a plan to seize Canton,
which, although discovered, has caused a con-
sternation among the mandarins, and suspen-
ded trade.

A deputation of Circassian Chiefs have
arrived in this country to plead their cause
against Russia. Lord John Russell has
written his incapacity to interfere in favour
of their nationality, and the people are in-
vited to consider the Circassian wrongs. A
Manchester meeting has resolved that Cir-
cassia deserves help, but there are difficulties
in the way. Can we undertake another
Euxine war? Russia struggles for a road
onward, southward, through Circassia, and can
only be repelled by force. Interference by
protests or protocols is useless with Russia,
which only bends to moral when backed by
physical force.

An organization connected with the Trades
of the metropolis, and other towns, is also de-
sirable, both for the collection and expendi-
ture of money, and we have referred to that
matter in another column. The advantages of
a central committee are not equal to the dis-
couragements it might inflict on local exer-
tions, if decisive control were assumed by its
members; and for all good objects a London
committee is decidedly preferable to one in
Manchester, exposed to those local differences
that will occasionally mar even a charitable
work.

BRITAIN, THE STATES, AND THEIR
STRUGGLES.

TIIE former report that the EMPEROR
NAPOLEON will interfere in the hostilities of
the Northern and Southern States revives. He
does not, according to rumour, desire to
monopolise the honour of settling this quarrel,
but requires the co-operaion of Britain and
Russia. An armistice is the present project,
and during the suspension of fighting, negotia-
tions would be tried. In the interval NA-
POLEON would extricate his tobacco from the
stores of Richmond, Virginia. One or more
ports would also be opened for the cotton trade.
('his is the programme announced by letters
from Paris, but the correspondents do not say
that it has been adopted by Britain or Russia.
Although some step of this nature has been or
probably will be followed; yet we cannot
offer any sanguine opinion of its success.
The plan will go to the hearts, and through
the hearts, of the active party in this country,
who run the entire length with the Govern-
ment of Washington, accepting the whole of
the animal, bristles and tusks, all in one lot,
as a very proper value for blood, slaughter,
war interminable, a desolating war. We have
heard that members of this credulous party do
4,0 t even consider us sound on slavery, and
such odds, ends, shackles, and trammels, con-
nected therewith as their Federal friends clung
to with a tenacity that would have been ad-
mirable in a better work. Errors of this kind
always occur. When enthusiasts get on a
hobby they ride as beggars de...on horseback, in
the same direction towards a personage who
may be nameless, and we confess to an utter
abhorrence of that road.
We cannot even stretch to'the magnitude of
the cosmopolitanism of our times. It is very
amiable doubtless in appearance, but everybody
cannot reach to its mark of transcendentalism.
We love all mankind, as in duty bound, and
the good of our own people a little over. It is
a weakness, but all vessels have not the same
capacity. For these large measures any ma-
terial will do, if it be cheap, ash or earthen
ware; for more limited purposes, men reserve
the finer crystal or the precious metals.
A sovereign may be spread out to cover a
perfectly cosmopolitan breadth and length, but
the thin leaf will only hide dirt, dust, and
rotten timber, and give no clear and useful
sound. It will want the ring of the concen-
trated little sovereign, and not possess itsl
use.

The cosmopolitanism that goes forth with the
same intensity of feeling in favour of all the
earth mistakes men's mission, men's responsi-
bilities; and the way to improve the world.
Christianity was to be preached to all nations,
but the preachers were to begin at Jerusalem,
A Alan is bound to help his neighbours, al-
though, men generally, overlook the duty; but
he is primarily bound to provide for his own
household. Even so we are all called upon to
oppose slavery as an evil, a sin, and a wrong,
unworthy of our times; but we are all more
responsible to provide against domestic starva-
tion. We regret the horrible sacrifices of
human life in Dahomey by a Pagan king, but
we are all in this country more concerned with
the many deaths happening daily from preventi-
ble causes in our country, and especially in our
large towns. Local responsibility and work
are the guarantees for the genedal good and
prosperity.
Nothing is easier than general talking of the
interests of mankind, but it is not nearly so
efficient as working for the parish, the city, the
country, the nation to which one belongs, yet
neglecting .no opportunity that may offer of
"helping mankind."
With this opinion of general duty we confess
guiltless of any sorrow at the possible formation
of two i epublics out of the once -United States.
The selfishness of Northern politicians has out-
raged all ideas of free trade, by taxes on British
manufactures, that are almost prohibitive, not
alone for revenue, but avowedly to bolster up
artificial trading; and as avowedly to strike
down the wages and work of British operatives;
and we prefer to the triumph of Federal poli-
ticians, the comfort and employment of our
working classes. The politicians of the Northern
States want to annex Canada, New Brunswick,
and Nova Scotia, and to preserve the Southern
States in union, for the purpose of forming a
Zolverein under one Government, which would
exclude British and other European manu-
factures from the American continent, except
on the payment of duties that are a robbery.
The British provinces will not assent to this
compulsory partnership; and if the Southern
States establish their independence, the main-
tenance of extravagant duties on our produc-
tions will become impossible, in any one of the
North American divisions, and so we have no
cause to mourn over the de facto division, even
if it become a de jure division of the union.
But would we promote free trade at the cost
of preserviug slavery? Assuredly not, for we
do not belong to the party in this country who
repealed the discriminative duties between free
and slave-grown sugars, in the interest, they
said, of free trade. The same men now pro-
mote, as far as possible, the cause of the
Northern States, in order, they say, to suppress i
slavery, at the cost of free trade. This pro.
ceeding is 'among political phenonvita, Only
intelligible to those persons who know how the
shares and stocks of the Northern States are
held in Britain. Many honest enthusiasts
hold none of these securities, and would not be
influenced by self-interest, but among those
who pull the wires, a majority will be found
to be deep in Illinois Shares and such other
things.
The alteration of our policy on the sugar
duties has caused an annual importation ever
since of twenty-five thousand negroes to Cuba
and slavery. We can redress that error with-
out a war. Let us, therefore, get out the beam
from our own eyes, and we will see more clearly
to help our neighbours.
Man proposes but GOD disposes, Southern
Propose a slave republic. It
politicians may
is a horrible inconsistency, and it will not
stand. If the Southern men are ever inde-
pendent and commence to work their system,
they must take down board by board, stone by
stone, and gradually give the negroes a home
and interest in the soil. They have not towards
the negroes that antipathy displayed in t:iose
Northern and Western States that refuse a

home to the black labourer, and from the day
On which they first feel that slavery is im-
possible, they will, for personal and selfish

reason, consent to the conversion of the negroes
into flee labourers and peasants.

MR. BRIGHT AND MR. BUXTON.

Mr. BRIGHT says that every man in Europe
who is not a foe to freedom applauds Presi-
dent LINCOLN'S proclamation; but this is only
saying to every man in Europe, " if you do
not agree with my opinion you are a foe to
freedom ;" and doubtless all the friends of the
ten hours factory bill, and the mining bill,
and the bleaching bill; and all those who
opposed, as we opposed at the time, the cruel
policy that for a farthing or a half-penny per
lb. on the price of sugars, has plunged two
hundred and fifty thousand native Africans
into Cuban chains or graves, having differed ,
from Mr. BRIGHT, were "foes
.to freedom."'
We shall not discuss the assertion farther, as
it respects men in Europe, but we have
' expressed our doubts regarding the character
of President LINCOLN'S proclamation; although
not in the bitter language in which it has
been denounced in the IN orthern States by Mr.
LORD GARRISON, whom we have known to be
a suffering friend of negro freedom for twenty
years; by Mr. WENDELL PHILLIPS, we under -
stand, who is the political leader of the
Northern Abolitionists; by Mr. BEECHER
STOWE, from his clerical platform; arid by Dr.
CHEEVER, from his pulpit.
We trust that the friendship of these men
for negro freedom is not disputed in Rochdale.
Each of them has suffered for the cause, and as
they must know their own country better than
our politicians, we take shelter from, this accu-
sation in their testimony.
But Mr. BRIGHT should read the papers.
He would learn from them that the North will
not consent to the policy avowed by Mr.
LINCOLN in his proclamation. Even in this
hour of peril the democratic party have had
large majorities during the October elections
of Indiana and Ohio, have irnproTed their
position in Pennsylvania and other Northern
States, and expected yesterday to carry New
York. Their " platform " contains a denun-
ciation of President LINCOLN'S proclamation,
and a refusal to abide by its terms.
Illinois declares that no more negroes shall
cross its frontier; lowa, that rejects the de-
mocratic and votes the republican ticket, will
not permit a negro to live on its lands; and
even Kansas, that was considered the battle-
field of freedom, rejects the poor negro, and
will not allow him l to labour and live on its
soil.

What can be hoped for in these circum-
stances better for freedom than a split of the
States; for when "all is over," boundaries
declared, and frontiers defined, and the quarrel
so far settled, the South may hope to live on
slavery, and yet learn a truism, that twenty-
six millions of whites may profitably keep four
millions of slaves ; but to eight millions the
possession can only be a perpetual loss, and
waste of strength, and therefore, in the pre-
sence of a jealous rival, in the North, they
must make haste to rear a coloured peasantry
out of a population of slaves.
Mr. Buxton is a higher authority than Mr.
Bright on the subject of slavery, and Mr.
Buxton on Wednesday said, "I am unable to
discover that this is a war with slavery ;"
adding, "President Lincoln's proclamation is
not an abolition of slavery." We leave Mr.
Bright to arrange with Mr. Buxton.

articles.title: CABNIENS' DELEGATES.
articles.text:
THE CABNIENS' DELEGATES.

TO TIIE EDITOR OF THE "BEE-HIVE."

Stu,--The delegates have got over the first portion of
their task, which they have accomplished in a praise-
worthy and painstaking manner, highly creditable to
their zeal and intelligence. On Wednesday laq, the
clauses they have adopted as amendments on those
contained in the present Hackney Carriage Act, after
having undergone consideration and discussions at
the various district meetings, where sonic verbal
alterations only were suggested, were finally passed,
and a sub-committee appointed to prepare them in
a proper shape to be submitted to the aggregate
meeting of drivers, which, I am glad to bear, is
about to be called on an early day, in a central
part of the metropolis. There is one hopeful thing
about the movement of these hitherto persecuted and
much abused class of mer, and that is, it is evidently
an earnest one, entered upon in the face of much op-
position and ridicule, but carried out in such a calm
and business-like manner, as to disarm all its oppo-
nents and convert many of them into firm friends. To
the surprise of the public, the cabman, instead of
being, as he was supposed to be by many, and
said to be by some who should have known
better, an " indomitable beast," has turned
out to be as good a specimen of humanity as "any
other man" in the same class of life, and endowed
with similar human feelings, ideas, and intelligence.
I speak of them in the same sense as did "the
unworthy son of a worthy sire," when in the
columns of his paper he called them by a brutish
name; I speak of them as a body, not wishing to
conceal the fact that there are, as in all other
glasses and grades of society, badly-conducted men
amongst them. Another cause for congratulation
lies in the fact that many influential proprietors in
the cab trade have expressed their entire opproval
of the proceedings of the men, and promised them
every as.istance. Much, however, yet remains to be
done before the condition of the cabmen can be
permanently improved. Although the delegates
have done much, and dolie that well, their actual
work has only commenced. The arrangements for
their aggregate meeting to petition for Parliamen
tary inquiry into their grievances, a necessary step
before an amended act is likely to I) e brought
into the House, and the arrangement of the evi-
dence, and by whom to be given, before that
committee, will rNuire constant attention; and
the raising the funds to meet the expenses connected
with this work must also engross the attention of
the delegates. These matters must all be weir
considered by the sub-committee that has been
appointed, and put into a proper shape to be !aul
before the body of delegates at their next meeting.
These delegates have up to this time done their
work so well, I cannot suppose for a moment
that they will prove themselves unequal to the
task still before them.

In connexion with magisterial cab law, an instruc-
tive case has just occurred. My readers will re-
collect a r-port inserted about a fortnight since,
and which was commented upon last week. A cab
driver was summoned before Mr. Maude, at South-
wark police cow t, for leaving his cab unattended in.
the station yard of the South Eastern Etailway, and
also for refusing to take a fare. The defence set up
by Mr. Smith, the Secretary of the South London
Cabmen's Club, was, that the railway station was not
a "place of public resort," within the meaning of
the Act, and that the driver paid the company a
weekly sum for the privilege of standing on their
premises. The magistrate, however, decided against
this view, and fined the driver Os. and costs, which
was paid. One day this week Mr. &nth received
notice from the police office to call and receive the
20s. and costs back again, as the magistrate had
since found out lie was not authorised by the Act in
convicting! Mr. Smith replied he was quite willing
to take back the money, but as the conviction and
fine took place in open court, and was reported in the
press, he should expect the acknowledgement of the
error in conviction, and return of the fine, to be as
publicly made. I believe this will be done.
Cheer up, Ctibby, "There is a good time coming."
November 6th, 1862. R. HARTWELL.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

SECOND EDITION.-SATURDAY MORNING.

ITALY.

TURIN, Nov. 6, (Evening.)
The Italian Government has addressed remonstrances
to the Prussian Envoy, who represents Austria at this
Court, upon the encounter between Italian carabineers
and Austrian soldiers upon the right bank of the Po.

MILAN, Nov. G.
The King reviewed the troops here to-day. Large
crowds of spectators were present, and the popular
enthusiasm ran very high.

Rots, Nov. 1.
Mgr. de Merode has disbanded the small remnant of
the Irish Volunteers called the Legion of St. Patrick,
which was already reduced to some twenty men. It
was very absurd to see them swaggering about the
streets of Rome in a gaudy uniform.

articles.title: SPAIN.
articles.text:
SPAIN.

MADRID, Nov. 5.
It has been decided in an extraordinary Council of
Ministers that the Spanish Government shall demand
the punishment of the Americans who have violated
the Spanish flag.

GREECE.
THE GREEK REVOLUTION.

PARIS, NOV. 5.
_La France of this evening contains letters from
Athens of the 28th ult., which state :--‘ The Provi-
sional Government is favourable to a monarchy, but a
very powerful Republican party wishes to establish a.
Federal State, endeavours to agitate the adjacent
Turkish provinces, and to raise Epirus and Macedonia.
It is not impossible that this party may obtain a majo-

NEW YORK, Oct. 25, Evening.
The Confederates have been routed at Pea Ridge,
Ar kansas, with loss of artillery and camp equipage.

INDIA, CHINA, AND AITSTRALIA..
REVOLT OF THE MAHOMEDANS.

SHANGHAI, Sept 19 (via Jubal).
The Tapeings have again retired from the vicinity
of this city, and the surrounding country is now quiet..
The Mahomedans who revolted at Shensi have suc—
ceeded in capturing the city and twenty-five towns in
the vicinity, killing all the mandarins, and destroying
every vestige of the Imperial authority. Nothing is
known respecting the movements of the army whick
had been sent to quell the outbreak.
CANTON, Sept. 26.
A serious conspiracy to burn this city and kill the
mandarins has been discovered. The conspirators are
in league with the Taepings. Numbers of them have
been arrestea. The city authorities are in a state of
great alarm. Rustonjee, one of the parties concerned
in the late 6pium frauds, has surrendered himself to.
the authorities at Hong Kong.

DlELBotrami, Sept. 25.
The gold fields recently discovered at Dustan (?)
have turned out a failure. The total shipments of gold
since the departure of the last mail amount to 100,750,
ounces.

ADELAIDE, Sept. 20.
Air. Mackinlay, the explorer, has returned to•
Queensland.

articles.text:
THE 8.41172 C NOTE FORG_ERIES.

On Thursday evening another man, named Henry
Williams, an engraver, of 85, St. Paul's-road, Ken-
nington, was taken into custody, on the charge of
being concerned in the engraving of the copper-plate
used in the forgeries.
On Friday the six prisoners, George Buncher,
Robert Cummings, William Barnett, Richard Brewer,.
James Griffiths, and Henry Williams, were placed in.
the dock, at the Mansion House, for re-examination.
On the last examination a young man named Henry
Brown, who had been employed at the mills at Laver-
stock, from whence the paper was stolen, was ex-
amined, and he proved that he had abstracted at,
different times a quantity of the genuine Bank note
paper, and he alleged that the prisoner Brewer' who.
was also employed upon the mills, was concerned with
him and had a guilty knowledge in the transaction.
His evidence also went to show that the other prisoners
were concerned in the affair. There were other wit-
nesses in attendance yesterday to confirm the evidence.
of the witness Brown, and another remand twit place.

GAME LAW RIOT AT BLACKBURN:

On Thursday eight men Swore charged before the
Blackburn magistrates with night poaching, of whom,
three were committed to prison. The court was
crowded during the trial, and the sentence was re-
ceived with loud groans ar.d hisses. When the
keepers left the hall, they were met by a vast crowd.,
of persons, who hooted them. A body of police came
to their aid, and acted as an escort; but before they
had gone 200 yards they were compelled to take
refuge, the crowd stoning them as they passed along
The keepers after a while were removed to the Town
Hall, whence they were conveyed home under the
cover of darkness. The mob, largely reinforced, at
five o'clock commenced smashing the windows of the,
Town Hall and Police-office and other buildings. A.
large force of special constables were sworn in, and.
the riot act read, but the disturbance still continued.
The military were telegraphed for, and at a late hour
on Thursday night a body of cavalry entered the
town.

articles.title: TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE IRON SHIP-BUILDING DISPUTE.

We have received the following letter respecting this
unfortunate dispute :
TO THE EDITOR OE THE BEEHIVE.
SlR,—Being in company, on Saturday, with several
influential men in connection with both wood and iron
Ship-building, I find the struggle between the two trade
societies likely to terminate in favour of the rightful
owners of the iron trade, viz., the iron ship-builders. I
have three proofs in favour of the iron men. In the
first place, Messrs. Wigram, of Blackwall-yard, find-
ing themselves defeated by the iron ship-builders keep-
ing away from their ship-building yard, and having a
first-class iron ship to build for the Peninsular and
Oriental Royal Mail Steam Company (the men they
employ being mostly wooden ship-builders and
labourers who have worked with iron ship builders)
they have contracted with Messrs. Westwood, Bailey,
and Co., London yard, Isle of Dogs, to do that part
of the ship the wooden shipbuilders are not capable of
doing. The wooden shipbuilders say they cia build
iron ships superior to the iron shipbuilders. Then the
iron shipbuilders say, why not the wooden shipbuilders
begin the ship and complete it themselves?' That
they would gladly do, providing they were capable.
So what the wooden shipbuilders cannot accomplish
the iron men must do for them, or sacrifice their
employment in Black wall, as well as Devonport ; as
no • doubt you remember the two iron-platers being
discharged from Devonport Dockyard because they
objected to do work for the wooden ship-builders to
finish. If the iron ship-builders do this, the cry would
be 'There is a tine ship we built- the wooden ship-
builders built that first-class iron ship.' Such would
be a falsehood, for they cannot build one by them-
selves. For instance, only look at the Trinity boat
(Beacon),' the wooden ship-builders talk so much
about their building; that was not built by them
alone, there being blacksmiths to do the angle iron and
fire-work, and a number of unprincipled men who
have been labouring with iron ship-builders and
gained a little knowledge of the work, to assist
them. Secondly, three of the wooden ship-builders
gave up the iron work last week, and say they
will not return to it, the reason being because
they cannot do it. Thirdly, thera is an agent
now in Liverpool from America who wants to engage
400 first-class iron ship-builders for the American
Government to construct an iron navy for them. Who
can blame them for leaving England to better them-
selves in a foreign land? Our iron ship-builders say
that the British Government has turned them out of
the royal dockyard, and put wooden shipbuilders on
their work. So our British navy is to be constructed
by wooden shipbuilders, and the American navy will
be constructed by our first-class iron shipbuilders;
men who have served a term of apprenticeship to
iron ship-building. The British Governmeat must not
complain when they find the iron navy now build-
ing almost or 4uite a failure by wooden ship-
builders in the royal dockyards, after spending so
many thousands of pounds on building them, and
find America and other foreign powers able to compete
and beat them with their iron built ships; for, depend
Upon it, they will be well built, and not only well
built, but strong and durable, as they intend having
nothing but first-class iron ship-builders to work upon
gum. The Yankees are not so foolish as 'to have
Wooden ship. builders to build iron ships at their ex-
pense. The iron ship-builders rejoice in having the
Opportunity of showing their skill to foreign Govern-
ments, as they are being deprived of their trade, birth-
right, and honest living by the English Government,
who hire wooden ship-builders in the royal dock-
yards. J. J.
Black-wall, Nov. 5.

articles.title: EDINBURGH JOINERS.
articles.text:
THE EDINBURGH JOINERS.

On Friday night a general meeting of the joiners of
Edinburgh. and Leith was held in the Leith Hall,
Leith, to hear addresses relative to the present position
of the joiner trade, Mr. Brown presiding. The Chair-
tan, in a few remarks, stated that this meeting had
been called by the Edinburgh Branch Society of
Joiners and Carpenters of Edinburgh and Leith, in
order to organise a trade society in Leith. Mr. Ross
then addressed the meeting. He said,—As regards the
union amongst operatives, he believed it was a com-
mon opinion that they wished to unite with the inten-
tion of carrying every thing before them by strikes.
He begged to irony that assertion altogether as con-
cerned the Joiners' Association. Their intention was
to prevent strikes. After reading several rules of the
society, to show the beneficial nature of their trade
union, Mr. Ross said, sixteen years ago the joiners of
Edinburgh had 3id. per hour; their pay had now risen
to 4:d, per hour, which was equal to four per cent, of a
rise. Look again at the Masons' Society, which was
organised sixteen years ago. At that date their
'wages were 41. per hour; they have now risen to 51d
Per hour, and in some cases 6d. per hour. This was
the effects or organisation. Why should there be such
a difference between masons' and joiners' ways? The
latter had a more expensive chest of tools to keep up.
The mu,-
as and Plasterers' Associations had been the
means ot reducing the hours of the workmen to fifty-
one hours per week; while the joiners had to work fifty-
seven hours. After a few further observations, Mr. Ross
concluded by urging those present to join the Trade
Society. Mr. D. Ramsay then rose and delivered a
lengthened speech on the benefits of combination
among rk
wo --n'en, and the great necessity that ex-
isted for a rise of wages in the joiner trade. The
present average of a journeyman joiner's wages was
ns. per week, which he considered insufficient to sup-
port a man having a family to provide for and educate.
The principles and objects of the Joiners' and Car-
penters' Trade Society were then explained; and an
opportunity given to those present to join the same.
After a vote of thanks to the Chairman, the meeting
aeparated.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8, 1862.

SUICIDE OF JOHN BALLARD.
[This man, who made himself so conspicuous in con-
junction with the notorious John Joseph Pomeroy
(afterwards transported for coining) for his opposition
to the men, and his steadfast support of the masters,
during the memorable lock-out of the building trades
in 1859-60, has destroyed himself under peculiar cir-
cumstances. It appears that neither his long services,
nor the aid be rendered to the employers, secured to
him the situation he held. The end of both of these
men (Ballard and Porneroy) is suggestive of the real
character of such sycophants.]
On Tuesday Doctor Lankester held an inquest at the
Prince Albert Tavern, Wharf Road, Paddington,
touching the death of John Ballard, aged 55, who had
committed suicide. It appeared from the evidence that
the deceased was a working smith and engineer. For
the seven years preceding the last two months he had
been foreman over one of the shops in the establishment
of Messrs. Cubitt, in Gray's-inn-road, but he was dis-
charged from that employment owing to some dispute
with superior. After his dismissal he took a loft in
Albion-court, Albion-street, Caledonian-road, and
entered into a contract with the Government for the
repair of some military bedsteads that had been used in
the Crimea. On Wednesday last he entered the loft at
an early hour for the purpose of commencing his day's
work. It was observed by the men employed in a
farrier's forge underneath, that he had not come down
at dinner hour, and it was found that he had locked
the entrance door on the inside. A ladder was placed
against one of the windows, and the person who
mounted it saw the deceased hanging from a beam.
From the position in which he was found, it would
appear that he had stood on one of the camp bed iteads
and thrown himself from the side of it after he had
tied the rope round his neck. In his pocket was
found a letter from one of the authorities at the Tower,
stating that he must take back some four or five of
the bedsteads which he had already delivered, in con-
sequence of their not being in accordance with the
contract. A relative of the deceased stated that this
contract had been a losing one, the price at which it
was taken scarcely paying for the materials. Subse-
quently to his discharge from Messrs. Cubitt's Ballard
had repeatedly threatened to commit suicide, and he
was very strange in his manner on the day he carried
his threat into execution. On this evidence the jury
found that he had committed suipide while in an un-
sound state of mind.

LONDON OPERATIVE BRICKLAYERS' SOCIETY.--The
No. 6 Lodge of this society, of which Mr. Henry
Noble is secretary, has removed from the Star, Black-
man .street, Borough, to the Marquis of Granby, Union-
street, Borough.
CABMEN'S FRIENDLY PROTECTION Socirrv. —The half
yearly meeting of this society was held on Thursday
evening, Nov. 6, at Uncle Tom's Cabin, Shoreditch,
when a report was read by M. T. Miles, the secretary,
congratulating the society on its position. The expen-
diture had been heavy during the past six months, but
a balance remains on that period of £8 17s. Id. The
report concluded with an urgent appeal to the cabmen
to join the society. The entrance fee is Is., and the
weekly contribution id. The report was seconded and
adopted, and the meeting concluded after the transac-
tion of some routine business.

How WORKMEN ARE TREATED AT CONSTANTINOPLE.
—The army of the Sultan Adbul-Medjid is to be en-
tirely re-clothed in Zouave costume, and for this pur-
pose some 2,000 additional tailors, besides the regi-
mental artists, have been engaged for a considerable
time at the Government workshops. They stitched
away until the time came when they thought some
money was due for their labours. Unfortunately the
regimental exchequer happened to be empty, which was
duly notified to the -two thousand tailors, with an inti-
mation that they would have to work on credit. This
the indignant artists refused and struck, whereupon,
without parley, each tailor was led out between a file
of soldiers, with an order that he should receive fifty
lashes on the soles of his feet. When a score or two had
got their allotted portion the rest gave in. The
Minister of War chuckles over the development of'
Turkish civilisation.

articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FORESTERS.
Balsron.—At the quarterly meeting of Court Duke
of Beaufort, held at the Three Compasses, Jacob-
street, on Tuesday evening, it was unanimously re-
solved—'That a committee be appointed to solicit
donations from each member of the above court, to
assist in alleviating the distress of the unemployed
operatives of the Bristol Cotton Factory, caused by
the cotton famine.' The 20th anniversary of Court
Philanthropic, No. 1,328, of the above. flourishing
ord6r, was celebrated by a dinner at Mrs. Charity
Bidgood's, the Crown and Dove Inn, Bridewell-street,
on Monday evening. The chair was taken by Brother
Thomas Webb. About 70 members were present, and
in the course of the evening the secretary read the
report of the expenditure of the Court, amounting to
£l6O for sick benefit, the amount in hand being
.£720, and at the same time mentioned that the profits
arising from the late fete at the New Gardens at Hop
field amounted to £206 6s. 9cl. -

DURHAM.—The anniversary diner of the Court St.
Nicholas, No. 806, was heid at the house of Br. Thomas
Clarke, Black Lion Inn, Durham, on Monday. Wm.
C. Blackett, Esq., surgeon, presided; Mr. John Stod-
dart, printer, officiating as vice-chairman. A sumptuous
repast having been discussed, and the usual loyal toasts
disposed of, Mr. Reed proposed The Ancient Order of
Foresters and the Officers of Court St. Nicholas.' He
stated that h had been a Forester for several Tears,
and was quite prepared to state that Forestry was
thriving in this country, and that if the officers and
brethren would only do their duty steadily, and work
harmoniously together, that court in particular would
continue to flourish, and enlist under her banner not
only the sympathy, but also the support of this great
community. The Court is said to number over 100
members and to have saved nearly £5OO.

Loyal Great Western Lodge was held on Tuesday
evening at the Cat and Wheel, Castle Green, Host

room was handsomely decorated with banners, and the
regalia and insignia of the Order. P. P. G. M.
Thomas in the chair; Brother Isaac Urch occupied the

HuLL.—The anniversary dinner of the Governor

articles.title: UNITED PATRIOTS' NATIONAL BENEFIT
articles.text:
UNITED PATRIOTS' NATIONAL BENEFIT

SOCIETY-.

The anniversary meeting of the members of this
Society resident in the district of Ashford, Kent, was
held at the Castle Hotel, in that town, on Saturday
last. A large number of the members sat down to
dinner, after which the cloth was removed and the
three club rooms being thrown into one large meeting
room, the same was opened to the general public, for
the purpose of entering into an explanation of the
position and advantages of this extensive and nourish-
ing society. Addresses were delivered by Messrs.
Charles Greenman and George Wheeler on the im-
portant results which had been achieved by this and
kindred societies in the alleviation of the afflictions
and misfortunes of the productive classes, of the par-
ticular and special claims of this society for their
approval and support, and of the paramount necessity
Which existed that each son of industry should take
advantage of the opportunities thereby offered for the
security of himself and the assistance of his fellow-
workers in the field of labour. The meeting was
attended by deputations from the local lodges of Odd
Fellows, Foresters, Druids, &c., the large room being
completely filled. Resolutions of approval and confi-
dence in the position and prospects of the Society
were proposed and unanimously agreed to, after
which the meeting broke up in the most cordial
manner.

FitND LY S
Fcrrieensy' PAIXENTS. —A case affecting the
Tradesmen's
Society, was heard before the
o
magistrates at the Moot Hall
rE
, Newcastle, on Saturday.
Thomas Robinson, an aged man,
employed in collect-
ing cottage rents at Spital Tongues Colliery, and in
attending to certain arrangements in a tunnel at that
place, stated that he had been a member of the society
for thirty-seven years, and that having become incapa-
citated by sickness in March last he received relief
from the society for six weeks, but that on applying
i for payment for two weeks n addition to those the
society refused to pay him, and declared that he was
excluded from the society in consequence of not having
paid up his subscription. He offered to pay the sub-
scriptions that were due on receiving the money to
which he alleged he was entitled, but the society de
clined to accept the proposal. 21r. Joel, on the part
of the society, endeavoured to show that the com-
plainant had followed his occupation during the. two
weeks in question, and was not entitled to rtneive the
benefits of the society, It seemed that he had kept
in his possession the key of a yard, but he denied
having performed any work, and the Bench, holding
that the possession of the key did not establish the
case of the defendants, ordered that the plaintiff should
be reinstated in the society from which he bad been
dismissed.

articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-

GENCE.

REIGHLEY CO. OPERATIVE SOCIETY. - The fourth
half-yearly meeting of this society was held on Mon-
day last, in the Temperance Hall, when the balance-
sheet was read, which shows that the amount
received for goods during the half-year is £2,999
35. 81d., and the nett profits £97 18s. 4d., which gives
a bonus of 9d. to each paid-up shareholder, and 7d. in
the pound to members on their purchases and sid. in
the pound to non-members, and £47 is. 51. to be
added to the stock.' After the appointment of officers
and other ordinary business, a proposition was sub-
mitted as to the advisability of purchasing property
suitable for all the requirements of the society. The
proposition met with a very favourable reception.

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE

THE LANCASHIRE DISTRESS FUND.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Sir,—The following letter was sent to the London
Trade Council on this subject by the late secretary, Mr.
G. Howell. The Council will feel obliged by :its in-
sertion in your paper this week. _

_ _ _
G. ODGERS, Secretary.
Bell Inn, Old Bailey, Nov. 3.
Gentlemen,—l trust you will pardon me for urging
upon you the necessity of doing something for the relief
of our starving brothers in the cotton districts. I have
been waiting for some time
.expecting to see the trades
of London take up this mo3t important subject. Perhaps
it is thought by some that it scarcely comes within the
scope of our Societies' questions. I must beg to differ
entirely from these gentlemen. If these men are re-
duced to poverty by the present depression in their trade,
they will be at the absolute mercy of their employers
when trade revives. For it must be remembered that it
will only gradually and slowly return to its wonted
prosperity. I cannot forget that before the present
crisis arrived, the employers tried to effect a large reduc-
tion in their wages. The men resisted it and offered the
most equitable terms in lieu of a reduction. They
offered to work short time, and so divide as equally as
possible among themselves the lahaur to be done, and,
of course, the remuneration for that labour. This the em-
ployers refused, and some even closed their mills. Thus
we see but little chance for the men from their employers.
It therefore becomes our imperative duty to hasten to
the rescue. It matters not whether they be Unionists
or Non-Unionists, we must not suffer them to be crushed.
Want knows no creed, nor should our benevolence;
or, rather call it not charity, it is but common justice.
It may be that some will differ as to the manner in
which the relief is, or should be, dealt out.. But that
cannot be an excuse for not giving. Better that it be
divided unequally or inefficiently than not at all.
Lotus all earnestly and perseveringlywerk to give them
tangible relief. Not such as is meted out by our poor-
laws, but sufficient to keep want entirely from their
doors, Gentlemen, take up this subject, and every true
Unionist will bless your efforts, and work with you to
make them successful.
Oct. 21.

articles.title: EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A SOLICITOR.
articles.text:
EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST
A SOLICITOR.

Mr. Edward. Capel Whitehurst, of Guildhall Cham-
bers, City, and Lower Belgrave-place, Eton-square,
solicitor, and the well-known Secretary of the Ballot
Society, was placed at the bar, at the Bow-street
Police-court, on Tuesday, charged with inciting the
prosecutor, Mr. George Blake Leheup Rogers, of
Grosvenor Hotel, late cornet in the sth Dragoon
Guards, to commit an unnatural offence. The case
excited considerable interest, from the high standing
of the prisoner, both in his profession and in society,
and from the fact that the prosecutor, also a person of
highly respectable [position, had recently stood
prominently before the public in certain proceedings at
the Westminster Police-court. Two solicitors were
engaged on each side—Mr. Smyth and Mr. Abrams for
the prosecution; Mr. Geo. Lewis, jun., and Mr. Bury
Hutchison for the defence.
Mr. Smyth said the charge which he had to prefer
against the prisoner was of a most serious and dis-
tressing nature. It appeared that the prosecutor, who
. . .

was a gentleman of weiath, had got into company with
some soldiers, one of whom was brought up at the
Westminster Police-court, upon the charge of robbing
Mr. Rogers of his watch. The soldier defended him-
self by making some charge against Mr. Rogers. The
case was adjourned, the soldier being admitted to bail
upon his own recognizance. That case was reported
in the newspapers. After the appearance of that re-
port Mr. Rogers received several anonymous letters,
one of which would be shown to have been written by
the prisoner. That letter contained a proposal of
an infamous nature. It commenced, If Mr. Rogers
really desires,' &c., and it closed with a pro-
posal that Mr. Rogers should, on the following
evening, at six o'clock, present himself at the top of
Constitution-bill, under the arch, wearing a pair of
white kid gloves, when the writer would introduce him-
self. That letter was directed to the address, 11,
Queen's-road West, Chelsea, which Mr. Rogers had
given at the Westminster Police-court, and which had
appeared in the papers. Mr. Rogers had, in the mean-
while, removed to the ,Grosvenor Hotel, and the letter
was forwarded to him there. It bore the postmark
October 26. A second letter, in the same handwriting,
bearing the postmark October 30, was received by MT-.
Rogers. Mr. Rogers handed over the two letters and
all the anonymous letters he had received to the police.
A third.. letter was received, in which the writer ex-
pressed his regret at learning that Mr. Rogers had been
ill, and proposed an appointment on that day at the
same place and hour. Mr. Rogers delivered that
to the police. On Monday Mr. Rogers received
a fourth letter in the same handwriting as the
other three. The writer suggested that Mr. Rogere's
change of address might be the 'cause of his
not keeping the previous appointments, and pro-
posed for that night (Monday) a fresh appointment
at the same place and hour. By the advice of the
police. officers Mr. Rogers kept that appointment.
He was accompanied by, an inspector ot police,
a sergeant of police, a person named Malcolm,
recommended by the police, and one other person.
Malcolm was concealed at a certain place in the en-
closure within th 3 rails and near the archway. Mr.
Rogers remained under the archway until the prisoner,
after passing him several times, said to him Are you
Mr. Rogers 1' Mr. Rogers replied in the affirmative,
and asked the prisoner if he was the writer of the
letters. The prisoner said he was. They then walked
arm in arm along Constitution-hill to the spot where
Malcolm was concealed, and a conversation took place
which Malcolm overheard. In the course of that con-
versation the prisoner proposed that he and Mr. Rogers
should dine together on the following day (Tuesday)
at an hotel, where they should pass the night. Mr.
Rogers then asked him whether he was sure who had
written the letters? He said, Yes.' Mr. Rogers
produced one of the letters, showed it to the prisoner,
and said, This is a matter requiring great confidence,
will you swear that you wrote this letter and the other
letters in the same handwriting ? ' The prisoner said
Yes, I will swear it.' The prosecutor then asked the
prisoner for his name and address, which the prisoner
wrote down in the prosecutors' pocket-book, C. C.
Whitehurst, 6, Lower Belgrave-place.' The prosecutor
then gave him in charge.
Mr. Rogers was then called and deposed to the facts
as above stated, with some further details of the con-
versation, utterly unfit for publication. He also
produced letters, the substance of which we suppress
for a similar reason.

Edwin Malcolm, commission agent, formerly a police-
constable, but having left the force for twenty years,
and subsequently manager of an omnibus company,
deposed to that part of the -conversation which he had
overheard.

The defendant entirely denied that he had been
guilty of any impropriety.
Jr. Lewis said he believed Mr. Smyth was about
to apply for a remand. The C 8.86 might as well be re-
manded upon the evidence now before the court. The
case would be fought out to the last.
The case was then adjourned, Mr. Whitehurat being
admitted to bail in two sureties of £250 each, and his
own recognisance for L6OO. Substantial bail, approved
by the prosecutor, was provided.

articles.title: CAUTION TO SECRETARIES OF
articles.text:
CAUTION TO SECRETARIES OF

TRA.D.E S 0 CIATI.ES.

William Pike, of 15, Bolsover-street, W., who had
been arrested at Patrixbourne, near Canterbury, and
brought to London on a warrant signed by Mx. Dele-
mar, one of the magistrates for the county of Kent,
was charged with embezzling several sums of money
belonging to the London Amalgamated Association of
Operative House Painters.—Mr. Eaden, 10, Gray's-
inn-square, attended for the prosecution, and said the
prisoner was appointed secretary to the association in
June, 1861, and he continued to act in that capacity
until the 4th of April, 1862, when he was sent to
Brighton with £lO to pay to a branch of the associa-
tion, and not returning on the Bth of April, a mes-
senger was sent to his residence, who found he had
left his home. Application was then made to his wife
for the books and papers belonging to the association,
which she gave up, and on examination it. was found
that the prisoner had kept no cash account in the
ledger for the past two months, and on further research
it was proved that from June, 1861, to January, 1862,
the prisoner had, in several sums, appropriated to his
own use £8 ss. id. belonging to the association.; and
from February to April 4th a further sum of £3 6s. 10d.,
together with the proceeds of two post-office orders,
one for £3 12s. id., and the other for Bs. Bd., and also
a sum of £l, which he had received at Brighton, the
whole of which moneys belonged to the association,
and amounted to £l6s. 12s. Bd. Mr. Eaden further
said he should only offer sufficient evidence for a
remand, by calling a witness who would prove the
admission by the prisoner of the facts as stated.—
Robert Shaw, of 18, Huntsworth-terrace, Portman-
market, said: lam secretary to the association. It is
not enrolled. A Mr. Thomas Adams and others are
the trustees. It was the prisoner's duty, as secretary,
to receive and pay moneys on account of the associa-
tion. I recollect the prisoner being sent to Brighton
with £lO to pay over to a branch of the association
there. I saw the prisoner on the 29th of April last, at
a meeting of the executive committee of the associa-
tion, where he was charged with having moneys
belonging to the association. I asked him if he had
cashed a post-office order on the Bth of April for
£3 12s. id., and made use of the money. He said
Yes.' I asked him if he had cashed another post-
office order for Bs. Bd., and kept the money for himself.
He said he had. I asked him if he had drawn from
the treasurer, since January last, 6s. 10d. more
than he had paid away on behalf of the association.
He said he had. I asked what had become of the
£8 ss. id. that was entered in the treasurer's cheque-
book, without the treasurer's signature. He said he
had appropriated it to his own use, being much pressed
at the time.—ln answer to the charge the prisoner
said, in a very defiant manner, 'He was not bound to
obey the rules of the association, as it was not enrolled.'
—Mr. Tyrwhitt said: He must not be allowed to make
private use of the money of the association, even if it
was not enrolled, and there being sufficient evidence
against him, he should remand him for a week.

FIRST DAY OF MICHAELMAS TERM.
Monday, being the beginning of Michaelmas Term,
the judges of the superior courts of common law and
equity breakfasted with the Lord Chancellor, in the
Middle Temple Hall, whence the noble and learned
lord, together with his guests, went in procession to
Westminster Hall to inaugurate the re-opening of the

articles.title: COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH.
articles.text:
COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH.

Sittings in Banco.—(Before Chief Justice Cockburn.
and Justices Wightman, Blackburn, and Mellor).

THOMAS V. SHIRLEY-BREACH OF PROMISE.

Mr. Sergeant Shea said this was an action for breach
of promise, tried at the last Lewes assizes before Mr.
Baron Bramwell and a common jury, when a verdict
was returned for the defendant. The plaintiff was
Miss Anne Thomas, a young lady twenty-three years
of age, who had filled respectable situations as a
governess in several privite families, and the defendant
is General Shirley, a gentleman of considerable posi-
tion and fortune, residing at Brookside Lodge, near
Rugby. The plaintiff, it will be recollected, entered
the general's service as a lady housekeeper (she having
advertised for such a situation), and afterwards, as re-
presented by her, passed as his wife. Under a promise
of marriage she yielded to his solicitations, and was
delivered of a child in March, 1862. The general, it
appeared, was a married man, though separated from
his wife, and it was urged on the part of the plaintiff
that she was not aware of that fact until some time
after the promise and seduction. The learned serjeant
moved for a rule calling on the defendant to show
cause why there should not be a new trial on the
ground that the verdict was against the weight of
evidence.—Rule refused.

articles.title: BAIL COURT.
articles.text:
BAIL COURT.

(Sittings at Nisi Prins at Westminster before Mr.
Justice Crompton and Common Juries.)
SABEY T. STEPIIENS—FATAL ACCIDENT AT ST.
MARTIN'S-HALL.
This was an action for the recovery of damages as
compensation for the death of the plaintiff's son through
the alleged negligence of the defendant. The
defendant pleaded not guilty. This was a second trial
and occupied the whole of the day. On the first trial
the jury were discharged without agreeing to a verdict.
The deceased was a carpenter, earning 335. per week,
and coatributed mainly towards the support of his
widowed mother, the present plaintiff. The defendant
was a zinc worker in Old-street-road, St. Luke's, and
had contracted to fix the zinc s-in lights in St. Martin's
Hall, for which purpose it was necessary to cut away
a portion of the roof, and in crder for the men to do
their work a scaffold was necessary. The de-
fendant, accordingly, procured the necessary materials,
and employed men, who constructed a swing scaffold
for the use of the workmen. On the 3rd January last
six men, including the defendant, were en the scaffold,
when one of the poles broke, and all the men, with the
exception of the defendant, fell to the ground, the
defendant escaping by holding fast to a gas pipe, sus-
pended as it were in the air, until a ladder was pro-
cured, and he was rescued from his perilous position.
The deceased and another man were killed, and three
others were seriously injured. The evidence went to
prove that the materials of the scaffold were good and
sound, and the negligence imputed to the defendant
was his not employing proper persons to construct it.
It was also urged that three poles instead of two
should have been used for the planks to rest on. The
jury, after being locked up about an hour, returned
into couit with a verdict for the defendant.

articles.title: BA.NKRUPTCY *COURT.
articles.text:
BA.NKRUPTCY *COURT.

(Before Mr. Commissioner GOULBURN.)
RE GEORGE STIFF.

This was an adjourned examination meeting of
George Stiff; described as of Beulah Spa Villas, Nor-
wood, and No. 334, Strand, newspaper proprietor.
The bankrupt, it may be remembered, was proprietor
of the Morning Chronicle, Weekly Times the _London
Journal, and the Guide. The total liabilities, accord-
ing to the accounts prepared by Mr. Joseph Hart, the
accountant, amount to £35,330; assets valued at
£23,770.

Mr. Linklater, for the assignees, said that in July,
1859, the bankrupt alleged tt at he had a surplus of
£22,000; but that in fact had no reality—no exist-
ence. The bankrupt had had the conduct of the
London Journal and Guid• from July, 1859, up to a few
days of the bankruptcy, and had made a net profit of
£4,900, which was equal to £l,BOO a year. In his
examination he stated the value of the copyright to be
three years' purchase. The fact, therefore, was that
on the 16th of July, 1859, instead of having £22,000,
he was utterly insolvent. Mr. Linklater then read
the report of Mr. Hart, and called attention to the
lavish expenditure of the bankrupt. There was a sum
of £2OO received by the bankrupt three weeks before
the bankruptcy, which was wholly unaccounted for,
which, together with a sum of £792 carried to sus-
pense account,' made nearly £l,OOO.
From the report presented by the accountant, Mr.
Hart, it appears that the loss on the Morning Chronicle
during the twelve months it was in Mr. Stiff's posses-
sion was £11,119 9s. 5d., and that by Mr. Stiff, in
September, 1861, reducing the price of the Weekly
Times, against the advice of his friends, from 2d. to Id.,
the paper had since been carried on at a great loss,
notwithstanding its alleged large sale.
The proofs of several gentlemen who had been pro-
fessionally engaged on the Morning Chronicle were
taken. The City editor claimed £63, and a further
sum in lieu of notice; and the foreign editor claimed
about £25. Mr. .Drough, who appeared for these
creditors, contended that the hiring was something
more than a weekly hiring, and asked for payment of
three months' salary, or £3O in full.
The Commissioner ordered payment in full as asked
for, a portion of the arrears—a proof to be made for
the difference.

The bankrupt then passed, and will come up for dis•
charge on December 3.

articles.title: SHOREDITCH COUNTY COURT.
articles.text:
SHOREDITCH COUNTY COURT.

BURNS V. EDWARD 9. -FRIENDLY SO CIF,TIES AND SURETIES
FOR THE OFFICIALS. -IMPORTANT JUDGMENT.
This was an action to recover £l5, balance of a bill
of exchange for £5O; plaintiff, one of the trustees
of the Loyal United Friends' Friendly Society,
and defendant a baker, of Lisson-grove. It appears
that the defendant had become surety on a bond of
£5O for a relative, who was elected treasurer in
plaintiff's society. This treasurer became a defaulter,
and the society applied to the surety, who, being unable
to pay the £5O down, accepted a bill drawn by plaintiff,
and payable in monthly instalment of £5 each. £35
had been paid, and then defendant stopped, and was
sued on the bond, but plaintiff was nonsuited, as the
society was not enrolled. Plaintiff now sued on the
bill; and, after hearing an elaborate argument,
His Honour delivered judgment. He said: In this
case I am bound to believe that defendant is liable
upon the bill which he has accepted, and as he has
paid £35, it is now too late to set up the question of
consideration. I find for plaintiff with costs.

articles.title: SOUTHWARK COUNTY COURT.
articles.text:
SOUTHWARK COUNTY COURT.

(Before Mr. Whitmo-e.)
THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF CARPEN-

TERS v. WILLIAM LEE.
This was a summons issued by Henry Juniper and
some other members of the executive committee of the
Amalgamated Carpenters' Society against the defendant,
William Lee, calling upon him to deliver up to them
certain books and monies which it was said he unlaw-
fully withheld and detained, on the plea that he was
still the secretary of the society, although, as alleged
by the plaintiff, he had ceaseft to be secretary, and
another person had been appointed to that office.
Mr. T. Salter appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr.
Joyce for defendant. The case created much interest
in the trade, and a great many of the friends of both
parties were present.
On the case being called, Mr. Salter, addressing his
Honour, said, he had held a consultation with his
clients, and as there were several knotty points in the
case, which would involve much argument, and being
desirous to save expense and litigation to the society,
he had advised them to allow the case to be settled by
an arbitrator chosen by himself and his learned friend
the counsel for the defendant. His clients had reluc-
tantly consented to this course, providing it was sanc-
tioned by the General Council of the Trade. To
obtain this consent it would be necessary to adjourn the
case for a fortnight. If at the end of that time it was
decided not to accept of arbitration, the case would then
go to trial. He believed the counsel for the defendant
was also willing that this courso should be adopted on
the same grounds.
Mr. Joyce having expressed his concurrence in the
course suggested,
His Honour said he would adjourn the case until
Thursday, the 20th inst. at 11. o'clock, when, if the case
came to trial, he would specially set apart that day for
its hearing.
Adjourned accordingly.

articles.title: GEO. HOWELL.
articles.text:
GEO. HOWELL.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHWE.
Sin,—l have been a reader of the BEEHIVE, the
real working man's paper, from the commencement;
and I can assure you I am well pleased with the in-
formation I have obtained from it. I believe it is the
only organ that gives us a fair and impartial represen-
tation in trade matters. It is the first to come forward to
ask for alms for the distressed workpeople in the time of
need, and fights our battles when the hand of oppres-
sion is engaged to screw us down. I think, sir, the
working men of this country ought to be pleased at
the efforts you are making to get subscriptions for our
distressed brethren in Lancashire and the district, and
for the support you are giving to the lila Lancashire
committee: for I think that committee, with the Rev.
E. A. Verity at their head, are the right men in the
right place, and are the most proper persons to judge
how their fellow men should be relieved, being a body
of working men.. I have no doubt you think it strange
that the trade societies of Birmingham don't send
their subscriptions to you; and my principal object in
writing is to explain our position. I can assure you,
the Birmingham people are not lax in their duties—
we have got a committee of working men that do credit
to the town. The workpeople in the various mann-
factories are giving well, considering the depression of
trade, those that belong to trade Societies and those
that do not. I cannot say that trade societies are sub-
scribing in bodies, or in the societies' name; but T
think it makes little difference so that we give some
way. I will speak for my own trade—the glass cutters.
I know there are but few, if any, but what are sub-
scribing weekly in their various manufactories, and
such sums are sent to the committee weekly or
monthly.

articles.title: I am, yours very truly,
articles.text:
I am, yours very truly,

HENRI' DAVIS.
Great Hampton-row, Birmingham, Nov. 1.

HIGHWAY ROBBERY.-011 Saturday, at 6 p.m., Mr.
J. H. de Kanter, of Java, was walking down Maiden-
lane, Highgate, on his way to St. John's-park; as he
neared the Smallpox Hospital he perceived, for the
first time, two men walking slowly in front of him.
He took no notice of them but continued his way, and
on coming up to them would have walked past between
them, the men having gone one on each side of the
road. But at this moment one of them put his arm
round Mr. Kanter's throat, and with his other hand
roughly stopped his mouth to prevent him calling for
help. The other one gave him a fierce blow on the
chest, which brought him to the ground. They then
knelt upon him and robbed him of his watch and his
purse and all else contained in his pocket, and then
made off in the direction of Kentish-town.
BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A CHILD.—A.s an intelligent
little boy, named Henry Scard, aged nine years, was
going to his school on Thursday morning last, singing
as he went along, in his childlike innocence 'Hurrah
for Garibaldi,' he was met near Fish•streetlill, City,
by an Irishman not worth the name of man,' who
caught him by the arm' and after shaking him well,
took him up and threw him in the middle of the street.
The poor child fell upon his head, and lay without any
appearance of life. A gentleman passing took him in
his arms to the nearest chemist's shop, but was advised
tattake him without delay to a hospital, where he now
IA dangerously ill from concussion of the brain. The
unmanly wretch who had caused this suffering ran
away after he had committed the cowardly deed.
THE LATE EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF CHILD DESER-
TION.—This singular case has bfen amicably settled.
The friends of the young lady who said the child was
given to her by a strange woman in one of the Great
Western Railway carriages, and who, on the other
hand, was alleged to have herself been the mother of
the child, have settled the matter by removing the
infant from the hospital. There will consequently be
no magisterial inquiry, and everybody who is familiar
with the remarkable circumstances in which the in-
teresting little stranger was introduced to the public is
left to form his or her own opinion as to its parentage.

articles.title: IIARYLEB ONE.
articles.text:
IIARYLEB ONE.

STEALING A CAB NO FELONY.-A young man named.
Frederica Andrews, labourer, was charged with steal-
ing a horse and cab, valued at £25, the property of
Robert Braine, cab proprietor, of 73, Upper Berkeley-
street. Prosecutor deposed that the prisoner, of whom
he had some slight knowledge, came to his stable, and
as he was going out prisoner jumped on the spring
and rode with him (prosecutor) as far as Conduit-street,
where the latter got down and requested prisoner
to look to the cab whilst he went to change his
hat. He had no sooner gone indoors than he
heard his cab go on, and on his getting into the
street he saw the prisoner driving at full speed.
He called after him, but in vain, got into a cab
and gave chase, and afterwards inquired at all the
cab-staads in the metropolis, but could hear nothing of
his cab, except that the prisoner had often done the
same trick before. At length, at two this morning, he
noticed his cab standing by a coffee stall in Oxford-
street, and inside was the prisoner regaling himself
with hot coffee and cake. A policeman was called and
took prisoner in charge.—Mr. Mansfield said it was a
most mischievous trick, to say the least, but as the
charge was laid as one of felony, he could not punish
him. He recommended a summons against the prisoner
for driving without a licence, and promised a severe
punishment if the prisoner were brought before him.

articles.text:
MARLBOROUGH-STREET.

IMPORTANT TO VOLUNTEERS.—APPLICATION TO THE
AIAGISTRATE.—A volunteer applied to the magistrate,
Mr. Tyr whitt, to be informed if, on a summons taken
out against him by his commanding officer to deliver
up his arms, the magistrate would allow him to enter
on his defence that he had been dismissed, that no
trial had been granted him, no question asked, and
that the colonel had refused him an opportunity of de--
fence. The applicant said that colonels of the regular
army had not the power of dismissing men without a
trial, goad that it could not have been the intention of
the legislature to grant this power to civilians, or a ,
colonel might dismiss the whole regiment. —Mr. Tyr-
whitt, after perusing the Act of Parliament, said he.
had no authority to interfere, and certainly should not
interfere with volunteer regulations.--The applicant
was said to have formerly belonged to the Queen's _
(Westminster) Rifles.

LAMBETH.

THE LADY, THE FRENCHMAN, AND THE BROOCH.—
Elizabeth Wilson, alias G-oodsell, who has been in-
custody since the 10th ult., on a charge of being con- -
cerned with a Frenchman, not in custody, in stealing
a diamond brooch of the value of .L 67 the property of
Mr. Richard Attenborough, was placed at the bar
before Mr. Elliott, for final examination. It will be
recolleczed V.a.t the Frenchman had purchased the
valuable brooch at the shop of Mr. Attenborough, and
requested that a messenger might be sent with him to
his residence in Walnut Tree-walk, Lambeth, where
he would pay for it. The house the prosecutor's mes-
senger was taken to was the one in which the prisoner •
lodged, and there, under pretence of showing the
article to a friend up stairs, he got possession of the •
brooch and slipped off with it. The defence set up for •
the prisoner was, that the Frenchman was a perfect
stranger to her, that she had merely picked him up,'
and he had only spent one night with her. This,
however, was proved to be untrue, for two months
before the ro?,bery she had shown another lodger in the
house a portrait of him, and said he was her intended
husband. It was further stated that the prisoner had
been seen in the house for some days preceding the
robbery, but Mr. Elliott did not consider the evidence
would warrant him in further detaining her.—Dis-
charged.

WESTMINSTER.
IIoRE CAB LAW.—Captain Elliott was summoned
or the non-payment of a cab-fare of Os. 61. Robert
Lawrence, driver, said that on the 23d ult. he was
fetched from the rank near the Victoria Station to
2, Carlisle-place, Victoria-street. The defendant and
a lady got into the cab. Previously to doing so, the
defendant asked whether he could fetch him back, to
which he replied in the affirmative. He conveyed.
defendant and the lady to 71, St. George's-square,.
Pimlico, and on alighting there the former told him,
to call for him at 10 minutes past ten. He returned at
that time, and remained waiting till fivetainutes past
11, when the defendant, another gentleman, and the
lady, got into the cab. The second gentleman, having
got out in the Vauxhall-bridge-road, the defendant and
the lady were taken back to Carlisle-place. Defendant
then tendered him 3s. 61. as his fare, but he told him
that he wanted 4s. or 55., as he had not had a job since
he set him down. The defendant said that he had.
given him 61. more than his fare, reckoning the con—
veyance to St. George's•square and back, the waiting,.
and extra passenger. As he refused to receive the
3s. 6d. in discharge of the fare, the defendant desired
him to return it, which he did, leaving him to his-
remedy. The complainant was hired at 20 minutes to
7 and discharged at a quarter-past 11, and his legal de-
mand, including 6d. for the extra passenger, was 9s. 6d.
—Mr. Paynter said that the question was whether the
hiring was continuous. As a rule it had been held that
where the driver was not paid when he first set down
it was.—Captain Elliott repeated that he did not
engage him for the whole time, and suggested that
there was nothing to show he had not taken half a
dozen other fares in the interim.—Mr. Paynter said, a
cabman was a public servant, who was bound to go.
wherever he was directed; the duty to be at a particular
place, at a particular time, would be incompatible with
other engagements. If he left his cab for hire during
the interim he might be ordered to another end of the
town and there required to wait. The only mode of
discharging him would have been to pay him at St.
George's-square; neglecting to do that the cabman,
according to the practice of that court, was still deemed..
to be in his service, and was entitled to receive the -
amount he claimed for time. The first contract did not
terminate unless the man was paid. Telling a cabman
who was unpaid to call again operated as a retainer.
Captain Elliott pointed out that when the defendant
was at Carlisle-place, after taking him home, he only
demanded 4s. or 55., and had now summoned him for
double the amount.—The cabman on being recalled
admitted thathe would have been satisfied withreceiving
ss.—Mr. Paynter said that under these circumstanceohe
should only make an order for that amount, which
Captain Elliott paid with the usual costs.

THE ARMIES OF THE POTOMAC.

It would appear Lona the papers that there is a great
outcry in favour of an onward movement by APClellan.
The only dispatches received from his army since the
last mail are as fellows :
FREDERICK, Mn., Oct. 20.—The indications of an
early movement are increasing. The recent reconnais-
sance has proved of much service in revealinc, the dispo-
sition of' the forces of the enemy, and furnishing much
needed information in regard to their future intentions.
The rebels, upon the return of the Federal forces, re-
occupied the positions from which they fell back, with
about the same force as before. They have three
pieces of artillery and one or two regiments of cavalry
near Halltown.
HARPER'S FERRY, VA., Oct. 21.—The Federal infan-
try now hold Halltown, and the cavalry pickets now
extend beyond there. It is reported by deserters who
have recently come in, that Stonewall Jackson is still
with a large force in the vicinity of Bunker's-hill.
The sutlers and others had introduced large quantities
of whiskey and other contraband articles into this place
- but the stringent orders of the provost marshal, toge-
ther with the vigilance of the guurds, are rapidly
breaking up the traffic. Several parties have been
arrested and imprisoned for selling liquor, and a consi-
derable quantity has been confiscated for hospital
purposes. Intoxication among the soldiers is becoming
rare. Yesterday all the shops on Bolivar Heights, of'
which there are a large number, were closed, and the
proprietors ordered to remove their wares at once. The
river continues very low, and fordable at almost any
point.

SIIARPSBURG, Md., Oct. 21.—There is nothing of par-
ticular interest transpiring here. The line of the. Potomac
is well guarded, to prevent the repetition of the recent
cavalry raid. All quiet along the lines.
FEDERAL RECONNAISSANCE.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 19.—General Stahl left Centreville
on Wednesday, with a force of cavalry and artillery for
the purpose of finding and fighting Stuart, who was
known to be moving south from Leesburg east of Bull
Run Hills, and threatening our advance.. At night we
concentrated at Chantilly, and on Tuesday morning
advanced to Aldie. Stuart declined the challenge
and fell back. There was skirraialiing with the
enemy's videttes and some prisoners were captured.
On Friday morning General Stahl advanced towards
Ashley's Gap, driving in the pickets of a force of infantry,
cavalry, and pa-finery under General Hill, occupying
i passes n the vicinity. At New Salem he captured a
number of pickets from the rebel force at Warrenton.
After a brief rest, General Stahl advanced to White
Plains, and encamped for the night, throwing forward
pickets to Thoroughfare Gap, and sending a 5m7.11 force
to look after a supply train of seven waggons, five-loaded
with forage and two with commissary stores, which had
left 'Centreville on the same day, for the use of his
command. The train was found and supposed to he safe.
It was halted at Newmarket about two o'clock won
Saturday morning, and at about half-past six o'block
was captured by 500 North Carolina cavalry, together
with 15 of our soldiers and teamsters. The ribels
conveyed the booty to Warrenton. On learning his
loss, General Stahl moved forward, hoping to recap-
ture the train. The enemy appeared intending to occupy
Thoroughfare Gap, to prevent General Stahl's passage,
and met our advance under Major Knox before we had
penetrated far. Major Knox charged at the head of his
force, and after a short skirmish the enemy fled. Our
forces pursued to the vicinity of Warrenton, but, after
vainly endeavouring to entice- the enemy out to _fight,
terminated the reconnaissance by falling back to Ce.utre7
ville, which place they reached at one o'elock this as orn-
ing. We captured about 100 prisoners, twelve hoi .sea,
and one caisson, and lost, besides- the train, two ho rses
killed. Our scouts now report rebel pickets within two
miles of Centreville, and a cavalry force at Bristow sta-
tion, So and from whish the rebels are moving train'.
