THE NEW YORK CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
_ _ _

At the recent meeting of the New York Chamber of
Commerce, convened in reference to the destruction of
American vessels by the Seeessioni.st steamer Alabama,
a series of resolutions were agreed to, the principal
points of which have been already publiehed. The fol-
lowing are the resolutions in extenso. They were sub-
mitted by Mr. A. Low, who presided at the meeting:—
Resolved :—That the Chamber of Cbmmerce has
heard, with profound emotion, the graphie account given
by Captain Hagar of the burning of the ship Brilliant
on the 3rd day of October instant.
That, in view of thieatrocity, it is ale duty of the
Chamber to announceefor the information of all who
are interested in the safety of human life—the life el-
shipwrecked passengers and crews—that. henceforth the
light of a burning ship at sea will become to the Ame-
rican sailor the signal that hires to destruction, and will
not be, as in timeepaet, the beacon to guide the generous
and intrepid mariner-to the rescue of the -unfortunate.
That henceforth self-preservation will be the first
dictate of prudence' '
as it is the first law of. nature and
consequently the destruction of the Brilliant can be only
characterised as a crime against humanity, and all who
have lmowingly and willingly aided and abetted must
be considered as perpetrators in the crime.
That this Chamber has not failed to notice a rapid
change in British sentiment, traesforraing a. friendly
nation into a self-styled neutral Power, the nature of
which neutrality is shown in permitting ships to go
forth with men, and in permitting an armament to follow
them, for the detestable work of plundering and des-
troying American ships; thus encouraging upon the
high seas an offence against neutral rights, on the.plea
of which, in the case of the Trent, the British
Government threatened to plunge this Government into
war.
Further, That :the outirage of consigning to destruc-
tion by fire, without adjudication, British and Ameeican
property together, is an aggravation of the offence
against the rights of neutrals, and ought to be
denounced as ,a crime by the civilised nations of the
world.
That this Chamber has heard with amazement that
other vessels are fitting out in the ports of Great Britain
to continue the work of destruction begun by the Ala-
bama, an enormity that cannotbe committed on the high
seas without jeopardising the commerce and peace of
nations.
Further, That it is the duty of the Chamber to warn
the merchants of Great Britain that a repetition of such
acts as the burning of the Brilliant by a vessel fitted out
in Great Britain, and manned by British seamen, cannot
fail to produce the most widespread exasperation in this
country, and hence they invoke the influence of all men
who value peace and goodwill among the nations to
prevent the departure of other vessels of the character
referred to from their ports, and so arrest the calamity
of war.
That it is the desire of this Chamber, as it is the
interest of all its members, to cherish sentiments of
amity with the people of Great Britain, to maintain
those cordial relations which have led to profitable in-
tercourse, and to strengthen the ties that knit them
together in mutual courtesy and respect.
That copies of the foregoing preamble and resolu-
tions,be sent to the Secretary of State and to the Secre-
tary of the Navy of the United - States, and to the
Boards of Trade of London and Liverpool; and that
the Secretary of State be requested to transmit
Copies of the same to *he diplomatic agents. of the
"United States, for didn't...lion in other commercial
countrigs.

Corrort ni SAN DOMlNGo.—Accounts from San
Domingo state that cotton planting is carried on actively;
and next year that country is expected to rank among
cotton producers. The cotton trees are stated to grow
spontaneously on all the south side of the island, and to
flourish in the poorest soil. That which is growing in
the vicinity is of short staple, but strong and fine, and
would improve with care in raising. On the extreme
eastern end of the island, in the dement of Higney, the
staple is describedias longer and finer—Jamaica paper.
The Journal de Loiret says that a gentleman in that
neighbourhood gave his servant a letter to post which
contained instructions to his agent de change to sell 100
shares of the Mobilier. The servant forgot the letter from
Sunday to Sunday, and at last, finding it again, at the
expiration of the seven days, in her gala costume, went
in all haste, knowing that it was a letter of import,
to fling herself upon her master's mercy to pardon the
mistake, but was astonished at the old gentleman's
seizing her in his arms, imprinting a kill upon her
cheeks, and premising to put 1,000 francs into the
savings' bank for her. It was not, however, a declara-
tion a love to cookey, but a ease of gaining 60,000
franca by the delay, and in consequence of the rapid
rise in that paper.
We (Array and Navy Gazette) are enabled to state that
on the occasion of the Prince of Wales attaining his
majority there is no intention (at all events such was the
fact up to Saturday) of making any naval promotions.
It was, we believe, at first intended to confer a certain
number of honours upon officers of the royal navy ; but
When it was considered that the Queen, the fountain of
honour,' was in a state -of affliction, and would be pre-
auded from tal(ing part in any act of rejoicing, the idea
was abandoned, and we have reason to think it will not
be revived until the marriage of his Royal Highness.

articles.title: COIVSUITATION ON GENERAL GyIRIBALDE
articles.text:
THE COIVSUITATION ON GENERAL
GyIRIBALDE

(From the Telegraph correspondent.) ,
LA SPEzzIA, Oct. 29.—The great medical congress of
La Spezzia was held this day; and the result, I am
• happy to say, was quite in favour of the patient.
Twenty-six doctors, derived from every class of the
• Italian schools, asssisted at this curious meeting, which,
''in more, perhaps, than one particular, rather resembled
a parliament than a medical consultation. Two most
important voices were absent—those of the French and
English surgeons; Mr. Partridge not being able tO each
La Spezzia till to-night—and, indeed, if it continues
to blow as hard as it is blowing as I write, he will
scarcely get here then—and M. Nelaton having re-
ceived two telegraphic despatches requiring his immedi-
ate return to France. Before leaving however, he had
examined the wound of General leaving,
At the
head of the profession, as represented here, was Pro-
fessor Porta, of the University of• Pavia. This surgeon
is the pupil of Searpa, to whose chair he has succeeded,
and whose ideas he has much d-veloped. With this
distinguished professor were Dr. Zanetti, of Florence,
and the usual medical attendants of the General—Zio,
Maestri, Bertani, et hoc genus omne—who, by a sort of
medical succession, deserve confidence as heirs, through
Porta, of whom they were pupils, to the system of
Scarpa. The examination was confided, of course, to
the senior, and therefore Professor Porta proceeded at
one o'clock to make the digital test. He is not very
polite ; and Garibaldi complained that the French
surgeon had put him to very much less pain.
Porta proceeded, however, with that savage civility
peculiar to doctors, and satisfied himself of the state
of the wound. Then came the congress—for con-
sultation must be a misnomer for such a vast collection
of talent. The debate lasted tw& hours, when it was
established without doubt that the digital examination
had failed to discover the actual presence of, the ball;
that, after probing to a certain depth, the finger met a
resistance, whicb might be the substance behind which
the ball was concealed; that thearticulation is uninjured;
that the general state of the wound is healthy; that the
ball may either remain in, come- away of itself, or after'
a. time be easily removed with an instrument; that the
cure is certain, though it may be slow. Then two
questions were put Is the General in sueli a state'
of debility that he would sink under two or three.
months' confinement'? ' Answer Certainly not.'
Is it probable that mortification, or even fever,
should supervene F'—`'Not in the least* likely.' The
result of the inquiry then resolved itself into this
verdict, that any operation whatever was totally un-
necessary; and that the present system should be con-
tinued.• For more than two hours did this surgical
debate last, and after that time a flood of medical talent
was let loose upon La Spezzia. Surgeons were' as
plenty as' sailors. Carriages full of doctors drove off,
and many table (notes are even novr echoing the opinions
of those who stay till to-morrow. The result of this
consultation—to look at it politically, and I regret to
say, that thelife of General Garibaldi was gambled with
here as, so much political capital—is a great triumphf or
the Ganibaldia.n as opposed to the Mazziniani party.

MARS.—On this planetorhich is now in its perigee
as well as in its perihelion, that is, at its shortest- dis- ,
tance from the earth and the, sum, and is visible about
10 p.m. in the constellation, of Pisces, where-it is easily
recognisable by its reddish light, Father Secelai has-just
published a few interesting remarks in the Giornale di
Roma.. Herschel, many years ago, asserted that Mars.
contained oceans seed oontinents, and that changes of
season could be distinctly observed on its.surface ; but
the accuracy of his. observations was doubted by suh-
sequent astronomers. In 1856 Father. Secehi began to
direct his special attention to this planets of whichite
made out a map in 1858 eleat his designs-presented such
discrepancies, compared with those of his predecessors,
and Dr, Mzedler's especially, that he heeitated•to publish
them. Now, however, that Mars is in so favoursble a
position, Father Secchi has found Maieller's designs to
coincide with the present appearance of the planet.
The chief difference between the two appearances. lay in
the white polar spots, which .Mmeller represented as
small brilliant circles, while Father Secehi found them
of an extremely complicated form. This is now easily
explained; in 1858 both poles of Mars were visible,
while now only one, the southernpole, is. turned to-
wards us. The. globe on which
,Father Secehi had
designed the appearances of 1858 l‘eing placed in a
proper position the equatorial regions of that psriod
coincide with those now visible e as for' the change-
observable in the white spots they are easily explained
by supposing them to have teen snow, which has now
melted away, owing to the proximity el the sun, and
the season of the solstice which now prevails in Mars.
Hence the supposition of the existence of water and
seas in Mars is confirmed, since without these snow and
ice could not exist; and in fact,, the blue lines supposed
to be water have not materially changed. And since, on
the other hand, the white spots seen by Father Secchi
in 1851, now present a. rose-colomedtint, there is ample
reason for adhering to Herschel's statement in favour
of the changes of season to which Mars is subject.
DEATH OF THE DOCTOR OF THE NOVADA.—The
death of Dr. Edward Schwarz, a Huegarian by birth,
which tobleplice at Vienna on the-22rtd of September,

talent, that he received from the Emperor himself the
appointment as' physician to the expedition. On the

Frigate Novara round the'Globe He further invented

but in the English language entitled A System of
AnthropometriCal Investi,gations,. as a me ,ns for the
Differential Diagnosis of Human Races,' invented and
established by-E. Schwarz. This 'instrument serves for
the measurement of the varieties in the construction of
the human body.

SILK AND VELVET.

Very attractive were the.eases in the south gallery
in which were displayed the gorgeous silk and brocade.
and rich velvets of our manufacturers; and no small
portion of the interest which attaches to the eourti•Of
France, Austria, Turkey, Italy, and some other foreign
countries is due to the silks and velvets welch are 'there
exhibited. From the Queen on her throne arrayed in
damask and brocade, to the factory girl, who can afford
to purchase a dress of plain or. checked gros de Naples,
this elegant material possesses charms and attractions;
and such is its nature th'it it can be, made to snit the
,tastes and the pecuniary means of all grades of civilised
society. It would be impossible to give an adequate
idea of the still and artistic talent, th; mechanical in-
genuity, and the amount of chemical knowledge which
has been brought to bear upon the producti els. of the
specimens of silk manufacture:in the present Exhibition.
The brocades and-:dareasks of Lyons, the r;ch coloured
velvets of Genoa, and the products of Spitalfields and
Coventry are things to be seen, and not described.
The display of furniture silks ma,: es op the brightest
portion of the Exhibition; and: the riekness of the
colour, and eleg ince of design of these fabrics win for
themselves universal admiration. The case of Messrs.
Walters and Co., of Newgate-street, and Braintree,
Essex, is exceedingly rich. The specimens in the case
were manufactured exclusively, and are publicly shown
for the first time in their present position.
Messrs. Keith and CO. are Successful as exhibitors.
They do not, it is true, make so prominent a display.
The silk trophy is this year replaced by a woollen one,
but the most superficial observer cannot fail to be
struck with the beauty and richness of the furniture
silks which are shown by these exhibitors. The width
of the fabrics, 63 inches and upwards, is evidence of the
skill of the Weavers: For colour and design and the
quality of material these silks merit the highest praise.
Messrs. Campbell, Harrison and Co. also, made a
very good show of -brocaded silk. In their-case will be
seen a black a brocaded silk thirty-six inches in width,
richly corded ground, With bouquets of flowers of every
variety of tint. Two of the most slelled workmen
were occupied three Months in the production of this
specimen. The nuraber of cards necessary to form the
pattern was 18,852, a single card being required to sepq-
rate the wasp preparatory to. each thread of the weft.
This is one of the most elaborate specimens of the silk
manufacturethat has been produced since the last Exhie
bition, 1851.

Messrs. Va-xasseur, Taylor, end Co. made a very good
display of silk fatrrics. The exhibitors had not pro-
duced any special articles for exhibitions r as was the
case of some few manufacturers, had made efforts which
are not Ekely to be sustained. The silk fabrics are such
as are produced in the ordinary way of business by the
firm, and for texture and colsur they leave nothing to be
desired.

Mr. Sherbrooke.Taylor, of 44 Friday •street, London,
has contented himself with the exhibition of Rich goods
only as are produced in the ordinary course of his trade.
The same mechanical skill which, can-produce a Email
brocaded pattern is equal, when the occasion requires,
for the production of a large and more gorgeous
pattern. Among the specimens shown remarkable for
their good•taste and excellent arrangement of colours
will be seen a rich dmeape, brocaded. with a clematis in
solid silver to a neat and chaste design, with great rich-
ness of material, instead of employing the larger and
bolder patterns which are usual in, this fabric. Near
this specimen is a lilac moire antique,, shot with solid
silver, also intended for Gourt trains, Other specimens
include a silver-gray satin brocaded with solid gold; a
rich ducape, a yard -wide, with an oak sprig in
natural colours; and a. rich moire antique, with the
blackberry brocaded in satin and tissue. There-• are-
several rich moire antiques in perfectly .new colours,
beautifullyrsoft and ladylike. Other branches a the
exhibitors' business are represented by pieces of satin
for dresses, ducapes, gros royals, g-ros d'Athenes for
dresses, and satin and grenadine handkerchiefs- for
gentleicaen's, wear made by power-looms.

The following.: spirited letter from General GariValdi,
written by the hand of his Secretary, Necchi, has-been
received by the-Mayor of Bath
. Spezzia„. Oct. 26,1852..
'ILC,NOIJIIAEZE Sin,—The General is deeply affected
by the noble sentiments that you, sir'." .and the liberal
speakers of England, have expressed for the cause of
Italy.. He thanks you all„and highly appreciates-your
love of truth and. liberty. The Roman question is an
intricate net [intricata matassa] that hypocrisy. and
despotism have embroiled with their perfidious bands.
Perhaps the English people might, by, their meetings,
urge their Government to endeavour to obtain,
gradually, or at, once, the return of the Frenclizoldiers
to their own country, and the evil government of the
priests would be at an end for even This would be
a moral victory., that would do honour to the English
nation.. But, the tyrants,,whether in,priestly or mili-
tary. garb,nre stubborn and blind. his for this-reason
that the General raised his standard, with the intention
of hastening to Rome and crowning Italy on. the
Capitol. Our Ministers., will not realise the dignity. of
this, nor do they yet realise it. They love .to dwell at
ease. They are willing to live initaly,but not todie for
b2r. They are not worthy to be at the head of a rising
nation, and have indeed reduced their, Government-to
French perfecture. My. General has narrowly escaped
with his life, They put him in prison, but they could
not bring hira.to trial, because his acquittal had.already
been pronounced by the world at large. He had every
legal right to gp to Rome. On the 30th of June, 1849,
the Roman Assembly, the only existing rule, after the
cowardly flight of the Pope and, his worthy cardinals,
invested General Garibaldi with. the Dictatorship,- and
he entered Rome to assert the rights of a peoble tormen-
ted by the oppression of the priesthood and the
dominion of foreigners. ' 'All this the General, for the
sake Of truth and ju.tice, was anxious that the English
people should become acquainted with.
Accept, my Lord Mayor, my sentimenis. of esteem
and respect. nYours,
`.C. ALIGLISTO, VECCIII.'

—His Highness the Maharajah Duleep Singh has be-
come the proprietor of Hatheron Castle and estate,
situate on the Cotswold Hills, about' two Miles from
the pretty little town of Fairford„ and iaine miles from

London„ on the .24tb, ult. However, on the, previous
evening his -Highness the Maharajah Duleep Singh
became the owner of the piLoperty; by private contract,'
at the price, it is said, of 5e225,000. The Maharajah is
welt known to be passionately fond of field Sports, and
he could not have chosen a more celebrated hunting ex
shooting country in which to take up his reeidence. It
is said at Cirencester that Hatherop Castle, spacious as,
it is now, is to be considerably enlarged, and 'that his
Highness intends to maintain a large establisianent.
, A ROYAL FUNERAL.— The Bing of Benin is justdeacl,
and his son proposes to inter him with unusual splendour.
, When a king dies here, a great grave isdug in the court-
yard, or some-where, near the royal wig wain. It must
be hollowed so. deep that the diggers are drowned by the
water which bursts it upon them, and there they lie,
after' concluding their work. Into this great hole the
'fiadoors lower the royal corpse, robed in all itg barbarid
finery, with lance, sword, 'row, and arrows. With the
dead king are immolated all his favourites and servants;
who are supposed to follow him to the other world; and
aerie him there; their presence being deemed necessary
/to complete his everlasting happiness. So far froM re-
garding this,practico as a Cruelty or even a necessary
-evil, the victims are said to be proud of the listinction,
and the Most violent disputes arise as.te who shall 'htve
the honour of entombment. When the .last man. has
descended into the grave, an immense 'stone is placed
over it. A few days later,- it is removed. One of the
great dignitar es of the state goes' to 'the mouth of the
-chasm, and asks in a loud voice; Who has gone to serve
the king?' The poor Wretches belOw, who arc eXpiring
by inches, reply according to the circumstances. Each
succeeding 'day the saute ceremony is gone through', and
the same question.askedrtill-all.inthat fearful pit have
joined the king, to serve him in the other world—dead
of' hunger or the-noxious miasma:of the vault IV-heil
no voice responds to the inquiry of the fradoor the great
slab is securely fastened, a huge fire is made upon it to
roast the flesh of an elephant, which is distributed among
the multitude•whe.throng to the festival. On the first
anniversary of the death of their king, these wretches,
in honour of 'Their late sovereign and "his' top faithful
followers, make dreadful sacritice of men and animals.
Never less than five hundred human beings are
slaughtered, and frequently thousands are massacred to
form a hecatomb to the; manes of their dead monarch.
The majority of those sacrificed are malefactors, or slaves
taken in war. If a sufficient number of either are not
forthcoming, the king sends his fair viragoes' into the
streets by night to decoy or seize men till the complement
is made up.—Livingstone's Negro Prince.
POLITICAL DUELS IN BERLIN.—The Yolks Zeitung
of Berlin, states that quarrels for political motives are
becoming frequent in that city. On Saturday last not
fewer than three duels took place there, between three
artillery 'officer's on one side, and as many students on
the other. The immediate cause of' those meetiegs was
a discussion relative to the late votes of-the Chambers.
Two of the officers were badly wounded, and the hurt el
.one of them, from a ball in the stomach, is considered
.mortal. One of the students was hit in the right arm.

articles.text:
DIBTRI- S-S
IN THE COTTON
DIAS IRICTS.

(From the Times Correspondent.)

ASIJTON-ITNDER-LYNE, Oct 20.
There is no Point in whi, h greater progress has been
made since my last visit here than in the matt r of
sewing claa-es, and, in comparison, with its population,
Aehten per, saps is as -well provided with these excellent
Lettitutions as any town in the district. There are
eleven of them in the town now, accommodating some
1,200 young women, and subsidised in turn by both
committees. Outside the town, but within the manor,
the Manorial Committee has also made grants' to four
small schools, and others aie likely to be established' in
small districts, which have hitherto been without the
fostering care of a relief committee. No feature in the
work of relief more deserves encouragement and sup-
pert, or promises to effect more lasting good than this.
i High wages and certain employment have attracted to
all these hives of minufactui ing industry numbers
of young worn; who live here without any natural
protectors, and it is needless to dwell on the
value in such a season of a mode of relief which not
only affords them the means of subsistence, but-
sa‘ es.them from numberless dangers and temptations,
' gives them instruction which will be useful to them
hereafter, and brings 'them within the reach of new
influences which may have the most beneficial effect on
their characters. Already, I ara told, a marked, change
is visible among them. Their somewhat roughand in-
, dependent manners are- softening down; they submit
more readily to control,. they appear to be anuiring
, habits of order mid neatness, and there is evidently
among them a warm appreciation of the interest taken in
their welfare. As a rule they are attentive and eager to
learn, and some have made such rapid progress .as to
astonish their teachers. Suggestions have been made
for giving instruction to the unemployed, women in
matters of domestic economy,, but none of them have yet.
taken a practical form. If &sensible scheme could be.
devised for the purpose, it would certainly be of great
service, for on all such points they are wofully igno-
rant. At 13 or 14 a girl he diese parts can swell
the family 'earnings by Bs. or 9s. a week, and
she is, sent therefore into, the mill at the
earliest moment -the law will permit. She has
but little chance of learning anything pf house-
hold duties, and, as a natural consequence, what-
ever domestic management falls to her lot is of the
•most extravagant character. The frying-pan is
almost her sole idea of cookery; when that can
no longer be supplied, she reverts to tea and coffee, till
pay-day comes round again. For every little job the
dressmaker and milliner are called in (many of these
young women when they first joined the classes scarcely
, knew -how to- hold a needle), and her hand-to-mouth
system of buying in all stores
,has made the fortune of
many a little shopkeeper. In justice be. it said that in
the matters of washing, scrubbing, and elbow-grease'
she is generally sound, and most of the cottages about
here are models of cleanliness. Some instruction in the
useful art of making a little go the furthest would be a
1 wiluable additioneto the present scheme but no one yet
seems to see exastly how it can be done. But even
within their present sphere of action, looking to the-
general success of these classes throughout the district,.
it may be said that they have already salved a very
difficult problem, mad that this important class of the
population is now provided for in such a way that
letnre good will be plucked from the present evil. At
the Ashton classes the young women attend five days
in the week for six hours a Say. Their time is divided
between sewing and instruction in reading,. writing,
and arithmetic and they receive from ed. to Bd..
per day according to their age or the necessities of:
each case. This, by the way, is not reckoned in
the general relief given, to the family, but is counted
as a premium for attendance. For the most part
the schools have been established by the, different
congregations of the town, and are under their manage-
ment, the relief committee in some cases finding all the
funds in others supplementing private subscriptions.
In the school managed by the curates of the* parish
church all corners are received without distinction; and
at the Christ Church School also, which is the largest,.
and accommodates now 500 woman. The Independents.
have a large school, where they maintain and occupy
all connected with their own congregation, and at their
own expense, without any grant from the public fund.
There is a weekly collection among the congregation—
said to be a wealthy one—by which the school is sup-
ported and a large amount of relief givenein addition
to needy operatives connected with thern community.
The whole-numberin the town is close upon 1,200, and
the Manorial Relief Committee subsidises four schools
out of the town, whichiprovide for over three hundred
young women. At the Christ Church sahool a warm
meal is provided every day for the 500 young
women, and within the last few thays a cen-
siderable quantity of warm clothing made in
the .sehool has been distributed. Materials, such
as flannel, calico prints,, and so on, are the great want
of all these classes. At the present prices,, to buy them
is more than their-funds will stand, and some have been
obliged, to take contracts for making up' shirts, icc.,
from which they gain no benefit except employment.
If anythmg, donations of materials are- more valued
than cast oft' clothing it. matters little what it. is,, some
use will be made of it by the managers. At one of the
schools-I saw a lot of coarse woollen wrappering, whieh'
had been sent down by. a large • chymical firm in Lon-
don. Its legitimate, fate to ordinary eyes seemed to be
dishclouts but the managers, experienced in all kinds
of shifts, had had it cleaned, and it was being made up
into warm winter petticoats for the girls. Except in. a
few instances of extreme destitution,. the Manorial
Committee has distributed no relief as yet except
through these sewing, classes, but in the course of the
next week its machinery will be organised for taking
charge of those cases which arse not reached by the
guardians or the other committee, more especially in
the few out-districts which are not included in the
borough, and which, have no local agencies of their own.
There is, undoubtedly, an ample field for both commit-
tees, and if their rivalries are only as keen in the work
of relief as they. are in other matters, the people will
indeed be well looked after. At the same time
each will have to act with great caution to avoid
crossing .the other's path and to- prevent imposition.
Among other things I saw in operation on a small
scale at Ashton an experiment which promises in its
-way, if successful, to be almost as valuable as the sewing
classes, if not more so. All who have followed the
course of events here must be aware that one of the chief
difficulties which guardians and others have had, to deal
with has been to provide occupation for the men to keep
them from the streets and the temptations of the ale-
house. The outdoor labour which has been found in the
shape of stone-breaking, street-sweeping, and road-
making will hardly be available much longer, and pre-
parations are being made in various places to assemble
them in schools which shall serve as it were, as an
educational labour test. Oakum picking has been the
employment given to, them here, and very unpopular it ,
Is from its association. with ordinary pauperism, but the
'guardians have just agreed to
,accept in its place an
equal attendance in some school. Two of these- have
been opened within the last week or ten days, one in
connection with the parish church, the other with Christ
'Church. Between: them they have already 50 deserters
from the oakum shed, and I have no doubt they will be
followed by others if they give a good report of their
experience.

desperate war ,with the fair sex, has damned himself to
everlasting fame, and greatly damaged the cause of the
Federals, by carrying his vengeance. towards women to
an extreme quite unprecedented in modern times.
Nothing can .be more unmanly or more 'impolitic than
this fellow's proceedings. .To insult and mortify the
ladies of New Orleans, he lately proclaimed that every
one, male or female, in New Orleans must register an
oath of friendship and fidelity to the United States, and
give in a 'list of his or her property, -which would be
. confiscated by any act or speech prejudicial to the
Federal Government. It was a bitter pill for the poor
ladies to swallow, but they were compelled to re-
cord a white lie or lose all they possessed. But a
forced oath .is not a binding one. The ladies ,of New
Orleans will feel that Butler has taken an advantage of
them to make them. do that which is as null and void in
law and morals as a forced si.,nature to a bill or testa-
ment. If the wretched tyrant flatters, himself that he
has really, gained a triumph for his cause by this brutal
proLeeding; he is miserably mistaken; and it does not
si e4k much for the American national character, that
he is suffered to hold .a post which he has so thoroughly
disgraced

(From the Times (Jemesponderrit)
EXPENSE OF LIVING.
It is not too much to say that the most fanatical he-
liver in the ancient "Union, be he Mr Seward himself,
would despair of the taith that is in him, and acknow-
ledge himself, in Victor Lingo's phrase, the 'somnam-
bulist of a vanished dream,' could he walk the streets of
Richmond this day, and gauge the spfrit and feeling of
its people after nearly nineteen months of such warfare
as the world never contemplated before. The streets
are crowded, the hotels refuse to contain their shoals of
guests; everywhere the quietness and confidence of a
people. secure in its- own strength is incontestably evident.
Everything necessary for life, most things requisite for
its luxurions enjoyment, as it io-interpreted on this Con-
tinent, are to be found in abundance. There is abso-
lutely only one commodity a which the absence is
gravely felt, that commodity being ice. Does the Fede-
ral Government hope by such a frail rudder to steer the
Southern Confederacy back into. the harbour of Union
Of course, with many of the supplies sucked in through
the moat ridiculous of blockades, and transported over
the enormous area which separates Richmond. from the
cities of the Southern seaboard, prices are high. The
board and lodging in the hotels amount to , 4 clop: per
say.; clothing and boots are extremely dear, but are to
be had by pay inc, for them; medical supplies are scarce,
but are constantly being introduced in- not insufficient
quantities across the Potomac and through the cities of
the coast. And here, from personal experience, I may
express my conviction of the utter impossibility of
blckading the Potomac and the Ohio, and shutting off
the South from supplies, along a .frontier which from
Fortress Monroe to. distant Kansas extends for some
1,500 miles. If the whole Federal navy was concen-
trated in the Potomfic,*it would be utterly inadequate
effectually to block the innumerable creeks and reaches
of that river.

articles.title: STATE OF PUBLIC FEELING.
articles.text:
STATE OF PUBLIC FEELING.

. I have travelled far and wide through Virginia; I
have conversed with men, women, striplings, and children
in that State and Maryland; L have seen men, formerly
substantial and thriving, whose everything has been
devoured by the Federals ; but never in one single instance
have I heard a word dregret hy reason of the war, a
timid note sounded in regard to its issue, a sigh breathed
over the departed Union, a gho•t of a desire expressed in
favour of compromise or reconstruction. On the contrary,
one universal chorus echoes through the length and
breadth of the land, 'The net is broken, and we- are
delivered Mr. Everett an& his votaries, who, still
believe in imprisoned loyalty as existing in the South,
might as well search in theßritish islands for a man who
desired them to, be annexed to Trance. So united,, so
homogeneous a community as the States of the Southern
Confederacy finds no parallel in our own annals. No
war that England has waged-for a hundred years has
met with such cordial, unanimous undivided support.
The war against the Freneh, Republic had its Charles
Fox; the war against Russia. its Richard Cobden. There
is no such -character in the Southern States. The
victory of the Federals in, this exasperated struggle
means, not the defeat of the Southern armies,—not the
possession of Richmond, Charleston, Savannah, Mobile„.
and New Orleans, which would no mere lead to a con,.
elusion of the war than the seizure of the Isle of Man.
A. Federal victory means nothing on earth but the ex—
termination and annihilation of-every man, woman, andi
child in the Southern Confederacy. There is no passion,
no frenzy, in the universal language. The intensity of
the hate flushes the cheek and clinches the teeth, but
finds little expression in feeble•words. If anything, the.
exuberance of animosity is more perceptible in the
flashing eyes and eager earnestness of the women; but
dab settled and unconquerable firmness of the men,
requires nothing to be added to it. The possibility of
Richmond's falling in calmly discussed, and preparations
have longtheen made for such a contingency.

NON-EFFECTIVE. BLOCKADE.

The fact remains that the-South, though sorely vexedf
by the bloekade,is penetrated. and reached by vessels
every day and every night, and that, consequently,..
there is nesuch scarcity as the Federal journals have,
loved to- paint. The influence of the blockade is felt in_
enhancedipriees, but even here there is a compensation.
-The South, cut off from external facilities, has, been
taught to,look to' itself for a thousand commodities which,
it once drew from the North, and of which it has now
,no alternative but to improvise however lamely and
inadequately, the inanufacture and production. It makes
but, little difference to a_nation which is receiving little
from. abroad that exchange on Europe should be at a
fabulous•premium. But it is a seriowa.wl momentous
circumstance for the importer,iftew York, and still
more serious for, the consumer whom he supplies, that
exchange on England should rise from.par or 109 to 135
and upwards, when it is considered that such is the
magnitude of. the New York imports that nearly a
millionrand-a-half of dollars are the weekly receipts
from Customs' duties upon them.
GENERAL
.LEE IN MARYLAND.

It appears to have been General Lee's principal de-
signovhen he crossed into.,Maryland, to seize .Harpers
Ferry, and to test the spirit of the Marylanders by his
temperate proclamation, .In order to.be unmolested. in
his attack on Harper's Ferry, he threatened Pennsylva-
nia, from Hagerstown, throwing Giiiernor .Curtis into
hysterics,, and animating Baltimore with the
.hope that
he would emancipate- tier from the iron tyranny .of
General Wool. He had little serious expectation. of
being, able to reach Pennsylvania, but if General Pope
had been continued in command, and Maryland had
.been more free, to act., there can be no doubt that Balti-
more and Washington would- have fallen. But when.
McClellan took tho field, and the army's confidence
again sprang aloft,, General Lee • had no other purpose
on the soil of Maryland than to,.capture Harper's Ferry.
General Jackson, after reaching Hagerstown fell sud-
denly and silently back upon Harper's Ferry, and
enveloped it closely upon every side.
At this • moment the fame- of-McClellan'. early ap-
proach, with the -design of' reinforcing Harper's Ferry,
overtook' General Lee. -He immediately threw General
G. Hill's division of from 12,000 to 15,000, men back to
a strong position, , 4 gutain,. where, on
September 14th, .... ' Itiii"ettecl them with
not less than 70,000. men.. The Southerners fellislowly
back before this imposing. force, but not without inffict-
ing upon it such a loss thati-t was not till September
the 'l7th 'that McClellan. forced on the miinentous.b4tle
of Antietam Creek. The morning, of the 17th found
General Lee strongly posted, but not.. With more than
45,000 men when the battle commenced.

articles.title: AN EPISODE OF THE. WAR,.
articles.text:
AN EPISODE OF THE. WAR,.

We come next to an episode in the war which ie
naturally ignored, by• Mr. Stanton and the Northern
press. It appears that, discovering that his enemy had
retreated across the river, GeneralM'Clellan, on Satur-
day, ;the 20th of September, threw some 3,000, men
across in pursuit. The movement was observed. by
General A. P. Hill, who left a few field-pieces in psi-.
'tion, from which he fired feebly upon the advancing
Northerners, giving orders to his men to retreat hastily
as they approached. The._Federals rushed on the guns,
and followed eagerly after what they imagined, to be a
broken and- paniestritck foe. But when they had got
about a mile and a half General Hill opened upon them
with grape and canister, and the slaughter is described
as having been the most appalling which the war has
witnessed. lum assured that not one-tenth of the in-
vading force escaped-- that the river was literally
choked with the bodies of the dead and dying, who had
rushed into the stream and struggled frantically with
each other to escape the pursuit. It is evident that the
lesson taught on that day -to General M'Clellan has
borne bitter fruit, and that his pursuit will henceforth
be more wary. In fact, there is great reason to sup-
pose thht his next move will be, not against General
Lee at Winchester, but against Richmond by some new
approach. •
PROBABILITY "OF SVC OE SS.

, „
Well may a nation be 'con i
fident of winning it in-
dependence which can exhibit'such 'spectacles as every
day prodtces wherever a Southern army is. in the field.
There, in poverty; hunger, and dirt, shoeless, with shirts
ragged and rent, often without hats, their feet bleeding
as they drag their weary limbs through dust and brier,
are serving in the ranks the gentlemen of the sangre azul
of the South. Many a man who, until the commence-
ment of this war, had scarcely a thought beyond the
Cafe Foy and the Boulevards of Parrs, and to whose
morning toilet every diversity of cosmetic Was as
necessary as water, bas for months been marching under
a musket, without one single change of rainmeut; feed-
ing often on green maize and raw pork, lying at night
on the bare earth, with a single blanket bet Ween him
and the canopy of heaven. Where all are fearless, it
were invidious to select one State in preference to
another as bearing away the palm; but it ,seems
generally conceded that General Butler has converted
the sons of Louisiana mothers, the husbands and brothers
of Louisiana wives and sisters, into demons of more than
earthly ferocity.
And these men, many of them bearing same of Eng-
land's most honoured names, and descended from Eng-
land's best families, are in the field, and have been so
for 19 months, fighting against mereenates who have
repudiated England as though she were governed by a
Nero, and have escaped from German penury and con-
scriptions. Whatever may have been the truth last
winter, it is not pretended now that the Northern armies
are not mainly composed of men of foreign birth
Where are the native Americans of weight and
influence in the Northern ranks? Why does not -Wendell
Phillips take the field ? Men older than he is are serving
by dozens in the Southern ranks. Where is Charles
Summer's musket? The Senate could spare Senator
Baker, in nowise Mr. Sumner's inferior in ihtellect, and
it were a noble answer to the South, which sneers at
non-duellists for want of courage, to show how one of
that class can comport himself upon the perilous edge
of battle:

articles.title: AG.RICUITURAL PB'OSPECTS.
articles.text:
AG.RICUITURAL PB'OSPECTS.

The week opened again very wet, with the wind front
the south-west, and drier in the evening. • Monday was
fair, but threatening,, and there was •:again rain at
night, and somewhat boisterous, still Mowing from the
south-west. Field work on all the light soil would be
proceeded with, and wheat-sowing on such land may be
considered nearly completed, but there is yet a great deal
to do on the heavy clays. The markets for wheat had
braced up a little, and if the condition were to improve
still more the millers would purchase more cheerfully.
Merchant's, too, are now disposed to take some quantity,
as shipping orders on the coast are dropping in from
distant consuming markets, the new freshening up, the
manufactured article, and causing it to be placed rather
more readily. Old foreign is used freely to give strength.
Wednesday proved' a doubtful day, wind north west,
with a white frost at night: The boisterous and wet
weather of the week completely checked the progress of
harvest on the high and late districts of Scotland, and
eats are likely to be secured in pooncondition, aaweil
as the barley still remaining out., The prospects are
thus not cheering for the Scotch farmers, those in, the,
early and southern districts having a poor crop of wheat
both as to quality and quantity, with prices generally
'very slow.

• Thursday, opened with some wet, as is so often the case
aSter a white frost, but it held up during the day, with
the wind round to the north-east and, north-west; while
the night proved wet and unsettled. Farmers watch
every dry day, and take advantage as often as they can
to get in their wheat. Agriculturists are again eneou-
ragedthis -week at the prospect of the barley marketrthe
demand having been well kept up throughout, and choice.
malting qualities have commanded a still further. en,-
hancement. The.proportion of such is, however only small
to the whole, probably being only about one-third,.
the remaining two-thirds consisting of secondary
qualities, which are, however, now more noticed, as,
these have been found to germinate well. They are.
giving satisfaction to the maltsters who have used them ;.
but those requiring the choice -pale malt for the ale.
brewers keep to theprimest sorts, and any white heavy
samples reallised higher figures than were at one time.
expected. The best-foreign descriptions-are command-
ing attention, but as yet they have arrived in limited.
quantities, the Snide being most in repute for pale ale.
The heavy Danish will serve for brown malt, whilst the
French will suit for general malting purposes. For a
few weeks more, at least, the demand may be expected.
to continue goad, until most maltsters have got a supply
to carry them on for a short time longer. The Yorkshire
and Scotch qualities are-coming into notice, as these are
growing kindly.
The week closed with thick, heavy weather, with the
wind from the north-east; barometer 30 inehes.—Nov 1.

BONDED ACCOMMODATION FOR SALT' IN CALCUTTA.--•
, Mr. Falk, of.the Liverpool Salt Chamber of Commerce,
had an interview on this subject with the council of the
Liverpool Chamber of Commerce. His object was to ,
induce the Liverpool Chamber to assist the Salt Chamber
in an endeavour to induce the government not per-
manently to • withdraw the bonded accommodation for
salt in Calcutta, as such a measure was very likely to
interfere seriously with, if not altogether to step, the salt
trade between Lieerpool and Australia, a very important
branch of commerce:. Mr. Falk stated that the bonded
accommodation in Calcutta. had bean withdrawn to suit
the wishes and convenience of the government agents
there, but that the system was highly initnious to the
general trade. He also stated that Mr. Tollemache, M.P.,
had been written to.on the subject, and that a com-
munication had also, been sent by the Liverpool Salt
Chamber.to the government.,

articles.title: LATER FROM ANXIVICA.
articles.text:
LATER FROM ANXIVICA.

• NETT YORK, Oct 24, Dvening.—Reconaaaissances
,
from General M'Ciellan's army continue to be made
but no general advance has taken place. General Burn-
side has been assigned to the ‘command of the defences
at Harper's Ferry: The Confederates are massed in the
Shenandoah Vadley. General Buell has relinquished
the pursuit of General Bragg, who has passed througb.
Curaberland Gap into East Tennessee. The Con-
federates carried immtnse trains of provisions out of
Kentucky. The S:.,nahern journals 'declare • that
Bragg's invasion of Kentucky was a failure and the
Northern newspapers denounce General Buell for not
having prevented General Bragg's escape from that
State. The Southern papers affirm that the reported
capture of large numbers of Confederate prisoners is
untrue. Large meetings have been held at Brooklyn.,
endorsing Pre•ident Lincoln's proclamation and de-
nouncing the Union as it was. According to intelligence
received here from New Granada, Mosquera had firmly.
'established his Gorernment throughout the country.
The Conservatives had been defeated with heavy loss in
a decisive battle. -
OCT. 25, Morning.—General Buell has been removed
from the command in Kentucky, and replaced by
'General Roseeranz. The Southern journals state that
the Federals have evacuated Corinth and Bolivar,
Mississippi. There has been organised resistance to the
'draught among the Pennsylvanian miners, but affairs
have now been adjusted. The returns of the elections
continue to show considerable Democratic gains through-
'Out the country. The New York Herald says that
-another convention of Governors wfil meet to con-
sider the removal of General M'Clellan' and urge
the enforcement of the Confiscation, .4.et. It is
reported that the Federals have captured an island
in Galveston Bay. Nashville is entirely cut .off
from communication with the North. 'Confederate forces,
numbering 1,000, crossed the Cumberland River, and
encamped seven miles north of Nashville, but were
driven back across the river bythe Federals. Semi-
offieial despatcheslrona Washington say that the Federal
Government would give nlf:a dollars for the
capture of the Confederate steamer Alabama, or 300,000
dols. for her 'destruction. The New York Tribune says—
Itr is believed in Washington that if the circumstances,
ofthe sinking of the steamer Blanche, in SPanish waters,
by the Fel era steamer Montgomery, are as stated, the
Federal Government will repudiate the action of the
captain of the Montgomery.'
EvEN'tNor.—At a Democratic' meeting held in
Brooklyn resolutions were passed pledging Democracy
torestore the Union as it was and. to maintain the Con-
stitution as it is, denouncing arbitrary arrests and inter-
ference with the freedom of the press. President
Lincoln's emancipation proclamation was declared un-
wise in policy and,bad in prinaiple, securing an united
South, but making' a disunited North. The name of
the Governor of Massachusetts was hissed by the
meeting. Mr. Horatio Seymour declared that Democratie-
relationsnips to the Government had changed within
the last few weeks, and thatDemocracynow.commanded
the situation. Thirty Federal machine workers at
Portsmouth, Virginia, have gone over to the Con-
federates. The superintendent of a plantation near New
'Orleans has been killed by negroes. It was rumoured
that the negroes afterwards revolted, and that the
military were called out The disturbance was quelled
after several were killed. The British steamer Rinaldo
arrived at New Orleans on the Bth. Semi-official
Washington dispatches. say that the • Mexicans were
making great efforts to resist the French invasion.

GUY FAUX DEHONSTI?ATIONS.

November the sth, the anniversary of that awful con-
spiracy which was to have blown Parliament and the
Constitution into the air, was commemorated in
that peculiar style which has of late years become
familiar to Londoners, and probably to the inhabitants
.of most provincial towns. On all such occasions the
Pope has naturally enough been the hero, although
there have been times, when, on account of strong
,political feeling, other persons have shared his glory.
'His Holiness divided the honours with Garibaldi, and
in many parts of the metropolis their respective
admirers indulged in pitched battles advocating the
,clainis of their friends. The Pope, when he was made
.a, 'Guy' by the Garibaldians, - was knocked to
pieces in many places by his Holiness's admirers,
who were disgusted at seeing him placed in so ignoble
a position, but wherever the Garibaldians proved the
stronger party, Pius the 9th - (in Some cases Cardinal
Wiseman) was paraded through the streets, and even-
tually condemned Ito flames. •Garibaldi was exhibited
in all sorts of costumes. The American question was
fully represented by the :Guys, and it would be difficult
to say whether Abraham Lincoln or Jefferson Davis was
the more caricatured. Both were surrounded by the
eniblems which are supposed t 6 be associated with their
respective States, and both were made as hideous as
their epponents could well render them. The dethroned
Ring of Greece came in for some notice; 'but as the
circumstances of his deposition have not yet become
very familiar to the class ,ofpersons who find amusement
in parading guys, no particular historical importance
attached to the few scattered representations of Klng
Otho. Minor guys of all sorts and sizes were.exhibited
in the streets; but as the morning was rainy and dull,
their merits were not as,
appreciated.

EXAMINATION OF THE PRISONERS.

On Wednesday the prisoners charged with being im-
plicated in the great forgeries on the Bank of England
were placed. at the bar, of the Mansion House, before the
Lord Mayor.
The prisoners arrested, and who have at various times
.during .the last few days have been placed atthe bar, are
George Buncher, butcher, of -Strutton Ground, West-
minster ; RobereCummings (a returned convict), electro
plater, having no fixed residence.; William and Ellen
Burnett, or Brook-street, Kennington-lane; and Richard
Brower, a mould maker, who bas been in the employ-
=ant of Messrs. Portal, of Laverstoke, Hampshire, from
whom a large quantity of Bank paper was stolen..
Another is John Griffiths, of 2, Brown's-buildings,
Winsor-street, Birmingham, who, hifying been examined
by the magistrates at Birmingham, was sent to London
to be Rxammed.

_
- Mr. Freshfield, solicitor to the Bank., who prosecuted,
said his Lordship would remember that on the last occa-
sion Burnett stated that the-female prisoner had taken
Part in the transaction' but that that was not a criminal
Part. The police had made inquiries, and had ascer-
tained that what she had done was done under the in-
fluence of her husband, or of the man whom she lived
with- Under those circumstances he thought she might
be discharged.
The Lord Mayor said he entirely concurred in the
suggestion, dnd Ellen Burnett left the-dock.
r
• Freshfield then proceeded to explain the
nature of the charges against the prisoners. He
said he had asked for remands from time to time,
because there was one of the leaders of the party
who was then at Birrain' ghara, and be was arlious
that all the offenders should be placed together at
the bar. There had been constant forgery of bank
notes, but up to July last it was of very little import.. 'W.
In that month, however, a robbery of hank paper took
place from Messrs. Portal
the contractors, when the
amount of forged notes coining in increased. Griffiths
was apprehended on Tuesday last at Birmingham,
actually engaged in printing bank notes from plates
which were around him: TT at once admitted that he
was guilty, and told the pc, e that he would tell them
all about it. He admitted ti ,-. he had. printed on common
paper, and in his possession was found some rupee
paper, which had been made by the Messrs. Portal for
the Russian government. It might Le mentioned that
all the notes had been manufactured from the same
plates, which was important, as showing the unity of
action between the various parties, although Griffiths
was undoubtedly the principal party. All the others
however, had aided or abetted in-the forgery.

articles.text:
GREECE;

The Hellenic Legation in Paris 13.9 s received letters
from the Previsional -Government which onfirm Gene-
ral Kalergis and all the other members in their respec-
tive functions.

Colonel Papadiamantopoulos, who is the mainspring
of the movement at At ens, has been named military
commandant of the Greek capi4l. Fringkatas 'has
been appo:nted Governor of th ; Palate, where every-
thing has been put under seal, in tt.e presence of Thiron
de Wendland, privitte secretary to King Otho, and who
signed the proces verbal drawn up on the occasion. The
Queen's jewels and a great number of valuable articles
were delivered to the Bardness de Plascow, Grand Mis-
tress of the Court, who, on departing, was accompanied
by an attache of the English Emb .ssy, by whom she
was conveyed to that Embassy in one of the Court car-
riages without any escort, through the crowd, which,
as stated, merely uttered some sarcasms against the
lady. The first measure of the Provisional Govern-
ment was to set all political prisoners at liberty.
The impression produced by the last letters from
Athens is that a certain division has begun to manifest
itself between the Canaria element, which is under
Russian tendencies, and that of Bulgaris, which has
French ones. Canaris had declined to form part of the
Provisional Government, and he appears to held apart
from Bulgaris. The oi her member designated to form
part of the Government (M. Roufos) was still at Patras,
and M. Bulgaris exercised a kind of dictatorship, very
mild, certainly, and willingly accepted in the capital.
Nothing certain was known at the ci4arture of the
packet of the state of the north-west provinces of Etolia
and Acarnania, where it is thought the revolution had
assumed a bolder character. Old. Grivas, a kind of
adventurous Garibaldi, had placed himself at the t ead of the
movement there. With him were his son and the revo-
lutionists in the affair of Nauplia,—men who felt no
great sympathy with those ruling at Athens. The Pro-
visional Government may, therefore, meet with some
difficulties in. that quarter.
A letter from Athens has the following particulars:—
All the foreign Ministers, and among them was the
representative of Bavaria, repaired on board the. King's
frigate to inform the King of the real state of things.
After having made them wait about half-an-hour, King
Otho at last consented to receive them. He was much
astonished to hear that he Must leave, and that he could
not preserve any hope. The King argued at length
against such an assertion, saying that the people were
for him and loved him, and that the army alone was
hostile to him. The Bavarian Minister then thought it
his duty to: speak, and expressed himself in such a
positive manner that the King could not entertain the
slightesthope. Turning, however, towards M. Mamiani,
Minister of Italy, he asked that diplomatist if this
revolution, so unexpected by him., would have happened,
had it not been for the excursion which he had made.
necisely the same thing would have occurred,' 'replied
M. Mamiani, 'only a little blood would have, perhaps,
been shed.' Otho ended by saying that he would reflect
as to whether he should stay or leave. During this _rather
warla discussion the Queen was much moved. The
Provisional Government sent an. officer named Saclour
Co Captain Palaska, of the Amelie, talline• on him to
give up the frigate, and to persuade the King to embark
on board a foreign vessel, but on Pala,ka refusing to
recognise the orders of a new Government, the officer
was obliged to return to give an account of Ihe failure
of his mission. The officer had hardly left the vessel
when the crew manifested feelings hostile" to their own
commander. The Government then gave the King four
hours to leave, and recommended him to embark on
board the English war steamer Scylla, which was an-
chored alongside the Greek vessel, as at the expiration
.of that period it would no longer answer for his life or
that of the Queen. That announcement at length de-
termined the King to leave, and the Amelie placed her-
self under the'orders of the Government. The departure
:of the King tranquillised the people, who were very
greatly exasperated, and had assembled on the shore
raising hostile cries. Atone o'clock, on the appearance
-of a supplement to the official journal announcing the
-departure of the King, the agitation all at one ceased.
Syra immediately sent its adhesion by telegraph as well
,Colchio, Nauplfa, Calavrita., and other towns.
The following is the first proclamation of the Provi-
sional Government of Greece, issued before that already'
known as having been issued at Athens :
Patras, the .Night of the 20th of October.
In virtue of the powers -confided by the people and
the army, and in consequence of the revolution which,
has taken place this night, as well as from the suspen-
sion of the civil authorities, the undersigned take charge
of the Provisional Government of this town and pro-
vince. Citizens Let us congratulate ourselves on this
salutary change, in which all the nation shares! Let
us consider it our first duty to watch over the safety of
citizens and public order. We invoke your patriotic
assistance in order to be -able to attain the more
general object—that is, until the nation shall have
decided in a National Assembly upon her future destinies.
Citizens! without order and tranquility we can do nothing
well, nor obtain our desired object. We are convinced
that you partake those feelings, and do not, consequently,
doubt but that you will contribute with zeal to maintain
real public. order, by which alonethe Greek nation, which
has been so long oppressed, rose unnyimously to reoon-
quer her rights until now trodden under foot. Long
live the country! Long live the nation!'
A despatch from Munich, .dated the 3rd inst.. an-
nounces that on that day a great family council was to
be held at the King's Palace. The council was to
decide whether it would be advisable for King Otho to
abdicate in favour of his brother Luitpold. Prince
Adalbert, the youngest brother, had postponed his de-
parture to Darmstadt to be presentat this council.

articles.title: PRINCE OF WALES AT MALTA.
articles.text:
THE PRINCE OF WALES AT MALTA.

VALETTA, Oct. 31.—The Prime ,of. Wales, who is
accompanying his sister' the Princess of Prussia, and
her Royal husband, the Crown Prince of Prussia, on a
Mediterranean tour, unexpectedly arrived here early
yesterday morning from Tunis on board the Royal yacht
Osborne, escorted by her Majesty's frigate Doris. The
Royal party arrived at Palermo from Marseilles, landed,
and went up to Mont R,eale. Haoring asked Sir F. L.
.M`Clintock to accompany them to Tunis, the Doris
.escorted the Osborne to that plF,e, where their Royal
Highnesses were ;buy well received by the Bey, and
.after visiting the ruins of Carthage, started for Malta
to replenish the yacht's fuel. When 175 miles to the
westward of the island the port paddle shaft gave way.
The Doris then took the yacht in tow, shortly after
which her Majesty's Ship Edgar, bearing the flag of
Rear-Admiral Dacres„ C. 8., was sighted and com-
municated an offer of assistance, which, however, was
declined. The Osborne has been taken in hand by the
dockyard for the removal of the disabled paddle, so as
to allow one wheel to work without the other., and it is
intended she shall leave• to-morrow afternoon or early
on Sunday morning for Sicily and Naples, escorted, as
before, by the Doris.
. _ _ _

On iuilval at Malta, the Governor, Sir Gaspard Le
Marchant, and his. secretary., Captain Brett. Admiral
Codringtcn and his secretary, Mr. 141unday, and the
Prussian donsul, Mr. Ferro, waited upon their Royal
Highnesses on board the yacht, and were most cour-
teously received; but, as their Royal Highnesses are
travelling incognito, the firing of salutes and other
public manifestations of respect were disper.sed with.
Soon afterwards the Royal party landed, and took up
their residence at the Palace, which his Excellency has
given up for their accommodation. Yesterday their
Royal Highnesses held a reception at the Palace, and
will hold another this evening. This afternoon they
attended a review of the troops in garrison on the Flo-
riana parade ground. The Prince of Wales and the
Prince of Prussia appeared in uniform, attended by the
officers of their respective suites. The Princess of
Prussia, who was looking remarkably well, and has, I
am informed, quite recovered her h:alth, proceeded to
the ground in Lady Le Marcbant's carriage.
The Prince of Wales appears to be in robust health,
and has wonderfully improved in general appearance
sinee his last visit, only a few months ago. His Royal
highness is accompanied by Lieatenant - General
Rnollys, Governor of his Royal Highness's household,
and Colonel Keppel, Equerry.

BRUTAL ACT.—A brutally wicked act was committed
by a Young man at Hull last week. A woman, it
appears, met him at night, and asked him to 'treat her.'
He gave her a bottle containing rum, as he said, but
which turned out to be laudanum, and shortly after
drinking some of it, she became seriously ill. On Friday
her life was still despaired of.
