articles.title: TIIE O'CONNELL STATUE IN .DUBLIN.
articles.text:
TIIE O'CONNELL STATUE IN
.DUBLIN.

The following letter has been addressed to the editor
of the Times.:—

Sir,—Your Dublin correspondent, no doubt misled by
the statements of journalists in the interest of a party
that would repeal ttie Emancipation Act, asserts that the
organisation to erect a suitable statue to O'Connell in
the Irish metropolis was conceived and has been 'pro-
moted in rivalry to the memorial to the lamented Prince
Consort. ilav,ng used my name in coma, ction with this
inaccurate version of the facts, I respectfully claim the
privilege of formally, and with as much emphasis as is
consistent w.th courtesy; contradicting the mi.represen-
tations of these so-calli d'Pro i estants,' whore opinions
-are so ingeniously introduced by your correspon.:ent to
procure for them the world-wide circulation of your
columns. The most active supporters of the movt ment
for erecting a statue to the Advocate of Civil and
Religious Liberty' are also the most active supporters
of the memorialoto t. e illustrious Prince, whose loss the
nation deplores, whose virtues, the Irish memor al
will worthily connueinorate. The Lord Mayor, the Lord
Chancellor, Mr. Justice Fitzgerald, the Pr sident of the
Lollege of Physicisns, and many others of the earliest
and most distinguished subscribers to the Prince Consort
Fund, were also among the first and most generous sub-
scribers to he O'Connell statue and to the Lancashire
Distress funds. I may be ptrniittod to add—as the
crime of originating a rivdhy ' to the generous effort
to commemorate the public sympathy for our bereaved
and son owing Queen is as factiously as it is I alsely
attributed to me by name—that my humble name is to
be found among the first subscribers to the Prince
Consort and to the Lancashire funds, and that I have
ever given to both committees my most sincere co opera-
tion. That I have taken an active, part in promoting
the manifestation of the gratitude of this nation to
O'Connell for his great services as the emaucipator of the
Catholic people of these nalms is most :true. That I
will continue to do so, no matter how my conduct may
be misrepresented, is 'also true; and I trust, that, as
your columns have been used to give currency to one of
the calumnies that have been invented by those who
seek to pet petuate strife between the two leading classes
of her Majesty's subjects in Ireland, you will allow me
to assure your readers that as 'loyalty to the Throne,'
obeiienoe to the laws,' and equal rights for all,' were
the leading principles of O'Connell's great career, those
who are most forward to perpetuate the memory of the'
greatest of Irishmen are among the most willing to
record in enduring marble' this nation's sympathy with
the Sovereign in her present deep affliction.
I am, Sir, your obedieut servant,
JOHN GRAY.
Freeman's Journri-office, Dublin, Nov. 4.

articles.title: YELVERTOY IistABBIAGE CASE.
articles.text:
THE YELVERTOY IistABBIAGE CASE.

• The judgment of Lord Ardmillanin.the Outer House
.of the Court of Session has been carried for review
before the Judges of the First Division of the Inner
House. The debate on the reclaiming petition or
appeal was opened on Monday by Mr. E. P. Maitland.,
Suiiciter-General of .Scotland, who stated that the
grounds of action on which the pursuer relied were
three „in number:—First, the interchange of mutual
consent between the parties, as .evidenced by verbal
acknowledgments, by correspondence, and by circum-
stances; second, marriage constituted by promise and
subsequent intercourse; and, third, the Irish cere-
mony. With the third ground he had almost nothing
to say in the present debate for this, court must, of
course, accept as evidence the opinions received from
the Irish consistorial lawyers, which were unfavour-
able to the pursuer; but it was necessary to keep the
point open lest the case should go to the House of
Lords, where the legal opinions would cease to be
evidence' and the House, being a court of law for the
United Kingdom, would look into that matter for
themselves. He maintained that Lord Ardmillan, in
his judgment, had decided several points against the
pursuer on which her case had never been rested, as,
for instance, the constitution of marriage by the inter-
change ofeonsent per verba de presenti, by cohabitation,
or by habit and repute, which were all grounds of ac-
• tion. which had been expressly repudiated. The So-
lieitor-General, in a lengthened speech, vindicated the
pursuer from the strong observations reflecting on her
character :which the Lord Ordinary had made' and
maintained that his Lordship's note was founded on a
series of misconstructions of the correspondence and
,evidence. The debate will probably occupy the Court
for the whole week, and a judgment is expected at an
<early period of the winter session.

Gastronomists,' -says tGalignani, will be -glad to hear
that truffles are unusually abundant this year. In the
market at, Perigueux, a few days back,. they were sold
at the unusually low price of 2fr. a pound. Speaking
of this aristocraticseasoning, it reminds one of the Brillat-
Savarin's maxim on the subject, altogether too selfish
for general taste :—To enjoy a truffied turkey the com-
pany should not exceed two—the turkey and yourself.%
DISASTERS AT SEA. —A letter from Hamburg of the
28th ult. says :---‘ The equinoctial gales have caused
great disasters in the German Ocean. More than a hun-
dred vessels have been wrecked, and in some cases the
crews were lost. A single steamer, on its way to Hull,
which was forced to put in here by stress of weathek,
saw no less than six vessels founder without being able
to render them the slightest assistance.'
THE DEAF AND DUMB.—At the last sitting of the
Academy of Sciences a paper 'gas presented by Dr.
Boudin, in which, after expressing his belief that sur-
domutism may henceforth be considered as one of the
probable consequences of marriages between near rela-
tives, he decidedly opposes the view adopted by some,
who consider the mfirmity in question to be hereditary.
The parents of deaf and dumb children, be observes are
generally in perfect health, and moreover deaf and dumb
parents not connected with each other by ties of con-
sanguinity very rarely get deaf and dumb children. He
then quotes an observation made by Dr. Perron, of Be-
sancon, of two brothers of the name of Vallet, splen •
idly constituted and enjoying the most perfect health,
who married two sisters, their cousins-german. The
eldest has had several children, only one of whom, now
aged 20, is deaf and dumb. The younger brother has
had six children, the first, third, and fifth of whom
could hear and speak, while the second and fourth were
deaf and dumb; the sixth, still in its cradle, does not
seem sensible of any noise they may happen to make in
the room. These cases are utterly in contradiction
with the doctrine of inheritance,

AN lINFLEASANT POSITION.—During the late hurri-
cane on the coast of Brittany the keeper of the light-
house at Blainville, opposite Coutances' was.deprived of
all, communication with the mainland for six days, and
was in the greatest want of provisions. When it was
at length possible to send him relief, he, his wife, and
maidservant were completely exhausted. Their pro-
visions had been c'onsumed, and they were existing on
rainwater collected in towels. The servant, a young
person only 16 years of age, suffered more than the
others, as well from hunger as from the apprehension of
being starved to death.
A Fox AMONG TIIIIKEYS.—A few day's ago a flock
of turkeys, 77 in number, b3longing to Mr. Bandy)
farmer, of Clapham, took their usual ramble over his
grounds, but not returning at the accustomed hour, one
of the labourers was sent in search of them. From
some unexplainable cause the turkeys refused to be
driven home; about twenty were carried in, the
remainder being left behind. On the following morning
Mr. Bandy discovered that a rapacious fox had been
busy with his turkeys; no less than 17 were found dead
and bloody in the field, showing the marks of Master
Reynard's teeth; several others were missing, making
the total loss 22. The dead fowls wore lying from 20 to
30 chains apart, some of them being found on the
adjoining farm of Mr. Gostling.—Bedford Times.
A correspondent of the Z eeman states that a threat-
ening notice Was posted on Saturday morning on the
gate of the Roman Catholic chapel at Doon, threatening
any one who would take the lands of Tormaline, belong-
ing to Mr. Laurence Marshall, J.P., from which it
would appear two tenants, named Hayes and Franklin,
were, some years ago, evicted. It is telieved that Mr.
Marshall is about to relet the farms, and it is with the
view of intimidating any one from taking them, in the
hope that the former tenants would be reinstated, that
the notice as posted.

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENCE. MR. WEITYSS JOBSON IN THE (WEEN'S BENCH.
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENCE.
MR. WEITYSS JOBSON IN THE (WEEN'S
BENCH.

Mr. Jobson applied .on the 4th Novembrr for a man-
damus against Mr. Arnold, and also Mr. Alderman
Carter, to compel them to hear his charge of perjury
against Mr. Disraeli, and decide thereon. He commenced
his rambling statement by observing that he applied
to their lordships to redress a wrong that had scarce y a
parallel. He said he was a citizen of America by
residence and adoption, and a native of the north of
England. He came to this country in 1859 to recover
property wrongfully- withheld from him that had been in
his family for centuries. Mr. Jobson then referred to
the proceedings taken against him by Sir James Fergus-
son, M.P., with whom he claimed relationship, and to Mr.
Disraeli's evidence in that case, upon which he four,ded
his alleged perjury. He proceeded to state that he was con-
victed by a jury packed for that purpose and by a judge
primed to condemn him. He next proceeded to inveigh
against the manner in which he was seated in prison,
and his being kept picking oakum and mending filthy
blankets. He denied that he had ever wr.tten Mr.
Disraeli a threatening letter, but he had written him com-
plimentary ones, for he had respect for his abilities though
he dissented from his p ditics. (Laughter.) Mr. Disraeli
had said that he solicited him to bring li;s case before
Parliament, and certainly he (applicant) thought he stood
on such good terms with the right hon. g• ntleman for
cutting up Lord Palmerst in; that he would have cone
it at once—(laughter) —and not have made it a harge
against him. (Laughter.) He never wrote the right
hon. gentleman anything that could be construed
into a threatening letter, but since his discharge from
prison he had written him a hostile letter, stating that
as he had prevented his case from being investigated he
would post the right honourable gentleman as a per-
jurer fill& one end of the kingdom to the other.
(Laughter.) Mr. Jobson, however, in reply to a ques-
tion by the Lord Chief Justice, admitted that Mr.
Alderman Carter had taken the documents from him to
read them, but declined to act next day, and his lord-
ship, after patiently listening to the applicant, sa d he
had not made but a case for the interference of the
Coi:rt. His case had evidently, on his own showing,
been investigated by Mr. Alderman Carter. Applicant
then asked the Court to allow him to proceed against
the gentleman at the Central Criminal Court, but they
declined to do so.

articles.title: GARIB2LLDP S HEALTH.
articles.text:
GARIB2LLDP S HEALTH.

The French medical journal, the Gazette des Hospitaux
publishes a long letter from the eminent French surgeon,
Professor Nelaton, containing a technical account of his
visit to Garibaldi. In describing the probing of the
wound, he says that the stylet penetrated the wound very
easily without causing the least pain. Piercing it trans-
versely, at 2f eentimetreshe was stopped by a hard body,
giving, on being struck, a dull noise, very different from
the sharp sound which results from contact with the
bone. 1. his, he has no doubt whatever, was the ball.
The general state of the patient is as favourable as
possible, when it is remembered that for 30 days he wagt
without sleep. There is no fever, the skin is fresh,
.s the appetite good. The sleep is uffident and resto-
rative. The countenance is calm, dignified, with-
out any expression of suffering.' An immediate
extraction of the ball would, he thinks, be inju-
rious. The proceeding most simple and devoid of
danger consists in dilating gradually the canal of thp
wound up to the point where the foreign body is present.
This .dilatation is to be effected by the introduction of
little cylinders of gentian roots of increasing size, for
which may be substituted in a few days a fragment of
prepared sponge. The probabilities are that the ball
can then be seen and touched and seized by the forceps.
With regard to the proposition of an amputation, Pro-
fessor Nelaton says, 'I do not admit this extreme
resource, except in the case contrary to all probability,
of some grave complication arising, such as a deep
abscess, abundant and inexhaustible suppuration, evident
deterioration of the constitution, in a word—a danger
of death. One word more. In my opinion the
general will recover, but his recovery will require
some months yet, and will leave a rigidity in the joint
of the foot, the inevitable ,consequence of an injury
which has affected the osseous joint surfaces. But this
demi-anatilosis will but slightly impede the function of
that member.'

articles.title: LYDIA.
articles.text:
LYDIA.

The Times of India in its overland summary, dated
Bombay, Oct. 11, says:—
Although an armistice had taken, place the ruler of
Herat, animated by the assurances-of help from the Shah,
has rejected overtures of peace on the part of the Bost.
In addition to 1.0,000 Persians with 60 guns encamped
at Meshed, a large force had been dispatched by the
Shah to Herat, which still continued invested. The
reports of native news,writers state that cholera was
decimating alike Affgh2ns and Heratees. At Peshawur,
the same visitation had attacked the troops.
The social aspect of the Himalayas is still surcharged
with heavy clouds. Scandal reigns at Simla. Additional
revelations as to the lateganabling transactions at that
-station have transpired. Sir Hugh Rose has taken
resolute action in the matter. Colonel Christie, whose
losses have amounted to £25,000, has been deprived of
the .brigade command at Delhi. The commander-in-chief
has also remanded some members of his personal staff
to their corps on account of their participation in high
play.' _

- A new sensation' has been imparted to the military
world of India by the expulsion of Col. Priestley from
i the United Service Club at Calcutta. So strong s the
pronunciamento against Sir Hugh Rose that the com-
mittee a the United Service Club have ever. determined.,
it is said, to request his excellency to resign the position
he occupies as president of the club, The partizans of
the ,Commander-in-Chief are irritated .at the non-inter-
ference of Lord Elgin in the imbroglio. The Viceroy, it
is rumoured, forwarded to the Commander-in-Chief the
legal opinion of the ,Advocate-General of Bengal, which
did not coincide with that of the Judge Advocate at
Simla' and Lord Elgin did not hesitate to remonstrate
against the policy pm-sued, in Colonel Priestley's case,
by Sir Hugh Rose.
The Viceroy, sick of the deadly climate of .Calcutta,
meditates' it is said, a sojourn at Ootacamund to recruit
his exhausted energies. Sir William Denison will con-
fer with the ,Governor. General, prior to the visit of the
former to Travancore and Cochin. Sir Hope Grant,
after a tour of inspection in"the Mysore country, ceded
districts, Hyderabad, and Kamptoe,-will meet Sir Hugh
Rose at Jubhulpore during the ensuirtg cold season.
The head-quarters' camp of the Commander-in-Chief
in India will move from Agra on the 10th of November
to G walior, thence to Jhansi, from Jhansi to Seepree,
and on to Saugor, Jubbulpore, Nagpore, Rewah, Allaha-
bad, and Lucknow, where his excellency will remain
until about the 9th of January, when he will return to
Agra to meet the Govenaor-General.
_ .

—lt is stated in Calcutta that Government securities to
the amount of about two crores of rupees have been pur-
,ehased on account of Government.

The sum subscribed in Bombay to the Lancashire
Relief Fund up to the present time is two lakhs fifty-
four thousand rupees.
The sale proceeds ,of the Banda and Kirwee prize
booty amounted to forty-two lakhs of rupees. The
amount realised from the sale of the Bhitoor jewels, be-
longing to the notorious Nana, is about four lakhs and
thirty two thousand.
On the 6th October an extension of the Grand
Indian Peninsula Railway, from Chalisgaum to Jul-
gaum, was opened for, public traffic—length of exten-
sion 58 miles.

The Government of Bengal continues to receive
liberal offers for the purchase of large tracts of waste
lands in several districts of Lower and Eastern Bengal.

According to the last advices from the Cape of Good
Hope four of the new French Indo-Chinese mail packets
arrived out there after a thirty-three days' voyage on
their way to India and China.
A CHURCH ON FIRE.—On the 2nd, at the commence-
ment 01 the afternoon service in Eglinton-street U.P.
Church, Glasgow, a cry of fire was raised, which speedily
caused such a commotion among the congregation that
the idea of proceeding with the service was abandoned
by the officiating clergyman. At the time of the first
alarm the minister was engaged in prayer, but he had
immediately to desist, and endeavour to prevent the too
speedy rush to the doors, by giving out a psalm to be
sung during dismission. This, however, proved a failure,
the crowds of people rushing to the doors, while the pre-
centor feebly endeavoured to engage the people in the
worship. Ii was at once seen that to proceed further
would be useless, and at the request of one of the elders
the cl rgyman desired the people to keep themslves com-
posed, and to dismiss quietly. The scene that ensued was
alarming in the extreme—several, leaping over the seats,
endeavoured frantically to secure an egress by the
windows. The West of England and other engines were
on the spot in a short period of time, and the firemen
commenced operations by tearing the rafters from the
building, while a copious supply of water soon had the
effect of extinguishing the flames. The accident is be
• !loved to have arisen from the heating-pipes getting over-
heated, and communicating with the timber in their.
immediate vicinity.—Glasgow Herald.
THE MAYORALTY OP BIRMINOHAM.—OH the 4th, a
private meeting of the Birmingham Town Council was
held to deliberate upon the choice of a gentleman as
mayor for the ensuing year. There was a large attend-
ance of members. Alderman Ryland nominated Mr.
Robert Wright, and Mr. Brinsley seconded the nomina-
tion. A. long discussion ensued, and, although no other
nomination was made, no decision was come to, several
councillors protesting that it was too premature to
decide on supporting any gentleman before the 10th of
November.

• The fever for slavery in England-shows signs of bay-
ing run its course. All has been said that can be said on
the dangers of breaking up a nest of thieves, and the
inroads made thereby on the domestic comforts of the
end ingered, Men have had time to look round, and
wonder how it was, that in the words of the Puritan
colonel who di d at Preston Pans, they have been so
miserably and scandalously befooled,' as to fight the
battle of what their forefather, and everybody but
themselves, have gloried in abhorring. 'I hey began
with ignoring principles. They tried to draw a veil
over the fact, that resistence to slavery is everywhere
the same natural right as resistence to the prairie wolf,
if all other chances are unavailing. They knew that
a great moralist of t,.eir own drank habitually to the
success of the next negro insurrection in the West
Indies;' and to that it would have come had the thing
gone on. The sum of all villanies,' like t..e t stablish-
meats of minor banditti, must have been quashed as
Heaven should enable. Nobody desires unnecessary
suffering; but thenuistnce must be abated. The man who
should say, If highwaymen were overpowered, think
of the cruelties which would be inflicted on th ir wives
and daughters,' would clearly be a trickster, to be
hooted do.n and pursued by whatever might be the
most humane formula of popular coatempt. However
weighty the interest at issue, it does not follow that
justice is to be so perilous to the outlawed. There *are
milder ways of doing the thing. It does not even follow,
that in the hands of good-natured people there shall be
much of m dice or ill-blood on any side, except as it
may arise from the ingrained tu, pitu.de of born and
hereditary felons. All the talk about horrors' and
'reprisals' and ' retaliations ' is the noise of rogues to
frighten fools. Everybody knows such tht eats are only
lip thunder. In particular, they never find their way to
the military on either side. Centuries ago, when Count
Wratislaw was taken prisoner by the Turks, he recounts
that he and his companions were ill-treated by the
civilian Tu- k, but the nflitary said, It is yours to-day
and may be ours to-morrow.' Let well meaning people
sleep in their beds; there will nothing come of all this.
—General T. .Perronet Thompson in Bradford Advertiser,

articles.title: HANCILESTER CITY BANK.
articles.text:
HANCILESTER CITY BANK.

Jonah Andrew, re gistered proprietor and mann ger of
the City Bank of Manchester, which stopped payment
on the 26th ultimo, was brought up on remand at the.
Manchester City police-court, on the 3rd, charged with
applying to his own use £37 16s'. entrusted to the bank
to retire a bill upon the Union Bank, Moorgate-street,
London.
Mr. Richardson, solicitor, appeared ?or the prosecution ;.
Mr. It. B. B. Cobbett defended the prisoner.
Mr. Sam. Lyon, traveller for Mr. Kean, tailor and
draper, King street, Manchester, said, on Tuesday, 21st
Oct., he called at the City Bank. He went there to
advise a bill. He saw Mr. Coulson, the prisoner's
clerk, who gave him a piece of paper to fill up. After
filling it up he handed it to Coulson, and left with it
£37 16s. and 2s. additional. On the Thursday following
he went to the bank again in consequence of a telegram
from London, saying the bill was not advised, and
showed the telegram to the prisoner, who told him he
was the proprietor and manager. He asked him why it
had not been advised in due course. He looked at the
telegram, 'and said, 'Perhaps you are not aware that
Spooner and Attwood have refused to honour my drafts?'
Witness told him the bill was payable at the Union
Bank, and he had nothing to do with Spooner and
Attwood. The prisoner replied, 'Well, there is no
money here, I have paid it all away.' He called a
clerk to prove that such was the case, and witness left
the bank.

William Coulson, a clerk at the bank, said he remem-
bered Mr. Lyon calling and paying the money. He
filled up one of the ordinary advice slips on the ceunter.
Witness handed it to Joseph Wadsworth, the cashier.
Had no instructions that day from the prisoner to send
the remittance to London. All the instruction he had
that evening from ;the prisoner was not to write to
London.

Joseph Wadsworth, the cashier, said he received the
advice slip and money from the last witness. The
money was put in the drawer. All the money in the
drawer was paid away that night except £2O and
country cheques to the amount of £l,OOO. The balance
was paid away next day to various parties except about
£4 and the cheques, and then the bank closed.
Mr. Richardson said he had served notices on the
prisoner and his solicitor to produce the advice note, but
they now declined, and he proposed to give secondary
evidence. He then recalled Mr. Lyon, who said that
the printed form he received was headed Speoner and
Attwood,' and he struck those names out and wrote over
them 'Payable at the Union Bank, Moorgate-street,
London.' He wrote John Williams on it as the drawer,
and his own name as the acceptor. He signed his name
at the bottom, but was not sure of the printed words
before his signature. He thought they were 'retire the
above.'
Mr. Richardson now asked for a further remand till
Thursday., to give time for witnesses to attend from the
Union Bank, in London.
The remand was granted.
_ _ _ _ _ . _ _ • _ . .

Mr. Richardson said he now proposed to go on with a
second case, in which Mr. John Wrigley paid the pri-
soner £l6 4s. with written directions to pay it to Messrs.
Mackey and Co., London.
Tb e magistrates thought this ease ought to stand over
with the other.

PROCLAMATION .OF THE EX-KING 4W GREECE.—The
Gazette de Trieste publishes the following proclamation
of thaex-King Otho to his late subjects Greeks!—
Convinced that after the late events in many parts of
the country, and especially in the capital, the prolonga-
tion of my stay in Greece would precipitate the inhabi-
tants in troubles of a sanguinary nature and difficult to
allay, I have resolved to quit for the moment this coun-
try, which I have always loved and still love, and for
the prosperity of which I have laboured .during nearly
thirty years without shrinking from any trouble or any
effort. Far from all ostentation, I had before my eyes
only the true interests of Greece, for I consecrated all
my cares to promote its moral and material development,
and I endeavoured especially that justice might be ad-
ministered impartially. When, moreover, political
offences were ,committed against my person, I always
practised the greatest clemency, and forgot what was
past. In returning now to the country where I was
born, I am saddened at the thought of the calamities
with which Greece, which is dear4to me, is menaced in
consequence of the late events. I implore the God of
mercy to deign always to be favourable to the destinies
of Greece.—Onto.--Port of Salamis, Oct. 24.'

RIGHT OF FEMALE MEDICAL STUDENTS.—A novel
case has arisen in connection with the University of St.
Andrews, Scotland, with regard to the right of ladies to
matriculate. It appears that on the 29th ult. Miss Eliza-
beth Garrett applied to the university authorities to be
allowed to matriculate, stating her purpose to attend the
courses of lectures given by the professors. No objec-
tion whatever was made by the clerk to the request of
Miss Garrett, who paid the usual fee, signed her name,
and received the customary card on matriculation. The
next day on of the professors gave her a letter to the
secretary authorising him to give her a ticket for his
class; another professor did the same, Miss Garrett
paying the fee and showing. the matriculation card. It
seems, however, that the privilege thus accorded did not
meet with the approval of the Senate of the University,
inasmuch as that body, at a meeting on the Ist instant,
passed a resolution to the effect that the matriculation
and class tickets had been given without sufficient autho-
rity; and further, that a committee should be appointed
to consider the question thus raised, to communicate if
they thought fit with the other universities, and if neces-
sary to take a legal opinion on the subject; and, in the
meantime, that the attendance of the lady on the univer-
sity classes be deferred. Miss Garrett is the same lady
who applied recently to the London University, with a
-view to matriculation, her application being rejected
only by the casting rote of the president. As regards
the University of St. Andrews, it may be reasonably
doubted whether the authorities have power to expel,
after having once granted admission. The point with
respect to the admission of female students to the
medical schools is exciting no small. interest in medical
circles, and the highest legal authority is being invoked
for its settlement.

killed; Mr. Robinson, the late Mayor of Richmond,

bruised and lamed. A cattle train ran into a passenger
train which was standing at the Moulton station. The
morning was very misty.

articles.title: STRANGE CAT.
articles.text:
A STRANGE CAT.

Tho subjoined advertisement, extracted from the
Tinzes, suggests various reflections to the thinking
mind :

'Lost, a Tom Cat, on the night of the 30th ult., from
6, Park Cottages, Park Village East, N.W. Light grey
coat, with black stripes; answers to the name of
"Johnny." Whoever will bring him to the above ad-
dress shall receive Ten Shillings Reward.'
There was, of old, a liquor which, our ancestors said,
would make a cat speak, and a man dumb.' It may, be
doubted whether even that beverage would make a cat
answer to a call. Cats are generally slow at answering
to their names; and it must indeed be an uncommon
Tom that answers to the name of Johnny. Tom and
Johnny in conjunction are equal to John Thomas; and
a light grey coat with black stripes would indicate a cat
less distinctly than a livery-servant. We may add that
the reward of ten shillings for the lost Johnny is liberal.
It shows dear Johnny to be made much of, insomuch
that one Johnny is considered worth ten Bob.

of a lady's letter always peeps out in the Postscript. It
may not generally be known, but there is an insinuating
motive in this. The dear creature, after indulgina in a-

thing she has of truth, or interest, to communicate, may
be taken literally au pied da la lettre. And who can say

not quite light in the end?

PARIS Permanent Universal Exhi-
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success iu stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions. .
The central position of Paris, and the vast number of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establishment there of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhi• ited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admissioa to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is opee, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, with liberty to re-export there
without payment of duties, or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.
The whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
course of construction) will be opened early in the sum-
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has alzeady been taken up.
A dmission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a Gener,sl Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be esta-
blished in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the same nature from different countries,
being placed in juxta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
will be charged, the space being taken for six years.
The first rate (£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
The second rate (£1 per square metre per annum)
'will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.

Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition and at the Offices of Messrs. J.

ROPEMAKERS' Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
BROTHER "WORKING MEN: It is with a feeling of
reluctance that We, the London Operative Ropemakers,
venture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowiag as we do the great depression of trade in
almost every degartment of manufacture, and yet we
feel encouraged to lay our eases before you soliciting
your sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are
well known by the London trades, and to many trades
in the country, for our willingness to assist others in
times of difficulty. We will therefore simply state our
case to you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of
your kind consideration
On the 11th of June last one of our employers offered
a reduction of seveupence per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a
well organised trade society, could not submit to any
reduction of wages, recognising, 63 fair workmen akould
do that a fair day's work is entitled to a fair day's pay,
and having enjoyed the present rate of wages for the
last seven years, and there being no reasonable plea
given why such reduction should take place.
Having sent deputations to the employers to reason
the matter with them and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
left us but to withcb aw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. H. Baker, Bermond-
sey. This is the eighth week of the strike, and our
men are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
justness of their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
sentation to obtain men their shop is sti 1 empty, for
as fast as the men come up from the countr, through
their agents and advertisements in the country local
papers, they (the men) after having the question of
dispute explained to them, leave their work, and by
our assistance leave London again, which creates a
large expense over the actual cost of keeping our own
members on strike. We have expended over £l5O,
large sum for only one firm, but then we are fighting
for the whole trade, for some of the other employers
have already given notice to their men, that as soon
as Messrs. Baker and Brothers get supplied with men
at the reduction that they will give no more for their
work than the Messrs. Baker's, and if we are com-
pelled to submit to this reduction we shall lose
£1,500 per year in wages (then leaving a large suiplus
of men out of work), a sum you will admit worth
st uggling for.
Having thus briefly staled our ;present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
another trades. solicitimt their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and ti acme against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
willing heart and ready heed to assist other trades
placed in similar circnrnstances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, bat
what lie have supported and sustained to our utmost
abiliOA We therefore make this appeal ' with some
:iegrea of confident, that you will readily respond to us
in our present difficulties, and show to the employing
classes- that there is a spirit of union aud brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
workmen.
We beg to remain yours very resoeetfnlly, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee; Richard Bur-
ridge, treasurer; Daniel Smith, secretary.
